title: Advanced Fluid and Particle Mechanics
syllabus_overview:
In this Developing subject, you will be asked to engage in the analysis of complex fluids, which are widely used in modern technologies and industries, particularly in foods, water, printing and coating materials, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and mineral processing. Understanding the fundamental principles of non-Newtonian fluids and particle mechanics in a fluid is crucial in these engineering practices. The subject will equip you with practical knowledge of fluid and particle mechanics in the context of chemical process engineering, where fluid (liquid or gas) interacts with particulate solids. The subject has three parts: it begins by covering rheological concepts of non-Newtonian fluids, such as viscoelasticity, physical properties, and quantities, with an emphasis on the design calculation of the flow. Basic principles of viscometry and analysis of rheological measurements are also introduced. Then, you are invited to investigate how complex fluids are understood within the context of microscopic aspects of surface and interface sciences. This includes surface and interfacial tension, surface chemistry, and their correlation to colloidal stability. The final section will provide coverage of single and multi-particles in fluid, solid-fluid transport, particle aggregation and agglomeration, and particle transport, slurries and fluid flow through a packed bed of particles are discussed in association with relevant case studies and numerical problem-solving methods using computational calculation. Completion of this subject will enable you to describe and model the physical behaviour of fluid-particle systems and perform design calculations and analyses of typical chemical engineering processes involving non-Newtonian fluids or complex fluid-particle systems.

Teaching Strategies:
Class notes will be available on Canvas for students to view in advance of classes. The workshops and tutorials will be offered in a face-to-face format, and students will be encouraged to participate in the classes which are organised for students to ask questions and to foster dialogic learning. Tutorial sessions will cover a summary of the class followed by a solution to the example and practice problems. Consultation sessions with the subject coordinator will be available for additional questions and discussions. Laboratory practicals are designed to provide students with hands-on experience working with a small equipment operation. Students work in a team to learn about its function and operational characteristics to explore the relationship between §the rheology of non-Newtonian, Newtonian and densities of complex fluids, the effect of particles on fluid degradation and surface wear characteristics. The laboratory class will be conducted in the science lab on the UTS main campus. Laboratory demonstrations and reports provide opportunities to increase understanding and enhance knowledge of complex fluids and particles in flow analysis. This is central to the two-part assessment submission, where students discuss how they used feedback and reflection to inform their progress.
learning_outcomes: Identify safety issues and hazards of non-Newtonian fluids and fluid-particle systems in viscous solutions. (B.1)
Analyse complex fluids and particulate systems in chemical engineering research and industrial processes. (D.1)
Communicate the design rationale for a solution to a complex fluids and particulate system. (E.1)
Design industrial processes for non-Newtonian fluids and complex particle operations. (C.1)
prerequisites: Academic requisite: 48641 Fluid Mechanics

title: Advanced Games Programming
syllabus_overview:
This developing level subject dives into the advanced games topics of artificial intelligence, procedural content generation, and networked multiplayer. You will learn these topics by utilising the industry-standard game engine, Unreal Engine 5, and the C++ programming language. You will learn skills and concepts through assessed weekly lab modules that will teach you skills and algorithms that are transferable between game development environments and that can generalise across many aspects of games development. You will further develop your understanding of these topics and combine them in a session-long group project that will culminate in a novel game or tool prototype that enhances your portfolio and prepares you for significant contributions to third-year capstone projects. The subject's development was supported by the 2019 Epic MegaGrants scheme.

Teaching Strategies:
Lectures will be used to introduce advanced games programming topics, establish common knowledge among all students, and facilitate class-wide discussion of these topics. Due to the complexity of the contained topics, most topics will require two or more weeks to be explored. Laboratory hours will allow students to further develop knowledge of the lecture topics through self-directed learning using freely available online resources. This will provide students with the opportunity to develop lifelong learning skills by enhancing their knowledge through hands-on skill acquisition. The quality of learning largely depends on the student; the effort that is put in will determine the knowledge and skills that come out of it. Games programming is a vast, complex discipline and this subject is a platform to facilitate students’ self-guided learning on both common core topics and student selected topics that they feel will complement their own unique skill set and career path, with the lecturer/tutors there to facilitate student learning. Laboratories will also be used for working on group assessments – sharing knowledge between group members, designing a game or game development tool, providing inter-group feedback on prototypes, and discussing progress and difficulties with teaching staff.

Understand advanced concepts in games programming and conduct self-directed learning to explore such topics in-depth. (D.1)
Critically analyse the prototypes of others and provide professional and constructive feedback. (E.1)
Iteratively design and develop technical demonstrations that combine numerous forms of fundamental and advanced game development techniques. (C.1)
Abstract and communicate the intent, benefits, and complexities of an advanced game or tool design to a wider audience of peers. (E.1)

title: Advanced Genetic Counselling
syllabus_overview:
This final genetic counselling subject equips you with the core competencies for supporting individuals and families living with psychosocial impact of genetic conditions. You will integrate your learning to prepare for graduation as entry-level genetic counsellors. You will engage in case-based learning to enhance development of communication skills across a range of contexts in which genetic counsellors practice. You will focus on increasing cultural safety and working with diverse communities to demonstrate your readiness to join the genetic counselling profession.

Teaching Strategies:
Core learning: Core learning material, activities and readings are undertaken in Canvas prior to weekly live and online workshops. Students will be provided with learning activities each week, including readings, discussions, reflection questions, case studies and videos that prepare them for the live and online sessions. Please ensure Canvas work is carried out prior to the live and online session so that you have spent time accessing and making sense of ideas. Attending the live and online workshops will allow you to test these ideas and get feedback from the academic staff and peers which will further consolidate your learning. Live and online workshops: Weekly live and online workshops provide students with opportunities to participate in discussion, role play and problem-based learning activities. The activities in the weekly workshops build on the Canvas work and allow time to clarify and ask questions on content learning. Students will work collaboratively in pairs, small groups and as a class during the workshops. Group discussions will often involve case-based learning activities. Students will participate in role play and learning activities to assist with the development of counselling skills in preparation for clinical placement. Feedback will be provided by the teacher and by peers. Block workshops: Students will attend a week-long block, during which they will participate in workshops that will include discussion, role play, simulation, problem-based learning activities, and practice of core counselling skills for genetic counsellors. When core counselling skills are practiced, the faculty member will provide live guidance on how feedback should be provided, so that students receive immediate constructive feedback from peers and from the faculty member. Research Integrated Learning: Taking an evidence-based approach to work with clients is an essential skill. Current research is integrated into the content provided in Canvas and workshops. Students are encouraged to read, discuss and utilise current research in counselling and communication in the context of providing evidence-based genetic counselling care. Reflective Learning: Students are encouraged to critically reflect on their learning and their skill development throughout the subject, to identify areas where they may improve their performance, and to assist in the development of lifelong learning. Reflective learning will be encouraged through specific activities including assessment tasks in which students will reflect on the development of core genetic counselling and communication skills over the duration of the session. Opportunities for reflection include the weekly reflective practice supervision groups that are part of 96101 Genetic Counselling Clinical Placement 4. Ongoing feedback: Verbal feedback will be provided throughout the subject during the block and live and online workshops. There will be weekly opportunities to discuss ideas and experiences and receive feedback during the live and online workshops. Opportunities for verbal formative feedback on assessment tasks are available prior to the due date and summative feedback is provided following final submission.

Apply reflective and inclusive practices in genetic counselling.
Adapt to changes in genomic healthcare field and identify professional development needs.
Demonstrate advanced client-centered communication and counseling skills for genetic counselling practice.
Advocate for clients and their families and address ethical considerations in genetic counselling practice.

title: Advanced Imaging and Specialist Recovery
syllabus_overview:
This subject equips you with advanced forensic imaging skills, crucial for careers in forensic investigation and digital evidence analysis. You'll learn to capture and scrutinise image evidence, mastering techniques for image enhancement and authentication. Through computer labs and practical exercises, you'll refine your ability to document complex scenes, analyse digital images as evidence, exhibit specialised search skills. and effectively communicate your findings. This training not only deepens your theoretical understanding but also prepares you to apply these skills in real-world scenarios.

Teaching Strategies:
Weekly online learning The weekly online modules deliver foundational and advanced theoretical content through interactive, self-paced materials. Each week, students engage with a blend of readings, short instructional videos, embedded quizzes, and collaborative discussion boards aligned with the practical and lab work. The content is designed using a flipped learning approach, allowing students to acquire core knowledge before applying it in hands-on settings. This strategy promotes active learning, critical thinking, and peer engagement, as students are encouraged to discuss concepts, analyze case studies, and reflect on their learning in preparation for practical application. Practicals Each practical session immerses students in authentic forensic scenarios, providing hands-on experience with advanced imaging equipment and techniques. Students work in simulated crime scene environments, using DSLR cameras, specialized lenses, 3D scanners, and lighting tools to document evidence and scenes under varied conditions. The teaching strategy is rooted in experiment-based and observation-based learning pedagogies: students learn by doing, testing hypotheses, and refining their skills through trial and error and guided reflection. Staff facilitate the sessions by demonstrating techniques, setting clear objectives, and prompting students to critically evaluate their methods and results, ensuring all required data and images are collected for subsequent analysis. Computer Labs Computer labs are student-centered, self-directed sessions where students process and analyze the data and images collected during practicals, using free, cross-platform forensic software. Each lab begins with a brief staff demonstration of key software tools and workflows, after which students independently manage, enhance, authenticate, and reconstruct forensic imagery for their portfolios. The facilitator’s role is to support troubleshooting, encourage reflective documentation, and prompt deeper analysis, fostering skills in digital forensics, critical evaluation, and professional reporting. This approach integrates guided learning with independent problem-solving, ensuring students develop both technical proficiency and the ability to critically assess their outputs in a forensic context.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced photography, digital imaging techniques, and analysis in forensic contexts.
Produce comprehensive forensic documentation in a professional format.
Assess digital imagery as evidence and discern information that is useful for forensic investigation.
Identify and explain various imaging artefacts and digital indicators and their relevance in a forensic context.

title: Advanced Haematology and Pathology Diagnosis
syllabus_overview:
This subject enhances your understanding of diseases affecting blood and organ systems, focusing on pathophysiology and diagnostic techniques. You'll learn to distinguish between healthy and diseased tissues, employing advanced microscopy and digital image analysis. The subject integrates interactive workshops and online learning led by field experts. You’ll gain professional digital competencies and diagnostic skills in line with modern laboratory practices applicable to the health sector.

Teaching Strategies:
In this subject, you will participate in a range of teaching and learning strategies, which will be used to enable you to learn, clarify, discuss and develop concepts learned in the subject. All the content of this subject will be delivered online via Canvas and Zoom. Lectures/self-paced learning (Canvas) Pre-recorded lectures and self-paced learning materials will be available online to introduce and present the subject content. These materials will be reinforced by additional online learning content made available through Canvas either before (for preparation purposes), during or after the lecture (for content review). Workshops (Online via ZOOM) Workshops will provide additional information to supplement the Canvas self directed learning. Instructions and advice will be provided about Assessment tasks. Feedback and Q&A about learning activities will be available. Practical classes (On-campus) During practical classes, students will actively engage with real-world case studies to reinforce their learning using modern digital software. This will help the students understand the key concepts and application of modern lab techniques that are used in the field to accurately and efficiently diagnose diseases. There is a strong focus on haematological and anatomical diagnosis of patient case studies through microscopy (digital morphology hosted by the AIFORIA learning platform) in conjunction with modern laboratory practices such as flow cytometry. syllabus_overview:
This subject enables you to create advanced web applications ready for production, focusing on server-side programming and business-to-business systems. You'll gain proficiency in internet technologies, encompassing web development stacks, n-tier architectures, transactions, security, and web-service integration. The subject simulates a tech startup or internal software project environment, where you'll develop and refine a prototype, ensuring it meets real-world standards of security, reliability, and maintainability. Through hands-on labs and group work, you'll enhance your internet programming, problem-solving, collaboration, and communication skills. Additionally, self-directed learning and professional community engagement are expected outside of class hours.

There is a one-hour collaborative lecture and a two-hour laboratory session each week. Preparation for the laboratory session includes expected participation in the collaborative lecture in addition to preparatory tasks such as programming challenges and independent research activities. The preparation may also include online readings or videos. Further independent study is also expected. The lecture is designed to provide: 1. A technical discussion and reflective analysis of the weekly themes. Prior preparation is important for involvement in this discussion. title: Advanced Interaction Design
syllabus_overview:
This subject delves into user experience (UX) in interaction design, crucial for technology adoption and competitive differentiation. UX reflects a user's interaction with digital products and varies widely in definition across academia and industry. You'll acquire conceptual tools to discuss UX effectively, identifying and critiquing digital technology experiences. Practical skills are developed by examining human-computer interactions, including mobile and pervasive computing, IoT, and more, focusing on user experiences in specific contexts and goals. You'll learn design methods like user research, sketching, and prototyping, applying these to create technology solutions that are not only functional but also enhance user engagement. By building on fundamental design principles, you'll be equipped to craft technologies that optimize user experience.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is linked with the undergraduate subject 31777 Advanced Interaction Design. While both cohorts will engage with the same lecture materials, postgraduate students will attend separate tutorials from the undergraduate students. Students will be asked to engage with pre-recorded video lectures on various topics and attend online tutorial sessions. The pre-recorded lecture videos will allow students to learn theoretical aspects of User Experience as conceptualised, researched and supported through the design processes of Interaction Design. In addition, online lecture discussions are held to help students clarify their understanding of the video lecture materials. Tutorials will provide students with continuous guidance and formative feedback as they practice the design skills. The learning activities are designed to iteratively build students’ skills, confidence and understanding in the subject matter, providing them with the best possible opportunity to succeed. Then, students will work individually and with a group on various problems that contribute to their overall assessment. Again, they will receive regular guidance and feedback from their tutor. With guidance from tutors, students are required to create and maintain a personal portfolio of their work in the subject throughout the session. They will be required to choose work samples they have created that through a guided reflection, demonstrate their learning and developing knowledge of the various tools and skills required in designing for user experience. Students are expected to use various online resources, including some provided through Canvas to access materials such as prescribed readings, videos, guides, and research materials to prepare for class assignments and individual work. Accessing and reading prescribed texts, as well as completing required set tasks before class will enable students to engage more deeply and successfully in the collaborative activities of the workshop and their weekly tutorial tasks. The subject values learning-through-doing. Students will be expected to participate regularly in online discussion forum, and to collaborate with others in a session-long group assignment to solve a real-life problem through design activities.
learning_outcomes: Describe the range of social/technical and experiential concepts that are important to consider when designing technologies that can be experienced positively by users. (B.1)
Identify the types of user experiences that are most appropriate for different types of human-computer interactions. (C.1)
Apply appropriate methods, concepts, and techniques to successfully design interactive technologies that can support engaging user experiences during use. (C.1)
Use appropriate conceptual tools to accurately describe, critique, analyse and evaluate user experiences that arise through, and during, interactions with information technology. (D.1)
Demonstrate awareness on how to design in a positive and respectful manner when working with, and for, Indigenous Australians. (A.1)

title: Advanced Journalism
syllabus_overview:
This subject prepares you with the multimedia journalism skills sought after by various organisations. You'll build a portfolio showcasing your ability to report and edit using text, audio, and visual media. Research projects delve into the evolving media landscape, scrutinising issues that shape discussions and policies about journalism's role and future. It also introduces you to further postgraduate study options.

Teaching Strategies:
Students will be exposed to high-quality reporting, editing and presentation across mediums and use the skills gained to develop their own reporting, editing and publishing. They will develop high level reporting and editing skills in lectures, seminars and workshops. Mandatory workshops will run, starting in week 1, throughout the session and aim to assist students to learn and/or refresh skills in the use of audio and video equipment. Students will be engaged via online and face-to-face learning with aspects of contemporary journalism practice and research to inform both their reporting and editing and the more reflective aspects of the subject. They will be expected to produce pieces of journalism and write reflective blogs that indicate their understanding of contemporary journalistic challenges, debates and opportunities. Students will develop their ability to identify journalism trends in lectures complemented by independent reading, participation in online discussions facilitated by the subject co-ordinator and use of online resources. Online Language Screening Task: An aim of this subject is to help you develop academic and professional language and communication skills in order to succeed at university and in the workplace. To determine your current academic language proficiency, you are required to complete an online language screening task, OPELA (information available at https://www.uts.edu.au/research-and-teaching/learning-and-teaching/enhancing/language-and-learning/about-opela-students) . If you receive a Basic grade for OPELA, you must attend additional Language Development Tutorials (weeks 4-12) in order to pass the subject. These tutorials are designed to support you to develop your language and communication skills. Students who do not complete the OPELA and/or do not attend 80% of the Language Development Tutorials will receive a Fail X grade.

title: Advanced Machine Learning
syllabus_overview:
Advanced Machine Learning deepens your understanding of sophisticated data models, algorithms, and theoretical principles, building upon existing machine learning knowledge. This subject provides a mix of theory and practical application, focusing on statistical learning theory and empirical risk minimization to refine your ML models and algorithms.

Teaching Strategies:
The study will be both theoretical and practical. As for the theory, the subject provides a systematic view of the whole lifecycle of a data model, from the design motivation to the dynamics in the learning process and the evaluation and how reliable the evaluation results are. On the practical side, learners will be led to translate mathematical notions into data structures and programs in a digital computer, which allows them to ‘open the hood’ of the data models and get hands-on experience to examine piece-by-piece how the models perform learning. Subject presentation includes weekly synchronous one-hour online workshops facilitated by an expert UTS academic(s) supporting self-study and online (LMS) learning activities. Regular formative quizzes throughout the semester will allow students to gauge their progress.
learning_outcomes: Design machine learning algorithms with practical implementation for professional contexts. (C.1)

title: Advanced Machine Learning Application
syllabus_overview:
This subject delves into advanced machine learning algorithms and machine learning operations (MLOps) concepts. You'll acquire skills to build, deploy, and manage models in real-world settings. The curriculum goes beyond basics, offering a deep dive into sophisticated algorithms and their practical uses through hands-on projects and case studies. A strong focus on deployment engineering prepares you to navigate the complexities of integrating machine learning models into production.

Teaching Strategies:
Blend of online and face to face activities: The subject is offered through a series of teaching sessions which blend online and face-to-face learning. Students learn through interactive lectures and classroom activities making use of the subject materials on canvas. They also engage in individual and collaborative learning activities to understand and apply text analysis techniques in diverse settings. Authentic problem based learning: This subject offers a range of authentic data science problems to solve that will help develop students’ text analysis skills. They work on real world data analysis problems for broad areas of interest using unstructured data and contemporary techniques. Collaborative work: Group activities will enable students to leverage peer-learning and demonstrate effective team participation, as well as learning to work in professional teams with an appreciation of diverse perspectives on data science and innovation. Future-oriented strategies : Students will be exposed to contemporary learning models using speculative thinking, ethical and human-centered approaches as well as reflection. Electronic portfolios will be used to curate, consolidate and provide evidence of learning and development of course outcomes, graduate attributes and professional evolution. Formative feedback will be offered with all assessment activities for successful engagement.

Apply effective collaboration and communication skills necessary for working in interdisciplinary teams
Design and implement robust and efficient systems for model deployment

This subject prepares you to tackle current macroeconomic research challenges by mastering analytical techniques for imperfect markets. You will build on prior knowledge from related subjects such as Intermediate Macroeconomics, Economics of Monetary Policy and Central Banking, and Economic Growth, Development and Sustainability. You’ll extend your understanding of interactions between the goods market, the labour market and financial markets, you’ll investigate new ways of explaining fluctuations in economic activity, and you’ll more thoroughly examine phenomena such as economic growth and inflation using detailed analytical methods. Learning unfolds through interactive lectures and tutorials, with a focus on relevant texts and articles.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject will be taught using a combination of lectures and tutorials. There is no course textbook. Students will read from texts and articles appropriate to the selection of topics.
learning_outcomes: Knowledgeably and critically read and analyse contemporary macroeconomic research
Understand modern theories of microeconomic foundations of market inefficiencies that contribute to macroeconomic fluctuations
Understand and apply dynamic analytical tools in economic analysis

title: Advanced Materials
syllabus_overview:
This subject comprises two interrelated parts: the creation of nanostructures, nanomaterials, and nanodevices through deposition, growth, and self-assembly; and the practical application of their unique properties. You'll learn how to tailor these nanomaterials for diverse uses, including innovative construction materials, medical prosthetics, and advanced electronic devices.

Teaching Strategies:
Practical work is an important part of this course in which students gain experimental skills that they will require in later stage subjects in their program. The practicals will also be used to assess the students’ skills in the laboratory and the report writing. During the laboratories, students work in the small groups of 3 or 4 to complete the experiments, which typically include synthesis and characterization of nanomaterials, followed by property testing. Each of the students will take different and complementary responsibilities within the group. Lectures will be presented with opportunity for student participation and are supported by a closely related laboratory program. Examples related to the students’ degree program are used to illustrate the importance of the topic. Selected videos are available in Canvas before or after the lectures. Students should watch the videos to reinforce concepts. Topics presented in the lectures are assessable in the final exam. The online quiz is used to provide early formative feedback to the students and teaching staff with regard to the students’ understanding of the subject. Canvas is used to post worked solutions to assignments, tutorials etc. and to keep students informed of their progress. Announcements are also made via this forum.

Apply fundamental knowledge and principles of materials science to address challenges in nanotechnology.

title: Advanced Manufacturing Technology
syllabus_overview:
This subject immerses you in the latest manufacturing processes and digital technologies that are reshaping industry norms. As a future designer, you'll understand how these advancements alter work, industry organisation, and your role in relation to products, consumers, and producers. You'll learn about the potential of new manufacturing tech, examine shifts in business models and production systems, and explore product design changes, equipping you for a forward-thinking career in product design.

Teaching Strategies:
A weekly lecture will provide the context for working with advanced manufacturing technologies and ensure the student is informed of developments in their use. This will be supported by a three-hour weekly studio that includes elements of workshop practice. Students will engage hands-on with industrial additive manufacturing and digital technologies through experimentation to explore the parameters of making with these technologies. Project work will then draw on these experiments, with students creating prototypes to demonstrate their knowledge of designing for specific industry sectors and consumer products. Studio time will provide students with the opportunity to take ownership of the ideas encountered in preparatory reading and research. Studio leaders will help facilitate discussion and offer expert insight and direction where needed, but students are primarily responsible for the collaborative and participatory nature of the tutorial. Outside of class time, students are expected to extend the enquiries made in the collaborative learning session with the independent development of their assessment projects. Studio leaders will be reviewing the work weekly and will provide feedback verbally. It is the student's responsibility to record any feedback provided both in studio and after presentations. Students will be expected to actively participate in collaborative peer review feedback exercises. Students will also be supported by the level 2, Faculty Workshop in the construction of models and prototypes. Grades, marks and feedback on final design submissions will be provided through UTSReview.
learning_outcomes: Develop professional written and visual presentation skills to communicate technical design tasks.
Demonstrate an understanding of associated digital technologies, such as robotic 3D printing, parametric CAD and 3D scanning.
Use prototyping as a key research method to work successfully with both industrial and consumer-grade additive manufacturing machinery.

title: Advanced Mathematics and Physics
syllabus_overview:
Delivered by the School of Mathematics and Physical Sciences, this subject equips second-year engineering and science undergraduates with the essential mathematical and physical knowledge needed in their fields. It offers a comprehensive set of mathematical tools for analysing electric and magnetic fields, circuits, and signal processing, alongside theoretical and applied quantum physics. The physics component introduces quantum physics, bridging from classical mechanics to its applications in semiconductor devices. Mathematics topics include vector calculus, complex variable functions, Divergence and Stokes theorems, Cauchy-Riemann equations, the Residue theorem, and Laplace transforms.

Teaching Strategies:
Maths: The mathematics section consists of two hours of lectures per week. Each lecture will focus on a specific maths topic. Tutorial problem sets will be assigned 3 times a year, these will completed and assessed online. A one-hour tutorial will also be available for students to seek help with these problems. Physics: The physics section consists of a 5 2-hour lectures and 4 2-hour tutorials tutorial for the first 5 weeks. The core material will be delivered via lectures, interspersed with demonstrations and explanations delivered by the lecturers. You will supplement the lecture notes by asking questions and discussing concepts and diagrams. The aim of this is to deliver a concise set of course notes while promoting attendance, active learning and exploration in the lectures and tutorials. Pre-learning: Prior to the lectures you will be given pre-work in the form of additional reading, problems questions and research tasks (some content will be obtained online). Some of the pre-work will also be crucial for you to complete prior to entering the subsequent classes. At the start of the lectures you will be assessed on your comprehension of the pre-learning through Q+A, quizzes and discussion. To give an example: the last century has provided diverse developments in the field of quantum mechanics. As part of the pre-learning in the physics section you will be asked to research historical developments in quantum mechanics and present the findings to the class verbally.
learning_outcomes: Solve core mathematical problems required in the engineering discipline;
Interpret how the quantum and physical properties of materials have relevance to the practice of engineers and applied scientists.
Solve problems in applied and quantum physics using a range of mathematical and practical techniques;
Evaluate how the quantum properties of electrons in solids can be used to develop new electronic devices;

title: Advanced Medical Biochemistry
syllabus_overview:
In this subject you will be introduced to the fundamentals of medical and clinical biochemistry, crucial for biotechnology, medical research, and pathology lab analysis. You will study biochemical abnormalities underlying diseases, their diagnosis, clinical analysis, and treatment, with a focus on kidney and liver function, diabetes, lipid disorders, clinical enzymology, and serum proteins. Emphasis is also placed on safety, quality control and automation. You will be offered insights into clinical biochemistry's role in health, ensuring precise and relevant testing, which will be beneficial for those aspiring to careers in diagnostic pathology, clinical research, or laboratory management.

Teaching Strategies:
In Advanced Medical Biochemistry you will have the opportunity to learn through lectures, laboratory practicals, and a journal club. In these classes you will be exposed to a variety of learning strategies which can be complemented by your own independent study, in order to help you maximise your learning potential in this subject. You are directed to check UTS Canvas and your official UTS student email regularly (at least once per week) in order to be up-to-date with the timetable and assessments. Lectures (2 hr/wk for 11 weeks): Lectures are delivered to you by experts in their respective fields and provide an introduction to the key concepts of Advanced Medical Biochemistry. Lectures will be delivered online and recorded. Some lectures may also involve preparation by you in the form of reading provided journal articles or patient case studies in order to discuss these in the lecture session. Laboratory Practicals (3 hr/wk for 5 weeks): You will generally work groups to perform laboratory experiments focused on the analysis of clinical samples for diagnosis of disease states, providing you with hands-on experience of diagnostic pathology and methods used in (bio-)medical research. These laboratory practicals will extend theory learnt in lectures, and help you understand and apply your learning. You will need to prepare for each session by reading the experimental protocol provided in the manual, and by completing a test on UTS Canvas before the session begins. Completing this pre-work and test will help you prepare for the experimental procedures and manage your time in the session in order to complete the required work in the timetabled session. For some of the laboratory practicals, you will also need to prepare by reading clinical case studies to understand why the relevant methodologies are being employed. By reading about the analysis of the results, you will determine what is the likely cause of a patient’s symptoms. Feedback for practicals are provided during the class and online for the written work by the demonstrators and assessors. Journal Club (3 hr/wk for 3 weeks): Journal Club is used in professional scientific fields of employment and is a regular meeting of a group of scientists to discuss developments in their field that have been recently published in the literature. Journal Club involves a person/team presenting a recently published journal article to the group, including context, aims, experimental procedures, and the important findings; as well as a critical evaluation of the study. The group then discusses the study drawing on their collective knowledge. Feedback is provided during the session by the assessor verbally and by online summary. You will work in teams to present at Journal Club. You will select a recently published journal article (within the last 3 years) on your choice of topic associated with the lecture series in Advanced Medical Biochemistry. In your team, you will present this article and associated, relevant information, as well as your critical evaluation (critique) of the study. This presentation will be a talk (oral presentation) with a visual component (e.g., PowerPoint) which will be delivered to the class.
learning_outcomes: Describe and perform and interpret standard biochemical laboratory techniques for analysing blood and urine.
Demonstrate effective collaboration and communication skills in diverse scientific contexts.
Describe and explain fundamental requirements of quality assurance, quality control and reference intervals within a medical science laboratory.
Apply research-based biomedical knowledge to explain common human biochemical pathologies.

title: Advanced Microscopy and Imaging
syllabus_overview:
This subject offers a thorough grounding in modern microscopy, combining theoretical principles with practical application using UTS's advanced research microscopes. You'll explore light and fluorescence theory, and techniques such as bright-field, DIC, phase contrast, and confocal microscopy, including live cell imaging. The course also introduces super-resolution microscopy and best practices in sample preparation. You'll learn to optimise data for image analysis and apply these skills in practical sessions, conducting experiments and analysing results to professional standards, ready for presentation at scientific forums.

Teaching Strategies:
Learning and teaching strategies At the beginning of this subject, you will be introduced to the content through the online learning space, Canvas. You will have the chance to engage with materials and meet your peers. You will be able to familiarise yourself with the central concepts prior to face-to-face classes, designed to help you further engage in collaboration and critical thinking. Canvas Pages for asynchronous learning: 5 online modules Online modules through asynchronous learning are provided as the foundation for your on-campus learning.The lecture series (online and CANVAS pages) have been designed to provide you with the background knowledge necessary for understanding the operation and application of the Microscopy techniques used in Medical Biotechnology. Online readings from discipline-specific reviews are made available to enhance the content that you receive. Asynchronous learning and interactive activities have been developed and tailored towards understanding advanced concepts in Microscopy. They are designed to educate and inspire you to engage in online participation and further discussion with teachers and your peers. You will gain an in-depth understanding of fluorescence and its uses in microscopy, as well as a grounded understanding of Immunofluorescence microscopy (IFM) and designing IFM experiments. Here, your knowledge will be tested and reinforced by online quizzes. You will learn about digital images, and the quantitative and qualitative data they contain. You will apply these foundation concepts to basic microscopic image analysis with the use of industry-standard software. You will also build on skills in graphing, statistics and referencing. You will have the opportunity for feedback to ensure you have the requisite knowledge to analyze, and present data and data-related statistics for a scientific poster. The online interactive modules will help you through the process of structuring and presenting a scientific poster correctly. You will be challenged to discuss and evaluate experimental design and image analysis in fluorescence microscopy with your peers and through online participation in discussions. Practicals: A two-day experiment The practicals give you the opportunity to learn how to prepare and label cells for cellular analysis by optical techniques. Fluorescent reagents, molecular tools and cell treatments will be made available. You will need to understand how the tools, reagents and microscopes work in order to perform the experiment correctly. You will explore the optical and digital parameters of research-grade fluorescence microscopes through experimentation. You will learn to microscopically image cells and the subcellular components which are vitally important for correct cellular function. You will learn about the use of relevant controls that are needed to validate your analysis. You will take images with industry-standard cameras and software. You will conduct a fluorescence microscopy experiment that aims to detect changes in cellular structure in response to a given treatment. The laboratory work is carried out in small groups but will be assessed individually. Computer class: 1 computer analysis session In the computer analysis session, which offers active learning of current computer-based analysis techniques, you will learn to analyse microscopy data using industry-standard analysis programs. The data that you analyse will include your own data that you have collected in the practical sessions and more complex data from real-life research projects. This data will be compiled and used to produce figures for the scientifc poster. You will learn how to present, describe and incorporate the data figures into a scientific poster and oral presentation. There will be regular feedback opportunities to ensure your analysis methods, results and poster preparation are of acceptable quality. Drop-in sessions and online tutorials Additional drop-in sessions will provide opportunities for further image acquisition using research-grade microscopes to ensure that you obtain high-quality image data (including replicates) of all your treatment conditions and controls. This image data will form the basis of your individual results that require analysis, interpretation and presentation in your own scientific poster. Additional drop-in computer sessions and online tutorials will aid you in the development of your image analysis methods and related skills, including interpretation and presentation of results. Attendance at these drop-in sessions is highly encouraged to maximise your learning outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Develop testable hypotheses that can be confirmed by appropriate statistical tests.
Prepare, fix and stain cells for microscopic analysis.
Evaluate, synthesise and communicate scientific research effectively.
Analyse and present microscopic data of high scientific quality.
Apply theoretical knowledge and practical skills in microscopy to acquire valid data.

title: Advanced Pharmaceutical Science
syllabus_overview:
From early preformulation studies to advanced drug delivery systems, this course provides you with specialist expertise to address challenges in pharmaceutical research and industry. In Advanced Pharmaceutical Science, you bring together the principles of pharmaceutics, biopharmaceutics and pharmacokinetics through an applied learning experience. You develop skills in the design and evaluation of conventional oral dosage forms, modified-release systems, parenteral formulations, and alternative routes of administration including transdermal, mucosal, pulmonary, and nasal delivery. You are also introduced to advanced and targeted drug delivery technologies and biological products. Through hands-on laboratory sessions using industry-standard methods, combined with interactive workshops, you apply scientific principles to real-world challenges in dosage form design and development. Emphasis is placed on quality control testing, in vitro product performance evaluation, and the relationship between formulation and drug bioperformance, in alignment with Australian and international pharmaceutical regulatory standards. The use of in silico predictive tools to simulate and predict drug bioperformance is also covered. Collectively, these learning activities enable you to develop the scientific knowledge and practical skills required for a career in pharmaceutical sciences and related industries.

Teaching Strategies:
In Advanced Pharmaceutical Science, you will engage with a variety of learning strategies designed to support your understanding and application of key concepts. The subject is delivered through eleven weeks of workshops and seven weeks of hands-on laboratory classes, complemented by weekly asynchronous online materials available on Canvas. Laboratory sessions are an essential component of the subject, as they reinforce and extend the theoretical concepts covered. Online materials Online materials will be available weekly and will be posted one week prior to the corresponding workshop topic. These materials will include videos explaining key concepts and quizzes. On-campus workshops You will attend 11 × 2-hour on-campus workshop sessions. You will be expected to engage with the online materials on Canvas prior to attending these sessions. During workshops, you will participate in problem-solving exercises and class discussions, receiving ongoing feedback through whole-class interactions and small-group activities focused on quiz and tutorial questions. On-campus laboratory practical classes · In Weeks 3–6 and 9–11, you will attend 3-hour on-campus laboratory classes focused on preformulation studies, quality control testing and in vitro drug product performance evaluation. · You will work collaboratively in small groups (4-5 students). These sessions are essential for reinforcing the theory learned through workshops and online materials to support understanding and application of key concepts. · You will gain hands-on experience operating standard laboratory equipment, develop an understanding of laboratory safety, and build teamwork skills. · You are expected to prepare for each session by reading the experimental protocol provided on the Canvas page. · Feedback for practical work will be provided during class and online, based on the data collected.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of the scientific and technological aspects of the design, manufacture, and evaluation of drug dosage forms and delivery systems.
Identify emerging technologies in drug delivery, including nanotechnology, biotechnology-derived products, and understand the principles underlying their formulation design.
Perform laboratory-based experiments to evaluate the in vitro performance and quality control of dosage forms, including preformulation studies.

Apply critical thinking and problem-solving skills to interpret laboratory data and propose potential improvements in formulation or processing, with the goal of enhancing the performance, safety, and quality of drug products.
Collaborate effectively in team-based settings to plan and evaluate drug product performance, demonstrating leadership, communication, and problem-solving skills.

title: Advanced Pharmacology
syllabus_overview:
This subject advances your understanding of drug and xenobiotic action from 91707 (Fundamentals of Pharmacology). It encourages you to adopt a problem-solving approach, with a focus on molecular pharmacology in relation to pathophysiological issues. You'll delve deeper into the role of receptors and ion channels in drug action, selective toxicity for treating infections, and factors influencing target organ toxicity. The efficacy of major drug classes for the treatment of cancer, mental health, and respiratory, cardiovascular, and metabolic diseases, among others, is critically examined. Tutorials and case studies reinforce the clinical relevance of the material studied, enhancing your ability to apply pharmacological concepts to real-world scenarios.

Teaching Strategies:
To utilise the class times efficiently, you are encouraged to always read the relevant materials before coming to class. You will find all of the relevant material for this subject, including recommended textbook, lecture handouts, and practical manual in Canvas. Please bring your relevant notes to every tutorial. You will have time during this activity to discuss the content with your peers and make further notes to consolidate your learning. Subject content will be delivered as interactive lectures which include discussion of cases and questions related to the lecture topics. In preparation for the interactive lectures, view the pre-lecture videos for selected topics in Canvas. In addition to the lectures, you are strongly encouraged to attend the tutorial and practical classes (see Program). These two-hour tutorials expand, reinforce, and supplement theoretical material from lectures by using clinical case scenarios. Consider these as revision activities about the completed lectures. In preparation for the tutorials, you must read the associated lecture materials. These tutorials will cover four major topics: neuropharmacology, cardiovascular drugs, antimicrobials, and cancer chemotherapy (and related drugs). During the tutorials, you should participate in the discussion of the answers to the questions about the clinical case scenarios and will receive feedback from your peers and tutors. Discussions will involve analysis of the clinical case scenarios and correlating them with the pharmacology of the drugs.
learning_outcomes: Explain the process of drug development, from discovery to post-marketing surveillance, including the role of clinical trials and biomarkers.
Analyse the pharmacological principles and therapeutic applications of drugs across various diseases.
Evaluate the complexities of drug addiction, including its treatment and the pharmacological challenges of dependence.
Describe the use of monoclonal antibodies as both diagnostic and therapeutic agents.
Communicate pharmacological concepts effectively to a non-specialist audience using various presentation methods.

title: Advanced Power Electronics
syllabus_overview:
This subject delves into the creation and deployment of power electronics interfaces for microgrids, smart grids, electrified transportation and modern power systems, a field gaining significant traction globally, including in Australia. You will explore technologies required for integrating renewable energy sources into the grid, managing energy storage systems, electric vehicles and improving grid stability and communication in smart grids. The curriculum empowers you to explore and develop innovative solutions for intricate design challenges. Upon completion of this subject, you will possess a comprehensive grasp of power converter principles, control strategies, modulation techniques and hands on experience of measurement and analysis. Moreover, you'll be proficient in modeling, simulating, and identifying crucial design parameters for control systems and prototyping.

Teaching Strategies:
A weekly learning schedule will be provided as a Study Guide with a list of topics, exercise problems and suggested readings for each week. Labs and quizzes inform the project and final exam. Face-to-face class time consists of tutorials and laboratories. The tutorials are an opportunity to meet with fellow students and academic staff to work on and discuss problems and raise any issues. Online videos and presentation slides on each topic will be provided. Prior to each tutorial session, students are required to go through online notes and videos. Continuous and dialogic feedback is central to these sessions. Laboratories form a significant component of the subject. They reinforce the theoretical material and are a lead-up to undertaking the group project. The labs will also provide practical experience in setting up and using specialised test equipment. Each lab requires a significant amount of reading, hand-analysis and computer simulation as part of pre and post lab work. Students work on the labs in groups of 2, and academic staff are available in each lab to review the lab work and provide immediate feedback. Students undertake a substantial group project that reinforces the theoretical content and culminates in a formal written and oral presentation of their work. Students work in groups of 2 to analyse a set of specifications, design, simulate, test and practically demonstrate a Power Converter System in the lab. Students are required to submit one Progress Report and one Final Report per group for assessment followed by a final group presentation. At the end of the project, an individual viva-voce will be conducted to assess each student’s individual understanding of the project. Throughout the project work students will reflect on the progress of their work in the project.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, design, simulate and test power converters and a control system in both the time-domain and frequency-domain. (C.1)
Measure time and frequency domain characteristics of power converters using appropriate laboratory equipment. (D.1)
Apply the mathematical tools associated with transform theory to the analysis and design of power converters. (D.1)
Model real and complex power electronic systems using a hierarchical approach, and be able to simplify them with practical assumptions. (D.1)

title: Advanced Primary Health Care
syllabus_overview:
This subject enhances your primary health care knowledge, preparing you for expanded roles in community pharmacy. You'll develop advanced skills in clinical decision-making, patient assessment, and service delivery, focusing on pharmacist prescribing. You'll cover the entire prescribing process, including patient assessment, clinical reasoning, therapy selection, monitoring, and follow-up, along with de-prescribing principles. You'll also learn to deliver advanced services such as travel health consultations and minor wound management. Through case-based learning and practical application, you'll refine your ability to provide timely, evidence-based care, positioning you to deliver high-quality, accessible health services in a pharmacy setting.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject takes a patient-centred, case-based approach to learning, with a strong emphasis on hands-on, practical experiences. Interactive workshops, supported by targeted lectures and independent learning, provide students with opportunities to develop and apply their clinical decision-making, prescribing, and service delivery skills in real-world scenarios. Strategy 1 Student preparation for learning: Students engage with pre-class content to build foundational knowledge in pharmacist prescribing and advanced primary health care services. This includes online and face-to-face lectures, clinical guidelines, case studies, and interactive resources covering prescribing frameworks, de-prescribing, travel health, and minor wound management. Strategy 2 Collaborative and interactive learning in workshops: Workshops provide students with a realistic, skills-based learning environment where they can apply knowledge in simulated patient consultations, prescribing exercises, and primary care service delivery. Students will: Complete weekly quizzes and participate in collaborative discussions to reinforce learning and apply key concepts. Work in small groups to assess cases and make prescribing and de-prescribing decisions using national guidelines. Engage in scenario-based role plays in the mock pharmacy, practicing prescribing, counselling, and service delivery (e.g., travel health, minor wound care). Participate in hands-on practical sessions where they use medical devices, diagnostic tools, and referral pathways relevant to expanded pharmacist roles. Strategy 3 Structured Feedback and Reflection Students receive regular formative feedback through structured activities, including: Weekly quizzes with automated and facilitator feedback, allowing students to identify gaps in knowledge and track their progress. Role plays and peer reflection, allowing students to evaluate their prescribing and patient communication skills. Immediate feedback from facilitators during workshops to refine clinical decision-making. Post-workshop reflections, where students assess their prescribing choices and service delivery to identify areas for improvement. This integrated, skills-based approach ensures students are well-prepared to take on expanded pharmacist roles in primary health care settings.
learning_outcomes: Implement pharmacist-led primary care services, such as travel health and minor wound management, within professional and regulatory frameworks.
Reflect on and refine prescribing and service delivery, ensuring alignment with professional responsibilities and the evolving pharmacist role.
Apply an evidence-based approach to prescribing within the pharmacist’s scope, integrating patient assessment, clinical reasoning, and shared decision-making.
Communicate prescribing decisions and care plans clearly to patients and healthcare professionals to support adherence and shared care.
Formulate individualised, patient-centred prescribing plans, integrating initiation, monitoring, follow-up, and de-prescribing, to achieve optimal medication outcomes.

title: Advanced Professional Practice
syllabus_overview:
This subject brings together knowledge and skills from across the Master of Orthoptics course to prepare students for professional practice as a graduate. Orthoptist-led screening, triaging, monitoring and management will be explored, considering development of appropriate protocols, and approaches to auditing practice to ensure best-practice care provision. You will learn about service delivery models across various settings including, relevant legislative and regulatory requirements for designing safe and efficient clinical services. Funding streams to support health delivery such as, Medicare, private health insurance, the National Disability Insurance Scheme, Worker’s Compensation and the Department of Veteran's Affairs, will be discussed. Approaches to complex and challenging circumstances including, the presence of a functional vision disorder, malingering and factitious disorders will be included. You will refine your communication skills to ensure you are able to provide accurate and accessible information to other health professionals, facilitating collaborative care arrangements. Health promotion and advocacy will be examined, and you will learn techniques to increase health literacy of patients, supporting adherence to orthoptic and ophthalmic therapies. You will explore the development of health partnerships that prioritise person-centred and culturally safe approaches, alongside the vital role of community-led initiatives to promote eye health for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and communities.

Teaching Strategies:
Preparation for Learning: Students will be provided with the details of preparation activities each week through the subject’s Canvas site. Activities are designed to help students prepare for their learning in lectures and workshops by engaging them with journal and other readings, videos, online resources and group discussion. Active Lectures: Lectures provide an introduction to topic content each week and guest lecturers are invited to share their professional expertise on particular topic areas at relevant times throughout the session. Lectures are active and require students to engage and participate in the analysis of case presentations, class discussion and other active and collaborative learning methods. Case-based Learning: Case-based learning is a form of problem-based learning (PBL) and a key learning strategy. Students follow the progress of actual cases they have seen during external clinical placements that are undergoing long term treatment. Through establishing a treatment plan and observation over the course of treatment, students gain insight into external factors that can influence patient outcomes, such as cultural norms and compliance and how these can be successfully managed. Through this students refine their skill in clinical reasoning and practice the application of theoretical knowledge gained throughout the course to develop appropriate patient-focused plans for their investigation and management of their patient’s ocular condition. Research-integrated Learning: Taking an evidence-based approach to the investigation and management of patient cases is essential for effective patient care and an important skill for Orthoptic students to perfect. Current research is integrated into content provided in lectures and pre-work and students are provided opportunities in workshop classes and through assessment to read, discuss and utilise current research in ophthalmology and orthoptics in the context of evidence-based patient care. Collaborative Learning: As health professionals, teamwork is an essential skill to ensure patients are managed appropriately within interdisciplinary teams of health professionals. Teamwork skills are developed through collaboration with peers in active lectures and workshops, conducted in collaborative POD classrooms, as well as through group assessment. Reflective Learning: Students are encouraged to critically reflect on their learning throughout the subject to identify areas where they may improve their performance and to assist in the development of lifelong learning skills. Specific activities where reflective learning is encouraged are; self-evaluation of their contribution to collaborative assessment tasks and skill achievement checklists and through post lecture/workshop review of learning questions on Canvas. Ongoing Feedback: In-class verbal feedback is an important teaching and learning strategy employed throughout the subject. Opportunities for verbal formative feedback on assignments are given prior to final submission and detailed summative feedback following final submission.
learning_outcomes: Design innovative models of eye service delivery that are aligned with clinical guidelines, regulation, legislation and funding schemes.
Advocate for equity in eye health care through health promotion informed by shared decision-making, community-led approaches, and partnerships that empower individuals and communities.
Reflect on the impact of advanced orthoptic practice across diverse healthcare settings, and its contribution to improved outcomes for patients and communities.
Audit clinical data and draw on best-practice evidence to evaluate clinical services and propose business solutions to increase efficiency and optimise outcomes for patients and organisations.
Communicate eye health information effectively and accurately using culturally safe, respectful, and inclusive approaches that promote health literacy and education.

title: Advanced Professional Practice
syllabus_overview:
This subject facilitates your professional identity as a genetic counsellor, aligning with the Australasian Society of Genetic Counsellors' 'Scope of Practice' and 'Code of Ethics'. You'll prepare for the workplace and potential leadership roles by applying knowledge of health literacy, education, and advocacy to genetic counselling. The curriculum emphasises the importance of interprofessional collaboration, workload management, continuous professional development, and reflective practice supervision. You'll also learn about the Human Genetics Society of Australasia (HGSA) certification process and engage with international peers to understand global professional roles and standards, shaping your perspective on the profession's future.

Teaching Strategies:
Core learning: Core learning material, activities and readings are undertaken in Canvas prior to weekly live and online workshops. Students will be provided with learning activities each week, including readings, discussions, reflection questions, case studies and videos that prepare them for the live and online sessions. Attending the live and online workshops will allow you to test these ideas and get feedback from the academic staff and peers which will further consolidate your learning. Live and online workshops: Weekly live and online workshops provide students with opportunities to participate in discussion, role play and problem-based learning activities. The activities in the weekly workshops build on the Canvas work and allow time to clarify and ask questions on content learning. Students will work collaboratively in pairs, small groups and as a class during the workshops. Group discussions will often involve case-based learning activities. Students will participate in role play and learning activities to assist with the development of counselling skills in preparation for clinical placement. Feedback will be provided by the teacher and by peers. Block workshops: Students will attend a week-long block, during which they will participate in workshops that will include discussion, role play, simulation, problem-based learning activities, and practice of core counselling skills for genetic counsellors. title: Advanced Programming and Use of Collaborative Robots
syllabus_overview:
This subject is designed to extend students' knowledge of cobots, focusing on applying cobots to industry relevant tasks. Through this subject, students gain experience programming cobots to perform industry-relevant complex tasks and troubleshoot emergent challenges related to cobots. Students are able to integrate a cobot with peripheral equipment to form part of a larger system, and utilise end-of-arm-tooling to perform physical operations such as materials handing and palletising.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject uses a combination of self-paced online content, interactive live sessions and in-person lab activities that are hands-on with cobots. The online component focuses on learning the technical concepts that underpin the programming and application of cobots in an industrial context. Concepts are presented using theory, case studies, videos and interactive practice activities. Learners will extend a basic knowledge of cobots to include industry relevant concepts such as how to identify and remedy common cobot programming challenges, and interfacing with peripheral equipment to perform more complex operations with cobots. The in-person lab sessions will build on this understanding through hands-on practical activities with cobots. Learners will complete guided activities that involve programming the cobots, solving common programming issues, interfacing with hardware such as end-effectors and IO, and integrating peripherals together to perform complete operations that are industry relevant. Learners are supported by staff in the lab where immediate support and feedback is provided. The assessments focus on completing the activities in the labs, with learners demonstrating their capability to utilise the cobots. The complexity of the lab activities increases through the course duration.

title: Advanced Project Management
syllabus_overview:
This subject is focused on the so-called “soft” aspects of Project management. In this subject, you'll grasp the intricacies of project management within a global business context, focusing on human and organisational dynamics, project governance, and the evolving role of project managers. You'll develop critical skills in teamwork, analysis, and research, enabling you to tackle complex business solutions effectively. Learning is interactive and collaborative, featuring in-class flipped learning sessions, discussions, and group projects that encourage critical thinking. You'll also undertake individual research, formulating and defending your own perspectives on relevant issues.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is taught through a one hour lecture and two hour tutorial each week on the City campus. The lectures and tutorials are structured to reflect how projects operate in the real world—blending theory, discussion, and scenario testing into one continuous and interactive learning session. Each week, you’ll explore key concepts in advanced project management, including leadership, ethics, stakeholder engagement, governance, and delivery frameworks. These ideas won’t just be discussed in theory—they’ll be applied immediately through realistic project scenarios, ethical dilemmas, or stakeholder challenges. You'll be encouraged to test your assumptions, make decisions, and reflect on the outcomes in real time. Workshops are highly collaborative and designed to simulate the workplace. You’ll work in project teams across the semester to respond to briefs, engage with case studies, and co-develop a group tender submission. These teams are expected to manage their own work through tools such as Kanban boards, team roles, and meeting notes—just as you would in industry. You’ll also complete individual reflections where you critically evaluate your leadership style, emotional intelligence, and decision-making. It is critical for assessment purposes these reflections are grounded in evidence from your team experience and supported by theory introduced in class. This subject integrates thinking and doing throughout. Participation, initiative, and reflection are essential—for both learning current practice, and for enhancing the skills expected of a professional advanced project manager.

title: Advanced Quantum Science
syllabus_overview:
This subject provides students with knowledge of advanced topics and techniques in quantum mechanics and quantum hardware. Students develop a grounding in the physical foundations of modern quantum technologies, as applied in the context of quantum circuits and devices.

Teaching Strategies:
Lecture material will be provided as videos made available through Canvas each week. Short, formative weekly online quizzes for each topic, linked alongside the lecture videos in the relevant Canvas page, will provide students the opportunity for immediate feedback on their progress in understanding and applying concepts covered in the lecture videos. These quizzes are designed to help students identify key concepts in each topic, and may be attempted as many times as required. Weekly practice questions and worked solutions will allow students to explore how to apply analytical concepts and techniques to concrete circuits. One two-hour workshop will be run each week throughout the session to discuss concepts from lectures. A second two-hour computer lab (tutorial) will be run each week throughout the session to learn and practise numerical methods for solving problems relevant to quantum information processing systems, and discuss problems related to their final project. Students are expected to have reviewed lecture and supporting material (e.g., videos and quizzes on Canvas) before attending workshops and computer labs. The scheduled time will be used for interactive discussion and application of practical methods. Example quiz questions and practice analytical questions (of the same types that will be included in progressive skills assessments) may be discussed during both workshops and computer labs to stimulate a deeper exploration of concepts and improve understanding. Developed understanding and skills, covering both concepts and analytical or numerical problem-solving techniques, will be assessed progressively through quizzes. For each half of the course, students will complete an in-class canvas quiz that will mainly focus on conceptual understanding (in weeks 5 and 11), and a take-home quiz that will mainly focus on analytical and numerical problem solving (due in weeks 6 and 12). These quizzes will comprise 60% of the overall marks for the subject. Students will then be asked to bring these different aspects together to undertake a final project which will serve as a "capstone" assessment for the course. Specifically, they will be asked to solve, using industry- or research-relevant analytical and numerical techniques, a problem relevant to a real-world quantum information processing application. This project will be assessed in two parts: submission of a short video presentation presenting the problem, describing the solution they have designed, and summarising and evaluating the results, along with their limitations and further possible directions (30%); and a short "live" viva "discussion" of their project with their assessors (e.g., their lecturers) (10%). Students will be assessed on their application of the solution technique, their clarity in explaining their approach and results, and their ability to demonstrate their understanding through answering questions. While students are of course expected to submit individual solutions to Problems Sets, collaboration during and outside workshop sessions is also encouraged to enable peer-assisted learning and feedback. Students are encouraged to make use of relevant online communication spaces in Canvas and Teams to facilitate collaboration.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and solve problems relevant to real-world quantum information processing hardware systems
Summarise, evaluate and communicate results from numerical and analytical investigations of real-world quantum information processing applications
Design and defend methodologies for studying performance of real-world quantum information processing applications
Explain key concepts relating to encoding, control, interactions and measurements in physical quantum information carriers

title: Advanced Quality Management
