title: Cost Management 4: Advanced Cost Management
syllabus_overview:
This subject explores advanced estimating and cost management techniques used by contractors, including tendering, cost monitoring, and cost control. It examines the practical challenges of cost estimation, project procurement, and strategies for achieving competitive advantage. The subject also covers key decision-making tools such as investment appraisal, feasibility studies, and cost–benefit analysis. Students will use contemporary industry software to undertake measurement and estimating tasks, and integrate estimating processes with Building Information Modelling (BIM) systems.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is delivered through weekly face-to-face learning supported by online resources. Learning activities include lectures presented by the lecturers and industry guest speakers, tutorial workshops, industry mentor sessions, and a combination of individual and group-based assessment tasks. Tutorial workshops provide opportunities for immediate feedback on group assessment work, as well as professional guidance and advice. Students are supported through Canvas, which provides access to subject materials, announcements, and ongoing communication with the subject coordinator. Students will work collaboratively in small groups to develop a tender for a building development project assigned by the subject coordinator. This process includes compulsory workshop participation, meetings with industry mentors, a tender presentation, and submission of a final tender report. In addition, two tests will assess students’ understanding of all subject topics and their ability to apply course concepts and skills.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of advanced digital technology in design, estimating and cost management
Demonstrate an understanding of PMBOK Competency Units/Knowledge Areas in Project Cost Management through active participation in in-class discussions and applied learning activities.
Understand the concept of bidding and tendering, early contractor involvement (ECI), procurement methods and infrastructure cost management
Use computer software for design, measurement, estimating, and construction programming
Understand the concept of investment appraisal and techniques

title: Cost Management Systems
syllabus_overview:
This subject equips you with management accounting and business strategy insights, focusing on cost management and analysis to meet organisational objectives. You will develop a comprehensive understanding of cost accounting concepts and decision-making tools, and learn to leverage Information and Communications Technology (ICT) to address costing challenges and improve organisational operations. You will engage with hands-on exercises, participate in case study discussions and collaborate in group assignments to refine analytical and critical thinking skills necessary for solving business problems.

Teaching Strategies:
Cost Management Systems is taught using a mix of face-to-face teaching, online resources and self-directed study. Lectures: Lectures provide the structure of a topic area, discussion of theory and practical examples. Tutorials: Students are expected to attend the lecture and review notes, undertake relevant readings and attempt all self-study tasks before attending the tutorial. Tutorials provide an opportunity to discuss concepts and ideas, ask questions about self-study tasks, and be involved in group-based problem-solving exercises and case studies. Discussion Board: Extensive use of the UTS Learning Management System Discussion Board is made to answer student enquiries. Self-directed study: Students will be required to undertake self-directed study in order to successfully engage in class exercises. For topic-related resources and learning content, see the UTS Learning Management System.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate data and cost information to solve practical costing problems and support tactical and strategic decision making
Apply a range of appropriate quantitative techniques and use costing information for business planning, performance evaluation and control
Apply Information and Communications Technology to support data analysis, decision making and communication.
Explain the role of management accounting and strategy in contemporary organisations to support the achievement of organisational strategies and goals

title: Cost Management and Analysis
syllabus_overview:
This subject equips you with essential cost management and analysis skills, vital for business planning and control. You'll master techniques such as cost classification, cost estimation, product costing, and variance analysis, applying them to real-world organisational challenges. Your learning will be hands-on, using industry-standard accounting tools and tackling problems drawn from professional practice, ensuring you're ready for the workplace. You'll develop analytical skills, Information and Communications Technology (ICT) proficiency for cost management, and the ability to think critically through a practice-based assignment, and problem-based quizzes and final exam.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is designed on the philosophy that, to become practice-ready: (1) students learn best by using cost accounting tools common in practice and; (2) students learn best by solving cost modelling and analysis problems sourced from professional practice. This strategy aligns with the UTS Model of Learning for graduates to be “work-ready” and to provide a “practice-oriented education”. The group assignment task is a cost system design and analysis case study designed to encourage critical thinking about the textbook and lectures' content. The subject is delivered through a three-hour seminar each week. Pre-assigned materials (readings, case studies and audio-visual) and learning tasks will also be made available for students to complete independently. Students of this subject are required to: Attend all scheduled seminars Complete all subject assessments Check for announcements on the learning management system regularly Read the entire subject outline Act in an ethical manner in the completion of the requirements of this subject and to not engage in any malpractice that will provide you with an unfair advantage over other students. In particular, the University has strong policies regarding plagiarism and cheating, which can lead to severe penalties or expulsion. It is expected that students will have read the online and/or other material that has been allocated for a particular week and are prepared to discuss those materials in seminars. Students must listen, take notes and actively participate in the weekly class. Students should be active in asking questions and participating in discussions. Students will need to learn a variety of theoretical concepts in order to solve the numerous and diverse practical problems contained in the subject.

explain how cost accounting techniques support the achievement of organisational strategies and goals
apply a range of appropriate cost analysis techniques to solve practical problems faced by organisations
interpret and critically evaluate cost information to support managerial decision-making

title: Course Design
syllabus_overview:
In this subject, you will study higher education curriculum models, theories and principles of course design, and apply these models to courses that are taught at your university. Through practical applications of key theories and concepts from this subject, you will develop your ability to design courses that provide integrated, coherent and engaging learning experiences that both fulfil the needs of your students and meet university and national requirements. You will examine the courses you teach and suggest opportunities for changes that enhance your students’ experience and align courses with university and national strategic goals.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject integrates distance study with intensive block face-to-face instruction in a studio format. Your distance study is supported by materials, resources and activities that you can access in an online environment in Canvas. These online resources will enable you to prepare for the intensive block, and to review content and submit final assessments after the intensive. During the intensive block, you will work collaboratively with other participants from Solomon Islands National University (SINU) on a range of authentic activities in a studio format to develop your understanding of models of course design. Before, during and after the intensive teaching block, you will engage in structured reflections in an individual journal. Both your journal and your action plan can form the basis for work in later subjects, which provide opportunities to revisit and revise your earlier work as your knowledge and skills develop. Teaching staff provide continuous formative feedback through online and in-class interactions, as well as structured written or verbal feedback on formal assessments. Although all formal assessment is individual, peer feedback and collaboration are integral to the intensive teaching blocks. All assessments are designed to focus on your personal professional development priorities for your tertiary teaching practice. If it is appropriate for your goals, you may submit your final Revised Action Plan assessment from the Advancing Teaching Practice subject as a component of the Poster Conference for this subject, by submitting a single integrated assessment that addresses the assessment criteria for both subjects. Submission formats are flexible for many assessment components and, where flexibility is possible, we invite you to demonstrate your skills in the format best suited for your personal goals.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on key principles of course design and the identify the impact these principles have on the student experience
Critically evaluate course or curriculum models and course design processes

title: Courts and Judges
syllabus_overview:
This subject will deepen your understanding of courts as a system of dispute resolution in civil and criminal matters by examining their structures, personnel, and core values. You will focus primarily on the Australian judicial system but use comparative examples to identify alternative organising principles and models of regulation. You will gain an appreciation of the interplay of values that underpin courts in liberal democracies, including judicial independence, impartiality, efficiency, accountability, and access to justice. Your learning in this subject will be informed by extensive sampling of the literature from different academic disciplines (eg law, political science, and history), case studies, group work, student-lead discussion and, when possible, guest lectures from past or present judicial officers. Assessment is focussed on continuous learning through regular quizzes, short answer questions, and class participation, supplemented by a research essay.

Teaching Strategies:
Strategy 1 Student preparation Extensive learning resources will be made available to students prior to class, including written materials, and questions and activities designed to guide reading. Students prepare for class by completing the assigned readings, considering the questions, and doing the activities. These test their understanding of the content of the readings. Strategy 2 Student Participation Seminar style classes are conducted in an interactive format. Student participation and engagement with the subject is encouraged by allocating responsibility for student-lead discussion, and by exploring, wherever possible, current and contemporary issues affecting the judicial system. Each student will be required to lead discussion in two seminars, namely, those for which they are also required to present written answers. Class discussions provide an opportunity for students to build on their independent study and critically explore, analyse and reflect on a range of relevant issues, as well as to develop and evaluate their own policy positions. Students will be able to gain valuable feedback from their colleagues and the teacher and at the same time develop their skills in critical analysis and evaluation. Strategy 3 Independent learning & skills acquisition through research Students achieve a sophisticated understanding of the judicial system by completing a research essay. By undertaking research into a specific area relevant to courts and judges, students are able to grasp and grapple with complex issues in the field, and make suggestions for reform. Strategy 4 Feedback to encourage critical reflection and self-improvement Learning develops in a rounded way with the benefit of ongoing feedback, which includes not only what needs attention but also how issues for attention might be addressed. Feedback comes from a variety of sources including from peers in the class who respond to a student’s contribution; the teacher in response to class contribution and written assignments; and a student’s own reflection on their work and participation. Subject Delivery 9 x 4-hour weekly seminars, delivered as 18 x 2-hour modules.
learning_outcomes: Construct and present clear, succinct, creative and persuasive written arguments relevant to the judicial system, which are substantiated by scholarship and research.
Demonstrate an advanced and integrated understanding of the structure and operation of the Australian judicial system in its legal, political, social and historical context.
Understand a range of methodological approaches to studying judicial systems in order to critically evaluate their legal, political, social and historical dimensions.

Conduct effective research by locating and synthesising multidisciplinary scholarship in order to analyse and critically evaluate institutions, policies, processes and laws that affect the operation of the judicial system.

title: Course Design and Assessment
syllabus_overview:
This subject enhances university teachers' ability to create effective higher education learning environments using the UTS model. You will apply constructive alignment principles to evaluate your students' learning context, determine teaching content, and assess the impact of various teaching methods. By aligning objectives with assessment, you will design a coherent series of activities for a chosen subject. The process involves exploring theory-based strategies to refine subject design and assess the efficacy of these choices, ultimately improving your teaching practice.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject uses an underlying philosophy of inquiry based learning and reflective practice. Subject participants are encouraged to reflect on their own teaching and learning context and developquestions or explore issues of importance to that context. Throughout the guided inquiry, subject participants are supported to find and share relevant resources to address their question or issue. Initial low stakes reflection on a subject outline offers opportunity to incorporate feedback into following assessment tasks. Face-to-face class time is highly interactive. Subject participants use classes to collaboratively workshop ideas for the design of subjects. They present ideas and issues in class and receive verbal feedback from peers and engage in conversations with peers around the literature on teaching and learning. Peer learning is also used via peer review of subject designs and regular conversations with participants from different disciplines on translating theoretical concepts in education to suit different contexts for learning. In some weeks, subject participants will be required to complete some pre-class activities which could include independent reading and online activities such as discussions, watching videos or other interactive tasks.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the design of a higher education subject to ensure alignment between the context for learning and intended outcomes;
Explain the design choices made by the subject designer by examining the educational and professional contexts affecting implementation of a subject;
Evaluate a subject design and suggest improvements consistent with the findings of the evaluation.
Describe the principles used in designing effective learning environments;

title: Create: Creating Interactive Multimedia Objects
syllabus_overview:
Are you curious about how to create engaging learning activities and environments? Understanding the theories of educational communication and instructional media is essential for designing effective learning activities and environments. This knowledge empowers you to create engaging and impactful educational experiences. This subject introduces you to the theories of educational communication and instructional media, exploring how these influence the design of learning activities and environments. You'll examine and critique examples of print, online, visual, and audio multimedia to understand their educational impact. You’ll design and develop your own interactive media object, such as an interactive learning activity, a screencast, an infographic, or something similar. You'll analyse, critique, and evaluate your design based on your understanding of learning theories. Additionally, you'll prepare and communicate a rationale for your interactive media object's design, ensuring it aligns with educational best practices and effectively engages learners.

Teaching Strategies:
Students engage in online or blended learning. There is a mix of group work activities and discussions, taking place both synchronously (in face to face sessions or online) and asynchronously. During these synchronous/ face to face sessions, there is an ‘expression session’ hosted by industry or other Learning Design professionals, and the opportunity for students to undertake online labs with specific Learning Designs and technologies. The learning management system (LMS) incorporates a range of other interactive activities, such as quizzes, multimedia presentations, short video and audio recordings and peer critiques. There is also regular formative assessment for students to track their progress.
learning_outcomes: Design and develop basic interactive media objects, taking into consideration accessible and contextual factors.
Analyse and critique interactive media elements and evaluate their effectiveness for learning.
Reflect and evaluate own and others’ learning and practice.
Prepare and communicate a compelling rationale for the design of an interactive media object.
Explain how instructional media and educational communication theories influence the design of learning activities and environments.

title: Creating Documentary
school: MAP and Sound and Music Design

This subject examines the theory and practice of documentary production. You will be introduced to the skills and techniques required for creating and critically analysing documentaries, including hybrid, animated and emerging non-fiction forms. Students receive formative feedback from the class lecturer and peers on in-class exercises and concept presentations relating to assessment items. title: Creating a Culture of Teaching and Learning in Healthcare
syllabus_overview:
Through a combination of applied and practical, action-based learning, this subject will enable you to empower yourself to become a change agent and innovator in your workplace in the teaching and learning context. You'll explore dynamic teaching and learning strategies, key change theories, and implementation strategies, developing the skills to lead and manage change, empower colleagues to actively engage in the spirit of inquiry, and foster a culture of educational excellence. Orientation week activities introduce the subject and peers, aiding assessment preparation. Weekly online resources, including readings and videos, support your learning journey and assessment success. Participation in Zoom meetings is crucial for collaborative learning and receiving formative feedback. A variety of feedback methods, including self and peer review, are designed to enhance your performance.

title: Creative Appeals in Advertising
syllabus_overview:
In this subject you will explore the appeals used in developing advertising messaging that is impactful and persuasive. You'll gain skills in identifying key attributes and articulating them through persuasive appeals, ensuring your message is both relevant and creatively expressed. Learning involves hands-on practice in message development, fostering a blend of analytical and creative thinking to enhance your marketing proficiency.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject introduces students to theories and practical frameworks that help practitioners to characterise the needs, wants and desires of a target audience as part of identifying the creative appeals to be used. This involves reviewing advertising campaign case studies, theoretical frameworks, and industry best practice reviews provided as pre-class activities, and using their interpretation of this content to inform discussion in class about the nuances of the appeals being used and the likely responses they will stimulate in the target audience. Discussion of the developing analysis for A1 will occur during the weekly seminars in the weeks before this assessment is due. This formative feedback will help students to focus and refine their analysis as they develop the report. Students also participate in creative workshops where they work collaboratively and apply appeals to a creative task to see the impact on the final ‘stimulus’ created.

title: Creating and Commercialising Ideas
syllabus_overview:
This subject is an elective option for postgraduate students, including the Entrepreneurial PhD. There is a lot we can learn from inventors, innovators and entrepreneurs who create change in the world. This subject takes students on a journey from developing an innovative idea towards a tangible outcome. Students start with generating ideas to solve a problem and learn a range of practical tools to refine and test their ideas – including rapid prototyping, user research and value proposition design. Students also get a deep understanding of how to bring their idea to the market. This subject is hands-on, dynamic and inspires entrepreneurial thinking.

This subject consists of six full days scheduled over 3 weeks, supplemented by online modules and activities. Learning will take place in a collaborative, immersive, experiential, studio‐based environment. Students will work with and receive feedback from peers, academics and professionals across a wide range of disciplines.

You'll learn to craft messages from a brand's attributes and unique elements, ensuring they offer clear benefits to the target audience. title: Creating Documentary
school: MAP and Sound and Music Design
syllabus_overview:
This subject examines the theory and practice of documentary production. You will be introduced to the skills and techniques required for creating and critically analysing documentaries, including hybrid, animated and emerging non-fiction forms. In this subject you will engage in sound and moving image exercises, culminating in the production of short documentary films. Throughout the subject narrative strategies, stylistic techniques and ethical considerations associated with documentary production will be a key focus and you will be encouraged to explore innovative approaches to the creative treatment of actuality.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject is delivered through engagement with online pre-class preparation materials, lectures, campus seminars, workshops and collaborative group activities. The online content provides theoretical, conceptual and practical contexts to enhance and support learning outcomes of seminar and activity-based work. The seminars are the venue for discussion, critique, short presentations and in-class exercises used to develop craft skills and strategies for working effectively in small collaborative groups on documentary productions. You will receive formative feedback from the class lecturer and peers on in-class exercises and concept presentations relating to assessment items. The subject has workshops facilitated by MediaLab which introduce new technical and software skills.

Describe and apply different techniques, approaches and forms of the documentary
Create and reflect on documentary work demonstrating creative and professional production skills
Analyse documentary films critically

title: Creative Arts 1: Visual Art
syllabus_overview:
This subject uses the NSW K-6 Visual Art syllabus to equip student teachers with the knowledge and creative skills needed to teach Visual Art at the primary level. It underscores the importance of art education and aims to boost your confidence in teaching art. You'll participate in weekly studio workshops to practice artistic techniques across various mediums. Concurrently, the course covers significant artists and art movements, introducing key concepts in art appreciation and critical analysis. You'll apply this knowledge by designing primary art programs and engaging in practical sessions and discussions. Reflection on your learning and teaching experiences related to the NSW K–6 Creative Arts: Visual Art syllabus is an integral part of the course.

Teaching Strategies:
A range of activities will be used to enable pedagogical and creative learning, including lectures, discussions, studio artmaking workshops and peer review practices. Lectures will focus on the methods and principles of primary visual art education as outlined in the NSW Creative Arts 1: Visual Art curriculum K-6. They will build student teachers’ knowledge of art by surveying key artworks, artists and art concepts from selected periods in art history and in contemporary art. Student teachers will participate in a studio art program, developing competency in a range of visual art media. Lectures and studio sessions will foster student teachers’ ability to create engaging art sessions around the needs of primary students at all levels. Students will be encouraged to reflect on their teaching practices and to be aware of research and thinking around primary art education. Students will experience art in a gallery setting and learn how to utilise cultural resources such as galleries, museums and their websites as well as other online and offline resources.

This subject develops student knowledge and understanding of the K–6 creative arts strands of music and dance. Students focus on specific musical and dance skills and techniques, and the pedagogical underpinnings of approaches to teaching in the creative arts. title: Creative Audio Programming
school: MAP and Sound and Music Design
syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces you to the principles of sound creation and composition using electronic and digital processes. It provides you with a foundation for computational approaches to sound manipulation enabling you to explore innovative approaches to sound synthesis, interactive systems, algorithmic and data-driven sound composition. You will investigate issues and current practices at the intersection of art, music and sound design, providing a context for you to develop your own creative sound works within the subject.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject is delivered through a combination of lectures, lab-based tutorials and weekly online modules. Lectures will incorporate a range of teaching and learning strategies including short presentations, videos, demonstrations, discussion of readings and listening lists, case studies and student group work. Lab-based tutorials offer hands-on tuition in which students work in small teams to sequentially develop their own creative work and engage in group sound-making activities. Weekly online quizzes help students engage in online materials, maintain progress and offer opportunities for feedback on learning. Assessment tasks promote cumulative skills development, integration of sound design and composition theory, and refinement of the final composition. The subject focuses on the music programming using the dataflow programming paradigm.
learning_outcomes: Relate technical and compositional concepts from historical and contemporary sound practice to new works
Design, plan, and realise digital music and sound design projects
Employ the language and concepts of electronic music production to identify and describe technical processes
Apply computational approaches to creative audio practice
Create novel sound compositions using dataflow programming

title: Creative Code
syllabus_overview:
This subject immerses you in the digital realm of design, where understanding interaction and expression through code is crucial. You'll learn to use code to create, read, manipulate, and display digital data, resulting in dynamic designs. By observing, making, and experimenting, you'll explore new expressive possibilities like generative graphics and interactive structures. The core theories and skills you acquire lay the groundwork for further study. You'll use P5.js, an open-source programming environment, to enhance your coding proficiency and bring your concepts to life.

Teaching Strategies:
Studio sessions will give you the opportunity to discuss questions about the weekly topic/content with your peers and with an expert studio leader, to collaborate on activities directly relevant to key ideas and to develop your skills as a design practitioner with assistance from your studio leader. Studio sessions will provide you with the opportunity to take ownership of the ideas encountered in preparatory reading, research and the lectures. Your studio leader will facilitate discussion and offer expert insight and direction where needed, but as students you are primarily responsible for the mood of the studio session. This can be a challenging subject as you will be presented with technically oriented material and an approach to thinking about design processes and outcomes that you may have not experienced before. Experimenting throughout the week is integral to developing your understanding of the material covered within studio sessions. This experimentation will be documented through your code diary. This may include thinking or working on material discussed in studio, working through textbook or online tutorials, or playing with your own code or examples from books or others peoples code to generate different outcomes. Exploration & curiosity is encouraged and there is an expectation that students will take an increasing level of responsibility for their ability to learn according to the demands of their own projects and its requirements. Feedback is given in studio sessions by the studio leader, but also in group discussion format. Some written feedback will be given in ReView, but feedback is primarily delivered face-to-face. It is the student's responsibility to make a record of feedback that has been delivered so that it can be accessed for the development of their work. Subject materials are delivered through Canvas and in the program of this subject outline.
learning_outcomes: Understand and apply design fundamentals and sensitivity to visual language within the design constraints and affordances of digital technologies
Have the capacity to document and reflect on process and outcomes
Demonstrate a basic understanding of the fundamentals and possibilities of the digital and code as a creative medium and the ability to apply this knowledge to creative projects
Demonstrate an introductory level understanding of programming fundamentals and problem-solving skills relevant to the design and realisation of code-based designs
Create simple generative and/or interactive works using code that successfully communicate concepts and ideas

title: Creative Coding
syllabus_overview:
This subject allows you to develop your conceptual and practical understanding of the key themes of code, data and algorithms within the context of designing and building a creative code prototype. It will advance your code and data literacy to enable you to communicate with programmers and technical teams in multidisciplinary environments. Conceptually, you will explore code, data and algorithms from historical and social viewpoints, alongside a variety of digital media contexts. You will develop a practical understanding of code, data and algorithms, through a process of 'learning by design' as you prototype your chosen creative code project. As you build your project, you will collaborate with peers to deepen your communication and literacy skills. You will critically reflect on your learning experience and demonstrate the development of your code and data literacy.

Teaching Strategies:
Face-to-face classes incorporate a range of teaching and learning strategies including case study analysis, presentations, hands-on coding activities and collaborative prototype development. These are complemented by preparatory work prior to attending classes using online resources such as websites and videos, and online technical skill development for certain software using digital resources. Initial classes introduce students to basic coding concepts through practical activities for a variety of coding environments which they can then choose from to create their prototype. As the subject progresses, more time is afforded to prototype development and code creation as they begin to iterate their prototype. Students receive formative and summative feedback throughout the semester, including from early weeks. Students are provided with formative feedback during classes as their prototypes are developed and become more advanced. Feedback guides both conceptual and technical improvements to their creative code prototype as a result of in-class project demonstrations and user testing. Students receive summative feedback in response to their submitted assessment items that is focused on assessment outcomes. Summative feedback may also provide information on specific aspects of the submitted assessment, strategies for improvement, advancements of strengths, and notable aspects of work. It is provided in written form and will be published along with grades.
learning_outcomes: Plan, design and build a creative code prototype
Develop fundamental code and data literacy including from historical and social contexts
Collaborate effectively with peers
Engage in self-reflective professional development
Communicate and articulate code concepts within the context of a creative code prototype

title: Creative Entrepreneurship

This subject equips you with entrepreneurial skills to create and assess business proposals that align with your talents and market trends. You'll learn collaborative project management and how to refine ideas through feedback. title: Creative Media Critical Contexts
school: MAP and Sound and Music Design
syllabus_overview:
This subject offers an introduction to the theoretical underpinnings, sector debates and broader contexts of media art. You will have the opportunity to examine the diverse forms and contexts of contemporary media art as you develop critical thinking skills in response to non-traditional media art works. You will explore the relationship between form, content, and context in media art and gain an understanding of the evolving curatorial and exhibition factors that impact the production of experimental media. You will apply critical frameworks to the evaluation and interpretation of contemporary works through field trips to view media art exhibitions, gaining a deeper understanding of professional artistic practices. Close analysis of current media art projects enables you to better discern the concerns and real-world issues at play in realising artistic concepts. You will then go on to develop strategies for applying innovative approaches and techniques developed by diverse media artists and curators to your own creative practice projects.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject is designed in a modular format, allowing academics from media arts, animation, and music and sound design to contribute content from their areas of expertise and research interest. This interdisciplinary approach fosters a rich learning environment and reflects the increasingly collaborative nature of contemporary art practices. The subject learning activities consist of regular face-to-face lectures and tutorials as well as field trips to relevant galleries and exhibitions. You will be required to engage with reading, viewing and listening material in preparation for lectures and tutorial discussions. Opportunities for formative feedback on plans for assessment tasks are afforded through tutorial discussions with peers and the class tutor. title: Creative Nonfiction Workshop
syllabus_overview:
Creative nonfiction exists at the crossroads of the factual, the personal and the imagined. In this practice-based subject, students write sustained creative work as they explore this popular and growing area of international publishing. Students consider the forms, possibilities, ethics and debt to fact of creative nonfiction. Students analyse and practise key techniques of sentence craft, voice and close observation. Students workshop their drafts into a creative work ready for pitching or submission.

Teaching Strategies:
Face-to-face classes incorporate a range of teaching and learning strategies, including discussion of lectures and set texts, in-class writing exercises that simulate selected genres and key techniques, and collaborative group work (workshopping in-class writing exercises and work-in-progress). Asynchronous recorded lectures and readings accessed via the subject site and the UTS Library supplement classes and provide students with the materials for independent class preparation. Workshopping of writing exercises and drafts of work in progress during class ensure there are opportunities for formative feedback before census date and throughout the session. Students are able to participate in online workshop discussion groups. Summative feedback is delivered via authentic assessment of assignments, which are designed to meet industry expectations.
learning_outcomes: Develop students’ own critical voice to reflect on their creative practice or the work of others.
Critically assess key theoretical or formal developments in the practices of creative nonfiction or adjacent genres.
Identify and evaluate a range of nonfiction genres and techniques and apply them appropriately to students’ chosen subject matter, audience and context.
Demonstrate advanced skills in navigating and applying the diverse formal and ethical possibilities of creative nonfiction, including its debt to the ‘real’.
Initiate, plan and compose a sustained and coherent creative work, applying the specialist techniques and skills of creative nonfiction.

title: Creative Practices and Methods
syllabus_overview:
In this subject, participants explore creative practices and tools from across many professional domains to generate, discover and explore new ideas, insights and solutions (as well as uncover blind spots). Participants are encouraged to cultivate a culture of curiosity, experimentation, playfulness and inventiveness as they develop their research, sensemaking and creative practices, and hone their ways of communicating concepts and ideas effectively. While creativity is instinctual, this subject also examines cutting edge insights drawn from fields such as neuroscience to inform and fortify the creative capability of both individuals and collectives.

Teaching Strategies:
This Key Enabling Methodology (KEM) subject is offered online and supported by face-to-face sessions. Participants explore emerging cutting-edge approaches and methodologies for investigating and creatively responding to complex real-world challenges. Participants also draw on their experiences in professional fields and organisational contexts to reflect on ways that these new approaches could enable them to innovate in practice. By doing so, participants develop a repertoire of approaches that can be strategically applied in their professional contexts. Through reflective tasks participants develop their creative intelligence – including professional judgement about how these approaches can generate innovation in real-world contexts.

In this introductory subject, you'll engage in a collaborative project addressing a real-world challenge, experiencing transdisciplinary innovation and complex thinking firsthand. You'll gain insights into the innovation ecosystem and the workings of transdisciplinary innovation. This practical experience will help you tailor your approach to Creative Intelligence and Strategic Innovation, guiding your journey through the program.

Participants undertake self-paced online study to examine selected cases of innovation that cut across disciplines, industries and sectors. They come together live online for six face-to-face sessions. These sessions immerses them in interactive learning with professional colleagues and academic staff (including ongoing feedback) and further hands-on engagement with concepts, frameworks and methods. Participants are supported to put their preliminary understandings of transdisciplinary innovation to practice by engaging in a short and experimental collaborative project within their professional cohort. Through guided conversation, including with their organisations, participants set their personal learning plans and chart a pathway through the program.
learning_outcomes: Examine real-world problem situations and the practices in play as complex systems
Question the assumptions that guide thinking and actions in professional practice by using a range of perspectives and frames

title: Creative Practice and Methods
syllabus_overview:
Creativity is consistently listed as a key 21st-century capability in that it allows us to view, understand and respond to challenges in new and more open ways. In this subject you'll explore the role creativity plays in the innovation process and discover your potential as a creative, transdisciplinary change-maker. You will examine what creativity is, and explore creative practice, process and methods from a variety of perspectives. You will learn how to remix and reimagine existing practice, applying new approaches to design your own creative method. You will apply these skills by collaboratively devising and leading your own innovation process in response to a complex challenge set by an external partner.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject uses problem-based learning strategies that involves students in researching and developing their own / group solutions to complex problems / scenarios. Learning takes place in a collaborative, immersive, experiential, studio-based environment. In each studio session students receive feedback and reflection from academics and industry professionals, whilst continuing to work on the problems / projects they are preparing and completing outside studio session times.
learning_outcomes: Develop and lead innovation processes that draw on and justify the application of diverse methods.
Create, apply and evaluate creative methods and approaches to investigate complex issues.
Communicate ideas in professional contexts using appropriate and creative strategies.
Reflect on and communicate insights about creativity in relation to self, others, and learning experiences.
Collaborate effectively in interdisciplinary teams to meet shared objectives and make appropriate decisions.

title: Creative Problem Solving
syllabus_overview:
This subject teaches you to navigate organisational challenges, disruptions, and opportunities. You'll learn industry-recognised tools for problem identification and analysis, and explore solutions using both divergent and convergent thinking. The subject emphasises change management strategies for implementing solutions with lasting positive effects, providing foundational skills for managing change within and between organisations, from spotting issues to developing creative solutions and impactful execution.

Teaching Strategies:
The teaching and learning strategies used in this subject promote the development and use of different approaches such as analytical, critical and creative thinking. The teaching and learning strategies are designed to enable students to make progress in their achievement and maximise their accomplishment of the learning outcomes. Students engage in the essential content through lectures, seminar-style discussions, case studies, group work and student-led dialogue through face-to-face and online collaboration. Students are expected to complete all allocated activities and readings, which will be available on the learning management system for each lesson before attending class. Completing activities and readings before class allows for in-class time to be spent on collaborative discussions that address interesting and challenging aspects of the material, and enable students to be creative in their approach to identifying and creating possible solutions to problems, disruptions and opportunities. Formative feedback exercises used during tutorials prepare and assist students with assessments. For example, students will be required to share and explain the tools and methods used to analyse problems and create solutions. The exercises aim to help students identify their strengths and weaknesses and target areas that need work. The practice case study exercises help tutors recognise where students are struggling and address problems immediately through individual and collective class feedback. Summative feedback provided to students for formally composed submissions such as the individual case study assessment (Task 1). The goal of the summative feedback is to evaluate student learning by comparing it against the prescribed assessment criteria.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate creativity and creative problem solving in the contemporary business environment
Make judgments and provide an appropriate technically feasible and economically viable implementation plan for the proposed solution
Assess and apply appropriate tools, methods, and frameworks to generate possible solutions
Analyse problems, disruptions, and opportunities for change and improvement

title: Creative Producing

syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces you to concepts, strategies and practices of content creation in established and emerging screen environments, enhancing your understanding of the creative producer's role in both domestic and global media landscapes. You'll hone your ability to initiate concepts and stories, and translate these into tangible media arts projects, both individually and collaboratively. Your skill set will expand to include creativity techniques, story development, pitching, financial sourcing, budgeting, scheduling, and navigating marketing, distribution, and legalities. You will also learn to foster ethical practices, build strategic partnerships, and adopt innovative methods in project development and distribution, preparing you for a dynamic career in media production. Learning is hands-on, blending theoretical insights with practical application to ensure a comprehensive grasp of content creation.

The subject explores key issues and concerns of producers. Weekly seminars incorporate a range of teaching and learning strategies, including lectures, short presentations, case studies and project-based learning. Collaborative in-class exercises embed oral, written, research and analytical skills relevant to each week’s topic. These skills are complemented by preparatory work using resources provided on the online subject site, and out of class project development activities. Students are expected to regularly check and engage with subject materials on the online subject site to effectively manage their learning experience in this subject. Formative feedback will be provided in-class on projects and exercises, including before census date.

title: Creative Production and Citizenship
school: MAP and Sound and Music Design
syllabus_overview:
In this subject you will examine your identity as a creative citizen, assessing practices, policies and established protocols within your industry as you consider what it means to be an ethical producer of creative content. Topics covered include indigenous creative practitioners and practices, gender and cultural representation, collaboration, workplace culture, intellectual property, the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) and sustainable production. These topics will be applied to ‘real world’ situations using problem-solving exercises with an emphasis on creative play and collaboration.

You will prepare for each week by engaging on-line with short readings, video materials and discussion prompts. There will be regular on-campus lectures, and weekly seminars will explore the theoretical and practical means by which we produce and craft interdisciplinary media projects. Through in-class screenings, case study analysis, game play and group discussion you will develop critical thinking and practical skills which are then applied to the production of original media projects. Formative feedback from tutors is provided pre-census date through engagement in weekly classes. Feedback is also given on summative tasks, in-class, before submission.

Apply critical perspectives on evolving technological, cultural and workplace environments to originate and produce innovative creative media projects.

title: Creative Production and Entrepreneurship

syllabus_overview:
In this subject you will explore scenario-based models of working in a changing commercial creative field. By investigating contemporary transformations in creative industries and developing creative business proposals in collaboration with your fellow students, you will develop approaches to managing the demands of clients while staying fiscally solvent and producing creative work. Alongside this, you will develop skills in collaborative project management, the production of promotional materials, and refining your pitches in response to feedback.

Students collaborate in small groups on a creative enterprise of their own design that will test their creative and business vision. Student groups also pitch their work to a panel of experts who provide detailed and interactive feedback. Throughout the subject, students will be encouraged to undertake independent scholarly research around creative industries and reflect on their own creative and collaborative practices. Feedback is also given on summative tasks, in-class, before submission.

title: Creative Production: Sound and Moving Image
school: MAP and Sound and Music Design
syllabus_overview:
In this subject organised around learning through creative exploration, you will gain basic skills in image and sound content creation, gathering, mixing, editing, and collaborative work practices. In classes that combine animation, music and sound, and media arts students, you will engage with relevant theoretical frameworks, sound and moving image histories, and the work of key practitioners in the field. You will get hands-on experience making sound and video projects in response to a thematic prompt. You will reflect on and gain a better understanding of your working preferences and how to be an effective collaborator. Framing your own creative output within the broader community of practice, you will learn how to apply established sound and image standards, producing short creative media projects that demonstrate a solid understanding of contemporary and historical practices.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject is delivered through engagement with lectures, on campus tutorials, technical workshops and field trips. Lectures are presented by a cross-disciplinary team and provide a focus for examining the theoretical and historical foundations for sound, animation, film and video. Tutorials are the venue for discussion, critique and the development of projects. They are also the place for debriefing and giving feedback on work produced and are used to introduce technical and workshop activities. Formative feedback from tutors is provided pre-census date through engagement in weekly classes. Feedback is also given on summative tasks, in-class, before submission. A staged approach to submission of assessment tasks is applied where you are required to share your work in progress in advance of the final due date, giving you the opportunity to respond to formative feedback before final submission. The workshop support resources allow you to gain basic technical proficiency with audio and video capture through short academically directed activities. The subject incorporates a range of teaching and learning strategies including online resources, audio recordings, videos, practical exercises, discussion of media arts examples and student groupwork. These will be complemented by independent student viewing and listening. An aim of this subject is to help you develop academic and professional language and communication skills in order to succeed at university and in the workplace. To determine your current academic language proficiency, you are required to complete an online language screening task, OPELA (information available at About OPELA for Students ). If you receive a Basic grade for OPELA, you will be directed to a language development intensive during Stuvac. If you do not complete OPELA you will receive a sanction preventing access to view your subject results and transcript in My Student Admin .

Collaborate on a creative media arts project.
Reflect on your own creative collaboration profile and working preferences.

syllabus_overview:
Where do creative project ideas come from? And how do you take them from concepts into work that can be used to attract creative collaborators? In this subject you will engage in iterative project development activities like pitching, workshopping and table reads, to evolve an original idea into a detailed proposal for a short media arts project. Working on a suite of industry-standard pitch documents, you will articulate a clear creative vision, define your project’s target audience, and address any ethical implications and feasibility issues that may arise.

title: Creative Technologies
syllabus_overview:
This subject immerses you in innovative ways to interact with digital environments, focusing on emerging technologies for future design applications. You'll move beyond traditional computing interfaces to a wider, more informed engagement with technology. Learn to design immersive experiences with virtual and augmented reality, and create physical interfaces using various controllers and sensors. You're encouraged to critically evaluate contemporary media technologies and explore existing projects that utilise speculative technologies.

Teaching Strategies:
Studio sessions will combine discussions around critical engagement with technology, presentation and discussion of art and design examples in the field of physical computing, technical demonstration and hands-on practice in iterative physical computing design practice. Your studio leader will facilitate discussion and offer expert insight and direction where needed, but as students, you are primarily responsible for the mood of the studio session. Emphasis is placed on developing each student’s confidence in processing and refining ideas, moving from research and conception right through to the creation and presentation of a prototype. Students are expected to commit 9–12 hours per week to each 6-credit point subject. This includes the contact hours. The 6–9 hours remaining each week are for the completion of preparatory activities and assessment tasks. This subject involves opportunities for students to benefit from peer feedback. Students will engage in low stakes collaborative peer feedback throughout the sessions. Projects and exercises cover ways of identifying and balancing the many requirements of successful communication of information and ideas as well as enhancing technical skill. The program includes pre-work sections each week that describe what you need to do to prepare for and bring to lectures and tutorials. Learning activities variously engage students in secondary research, online discussion, peer-group critique on work in progress and presentations. At the end of each session, please read the Pre-work section for the next session. Pre-tutorial resources and subject materials are accessible via UTS Online. Students will have several opportunities to receive assessment feedback during the subject. The feedback provided will vary in form, purpose and in its degree of formality: Formative feedback will be provided during the learning process, typically provided verbally by the subject's teaching staff. It will address the content of work and a student's approach to learning, both in general and more specific ‘assessment orientated’ terms. It is designed to help students improve their performance in time for the submission of an assessment item. For this to occur students need to respond constructively to the feedback provided. This involves critically reflecting on advice given and in response altering the approach taken to a given assessment. Formative feedback may also, on occasion, be provided by other students. It is delivered informally, either in conversation during a tutorial or in the course of discussion at the scale of the whole class. It is the student’s responsibility to record any feedback given during meetings or studio sessions. Summative feedback is provided in written form with all assessed work. It is published along with indicative grades online at UTS ReView. Summative feedback focuses on assessment outcomes. It is used to indicate how successfully a student has performed in terms of specific assessment criteria.
learning_outcomes: Gain the technical skills to make and develop projects using of emerging technologies.
Identify, contextualise and analyse relevant works that demonstrate emerging and speculative technologies as expressive and communicative media
Understand and apply design principles and fundamentals within the design constraints and affordances of emerging and speculative technologies.
Research and plan a simple project for physical interaction with a virtual environment
Reflect on process and outcomes
Develop skills to produce an aesthetically resolved outcome and the ability to communicate ideas

title: Criminal Law and Procedure
syllabus_overview:
This subject examines the principles of criminal law and procedure by exploring specific criminal offences and defences, and aspects of police powers and prosecution. You will engage in both statutory interpretation and case law analysis. Criminal Law and Procedure is one of the subject requirements for admission as a legal practitioner in all Australian jurisdictions. Through seminar discussions, you will consider the aims of criminal justice, the broad factors that shape criminalisation and its particular impacts on First Nations people. You’ll develop legal problem-solving skills in interpreting factual scenarios, identifying relevant legal issues, and applying rules to the facts to formulate a sound legal position. These techniques provide a foundation for legal problem-solving in many other law subjects.

Teaching Strategies:
Strategy 1: Student preparation Students are expected to complete the prescribed Canvas module (reading, questions, exercises etc) prior to each class. The readings and exercises contained in the Canvas modules constitute the minimum, essential preparatory work to enable a thorough understanding of the topics covered in the course and to facilitate participation in class discussions. Students should take notes from these pre-class readings and exercises and outline preliminary answers to discussion questions and problem questions prior to class. These notes should assist with preparation and comprehension of the material in class and collaborative discussion and problem-solving exercises, and may then be augmented by any notes taken during or after the class. These notes should also be a useful foundation for examination summaries. Additionally, there may be self-learning modules which require students to undertake prescribed reading and/or exercises for certain topics which are not scheduled to be discussed in class. These topics complement the topics discussed in class, and are examined by students independently without instruction from the lecturer, although students are encouraged to ask questions or raise issues via the discussion board. Self-learning modules may also be assessed. Strategy 2: Interactive class discussions The interactive seminar format assists students to consolidate and develop the knowledge acquired through engagement with the pre-class modules. Seminar discussions encourage and develop students’ capacity for critical thinking and oral communication. The modules on Canvas contain discussion questions and problem questions for each class. Students are expected to engage with one another and their seminar leader in responding to these questions. This necessitates actively participating in class discussion through answering questions generally asked of the class and working on responses within designated small groups. The discussion questions generally relate to rules of criminal process, aspects of criminal liability, the elements of criminal offences, the decision and reasoning in specific cases, and critical commentary on the policy and development of such laws. The problem questions require students to respond to factual scenarios that raise legal issues and apply legal problem-solving skills to formulate legal advice. Strategy 3: Problem solving The ability to solve problems is an essential skill in lawyering. Problem solving involves interpreting facts, identifying and analysing legal issues, and applying relevant law to the facts. Students will practice these skills in seminars and pre-class activities to develop their capacity to identify legal issues arising from a factual scenario and apply relevant statutory and common law rules in criminal law to resolve those issues. Students gain relevant, practical skills in legal analysis, problem solving, and presenting legal advice. Students may be asked to suggest a response to the problem based on their own work prior to class, or be given the opportunity to examine the problem in class individually or collaboratively within small groups. Strategy 4: Feedback Class participation feedback: Students reflect on their class participation in an ungraded self-assessment form and, following this, are given feedback from their Seminar Leader on how they are performing relative to the assessment criteria for class participation. Students are expected to reflect on and action this feedback in order to further strengthen their class participation. A final mark for class participation will be released at the end of the session. Ongoing feedback: Students will have opportunities to develop and hone key legal skills during this subject. These skills include critical thinking, problem solving, statutory interpretation, and case analysis. Feedback on the development of these skills will be provided during seminars either individually, in groups, as a class, or in a combination of these. Students will also receive written feedback on their mid-semester assignment. This may be provided to students by means of a detailed marking guide posted upon return of the assignment papers, to each student through individual comments on marked papers, and/or by other appropriate means. This feedback will assist students to identify aspects of legal analysis, written expression and problem solving that need to be improved in preparation for the final examination. Each class offers students the opportunity to ask questions about any aspect of the material being discussed. Further, students are encouraged to utilise the Discussion Board to ask and answer others’ questions about the subject and its assessment, both generally about criminal law including recent or topical developments, or specifically about any of the topics being taught in class. The questions posted on the Discussion Boards will be accessible to all students, and students are encouraged to respond to their peers’ questions or comments. The teaching team will endeavour to respond to unanswered questions or correct mistakes in a timely way. Self-reflection feedback: The class participation self-reflection and feedback, weekly ungraded quizzes (see below), in-class discussions and exercises, and online discussion boards all allow students to receive timely and relevant feedback on their progress throughout the semester. Students are encouraged to use these sources of feedback to regularly self-assess their progress. Strategy 5: Quizzes Students are provided the opportunity to undertake ungraded online quizzes which provide ongoing, formative feedback on their understanding of criminal law and procedure at regular intervals during the session. Subject Delivery: This subject is delivered online and in person.
learning_outcomes: Explain the structure, rationale and principles of criminal law and procedure in New South Wales through interpretation of selected provisions of the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW), analysis of common law doctrines and rules, and engagement with critical commentary
Communicate clearly and succinctly using appropriate expression when responding to factual and legal problems and when using the terminology and concepts appropriate to criminal law and procedure

Formulate logical, reasoned, justifiable and persuasive arguments regarding the application of criminal law to factual problems, as well as the theoretical and policy issues surrounding the laws and their application
Interpret facts, identify and analyse legal issues and apply relevant law to the facts to resolve criminal law problems

Critically analyse the policy, development and application of criminal law and procedure, including evaluating the social, political and historical context in which the laws function, and their effects on society as a whole and disadvantaged groups in particular

syllabus_overview:
This subject offers a comprehensive look at media post-production, with an emphasis on editing and sound design. You'll explore the full spectrum of media production, from pre-production to post, including new workflows for innovative and spatial media. Through practical scenarios, you'll refine skills in data management, asset handling, and collaborative processes, covering everything from data wrangling to editorial tasks and final outputs. You'll also engage with cutting-edge production models and the technologies and challenges associated with multi-channel, immersive, and complex media projects, including augmented and virtual reality.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is structured to encourage students to learn through hands-on learning, experimentation and collaboration. The subject uses a studio model for media production activity where theory, practice, collaboration and reflection are integrated. Both making media and speaking to one’s own and other's media work will be a focus of the studio. To these ends, students will receive feedback at all key stages including early in the session. Face-to-face seminars include short presentations and case studies to introduce creative techniques in media production; and examine issues connected with low & micro-budget production. Students work through a series of small contained creative exercises to develop their skills and experience in micro-budget techniques. Face to face classes are complemented by independent student reading, out of class production activities and participation in online discussion and forums that help build understanding in micro-budget production in the context of industry, career and creative sustainability. Students develop the ability to evaluate their own and others’ production work through a reflective practice approach to learning, whereby ongoing individual and group production work will be integrated with and informed by theory, discussion and reflection on one’s own and other's creative processes. Throughout the process, the work produced will be viewed with the intention that the students reflect on and articulate their learning.

title: Crime Scene Investigation
syllabus_overview:
This subject deepens your understanding of forensic science principles at the crime scene, focusing on the concept of trace and its applications. You will develop practical skills in scene examination, with online learning materials on Canvas supplemented by hands-on sessions in the Crime Scene Simulation Facility. By integrating theoretical knowledge with practical experience, you will gain the foundational skills crucial to crime scene examination.

Teaching Strategies:
Asynchronous learning via Canvas: Announcements, assessment information, and mandatory subject materials and activities will be made available on Canvas. You will learn asynchronously through use of videos, activities and readings provided on Canvas. These materials introduce and explain key principles in crime scene investigation and relate the concepts to modern professional practice. Discussion Boards on Canvas also offer opportunities for questioning and clarification of the subject material. To develop a complete understanding of the content and make the most of the practical classes, it is strongly recommended that the online materials are completed prior to the practical classes. A Canvas module on careers within various forensic roles is also provided; these materials contribute to your understanding of professional practice and industry expectations of graduates. Practical classes: The practical classes will take place on campus in the Crime Scene Simulation Facility, where you will put into practice the knowledge gained from the Canvas materials, and consolidate how to conduct key practical techniques that are crucial to every Crime Scene Investigator. There will be formative feedback provided throughout the practical sessions, along with assessed practical classes, that lay the foundation for the more advanced crime scene subjects. This ensures that all forensic science students, regardless of their major, have a solid foundational understanding of crime scene investigation, given that this is the first stage in any forensic science investigation. You will work in groups to develop important practical skills that are highly sought-after by future employers, including an understanding of teamwork in a pressured environment. Attendance for the practical sessions and crime scenes is strongly recommended, and the completion of Canvas exercises delivered online is crucial before entering the laboratory sessions.

title: Crime Scene Investigation and Management

Students develop a deep understanding of crime scene management, learning to handle common scenarios, identify hazards, and process evidence in realistic settings. These workshops are not assessed and allow students to practice techniques in simulated crime scene environments, use equipment and ask questions. The final online workshop will deliver a tutorial-style learning experience whereby the students learn how to prepare and present a brief of evidence.

title: Criminal Justice in Action
syllabus_overview:
This subject provides a comprehensive and critical examination of the criminal justice system, focusing on its foundational principles, key actors, and processes. Students will explore criminal law alongside the operations of the criminal justice system and a range of professions and their professional practices. The subject examines punishment, rehabilitation, and public protection strategies, as well as comparative perspectives on criminal justice systems worldwide. Through an evidence-based and scientific lens, students will critically analyse contemporary challenges and innovations shaping criminal justice in the 21st century. This subject encourages informed and constructive engagement with the system, promoting balanced perspectives that support effective and just responses to crime, disorder and threats to public safety & security.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject adopts a blended learning approach designed to support active and engaged learning. Each week, students will complete a pre-recorded online lecture, which introduces key concepts, case studies, and practical examples. This is complemented by independent study activities and curated key readings that deepen understanding of weekly topics and promote evidence-based thinking. To reinforce learning and support critical engagement, students will also participate in a 1.5-hour face-to-face seminar each week. These seminars will provide opportunities for discussion, collaborative problem-solving, and the application of theoretical and legal knowledge to real-world criminal justice practice. The blended model ensures flexibility, while also fostering the analytical, communication, and professional skills necessary for work in the justice sector.
learning_outcomes: Explain the foundational concepts and structures of the criminal justice system and how they interact to address crime and maintain public safety.
Analyse key categories of crime and the legal frameworks governing their prosecution, including violent, sexual, acquisitive, and drug-related offenses.
Describe and compare international criminal justice systems, and explain emerging trends using a balanced, evidence-informed perspective on reform and policy.
Critically assess the role of law and justice in relation to Indigenous Australians and other marginalized groups within the criminal justice system.
Evaluate the processes and authority of law enforcement, courts, and sentencing practices, applying evidence-based approaches to their effectiveness and fairness.

title: Criminalistics
syllabus_overview:
This subject advances skills introduced in 65242 Principles of Forensic Science and complements learning in 65342 Crime Scene Investigation. In this subject, you will learn how to analyse, interpret and report on forensic traces including fingermarks, tool marks, shoe marks and biological materials. Through mock casework in the practicals and workshops, you will gain hands-on experience with decision making, processing, and interpreting forensic traces in the context of different case scenarios – key skills for a career in forensic science.

Teaching Strategies:
All learning materials, including recorded lectures, interactive support materials, additional multimedia and electronic copies of subject manuals can be found under Modules on Canvas. Detailed assessment task information is located under Assignments. Recorded lectures: There are 9 recorded lectures throughout the teaching session that students can watch in their own time during that week. The lectures provide students with the theoretical knowledge required to analyse, evaluate and interpret a variety of forensic traces, as well as introducing emerging techniques or concepts in forensic science. The topics discussed in these sessions provide the foundation for the workshops and practicals, where students apply their new knowledge. The lectures are broken into blocks of information, Q&A and application/activity. The lectures are supported by interactive online tools and summary modules in Canvas to give students an opportunity to revise and reflect on the learning materials in a student-led environment. Workshops: Six 2-hour workshops are scheduled during the teaching session. These workshops provide students with a smaller and supportive class environment to discuss and practise more difficult professional skills or concepts in collaborative groups and an opportunity to receive real-time feedback from peers and academic staff. Students are placed in charge of their own learning with a classroom focus on peer learning and application. Practicals: Practical sessions run for 3 hours and are scheduled for 9 of the 12 session weeks. The practicals allow students to gain experience with the analysis and interpretation of a variety of forensic traces in a collaborative professional setting. Teams of students are assigned simulated exhibits to examine over four 2-week periods. Early practicals focus on building foundational skill sincluding laboratory documentation, ACE-V and developing examination strategies. Students apply these skills to a mock case - from receipt of the items through to laboratory analysis, interpretation, and the preparation of an expert witness report - in the second half of the semester. These classes are student-led with one-on-one and group support provided by teaching and professional staff. Students are also encouraged to seek solutions to any issues they encounter in the laboratory or unusual results they obtain. The assessment for these cases is designed to introduce students to expert testimony formats and forensic interpretation. Self-directed learning support: Online learning modules, including quizzes and multimedia, that supplement the concepts learnt in face-to-face classes will be available on Canvas from week 1 onwards and can be accessed or revised at any point during the semester. This includes interactive revision modules on core skills required in the practicals that provide immediate feedback. Links to further reading, podcasts and vodcasts are also provided to students to expand their learning outside of the classroom.

Clearly communicate expert opinion to a lay audience in a variety of formats.
Describe the common types of forensic traces and the basic processes that lead to their creation.
