title: Media Law and Accountability
syllabus_overview:
This subject explores the legal and ethical boundaries of free speech and public communication across journalism, media, advertising, public relations, and digital platforms. You'll learn about both the limitations and protections in public discourse, critically assessing potential legal reforms affecting media and the internet. Key issues like privacy, data use, freedom of information, defamation, and copyright in a digital society are scrutinised through case studies and inquiry reports. You'll reflect on balancing ethical considerations with maintaining free speech and an open democracy.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject integrates legal concepts, practical skills and scholarly literature. Teaching strategies will incorporate interactive, collaborative learning through the use of online platforms and active learning activities in class time. The program will differ according to each week but it will broadly involve lectures, collaborative problem solving, reading, independent research in online and face-to-face contexts, pre-class online discussions, online polls, formative quizzes and peer-learning activities. Through these learning strategies, students will develop an understanding of the basics of media law in both a theoretical and practical sense.
learning_outcomes: Construct clear and persuasive scholarly analyses and arguments.
Examine, evaluate and explain key media laws and relevant ethical codes and critically assess proposals for reform.
Apply relevant laws and ethical frameworks to contemporary problems emerging from professional practice.
Apply relevant cultural protocols in professional practice.
Interpret a variety of legal and policy texts including judgements, legislation and explanatory memoranda.

title: Media Law
syllabus_overview:
This subject analyses and evaluates certain legal restrictions on free speech affecting the media. You will examine the law of defamation, contempt, vilification, censorship, counter-terrorism measures and privacy. The legal framework consists of a wide range of federal and state/territory laws, both legislation and common law. You’ll explore whether the law strikes an appropriate balance between free speech on the one hand and relevant competing interests on the other. You will learn from industry guests who are current practitioners to consider how they apply the law, and what might be involved if you choose to pursue a career as in-house counsel. You’ll also learn through in-depth consideration of some of the leading cases as well as the broader constitutional and policy context. This allows you to develop a coherent understanding of the nature, scope and application of current laws. You will identify emerging issues and challenges of regulating the media and free speech – notably, those posed by online communication – and evaluate proposals for reform. This is an essential subject for students who would like to work in a legal, regulatory, editorial or executive role in the media, and will benefit those interested in related communications roles across a range of industries.

Teaching Strategies:
Strategy 1: Student preparation and blended learning Students engage in independent study to develop, deepen and consolidate knowledge and understanding of relevant issues. Students are expected to read and engage with media and other sources to enable active participation and learning in seminars and lectures. To assist preparation, students can ask questions on Canvas and receive guidance from their peers and/or the teacher. Information provided in Canvas includes an outline of each topic with key issues and questions to be considered in class as well as information about seminar participation activities. The blending of offline and online preparation and learning will enhance student participation in the class discussions and promote further learning. The use of discussion board posts and critical reflections on other students’ posts will help guide students on the identification of legal issues that are relevant to this subject, including issues featured in the media throughout the subject, and will help develop their capacity to analyse these issues. Strategy 2: Participation in lectures and seminars The major component of each class will be seminar discussions on set topics based on readings that students have completed ahead of class. Seminars provide a key learning experience in this subject. Students participate in seminars by contributing to class discussions to facilitate in-depth critical analysis and evaluation of selected issues, testing of ideas and arguments, keeping up-to-date with media law developments as well as developing oral communication and collaborative skills. Each class will include some content delivered as a short lecture, and there may be additional lecture content posted online. Lectures introduce topics and assist students to navigate the complexities of media law and policy. Students participate in lectures by seeking clarification on complex concepts and by discussing selected contemporary issues which places the law in context. Strategy 3: Workshop with industry guests The subject includes a strong emphasis on the practical application of the law and, in particular, how restrictions on speech affect media organisations and other platforms used for the publication of news and information. An industry guest who is a current practitioner will (if available) present a workshop on a major topic covered in the subject (defamation or contempt). The objective of these sessions is to give students the opportunity to consider how practitioners apply the law, and what might be involved if they choose to pursue a career as in-house counsel. Subject Delivery: In general, face-to-face classes will be offered for each of the three-hour weekly sessions.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and evaluate a range of perspectives and opinions relating to the issues and challenges of regulating free speech and the media.
Construct clear, succinct, reasoned, justifiable and persuasive legal and scholarly analyses and arguments.
Examine, evaluate and explain key media laws, related principles and concepts and the broader theoretical, constitutional and policy contexts informing the regulation of the media and free speech.
Identify, analyse and apply relevant media laws and generate solutions to contemporary media law problems.

title: Medical Biotechnology
syllabus_overview:
This subject allows you to apply your scientific and molecular biology knowledge to the discovery and development of medical biotechnologies. You'll enhance your laboratory skills through cell culture techniques in the HIVE laboratory, exploring treatments for diseases like cancer and respiratory disease. Through practicals, workshops, and inquiry-based activities, you'll master experimental design, data analysis, and interpretation, contributing to biotechnology research projects. You'll also learn about the clinical translation and commercialisation of new discoveries. Assessments focus on developing research skills, literature critique, experimental planning, and scientific communication, including ethical considerations. You'll stay abreast of clinical needs and advanced technologies for biomarker and drug discovery, understanding the development of cell-based therapies, biologics, gene therapies, regenerative medicine, and drug repurposing. This equips you with the expertise to innovate in medical biotechnology research.

Teaching Strategies:
Medical Biotechnology is delivered using a combination of online self-directed learning, interactive workshops, laboratory practicals (group research project) and assessments. Introductory Workshop (1h) x 1 We will meet in Week 1 for a brief introduction to the subject and assessments. Workshops: In-person (2h) x 10 Face-to-face workshops will guide you through activities directly related to your research project and assessments so attendance is strongly encouraged. You will work collaboratively in a group to complete tasks using creative and conceptual thinking. Some workshops may require engagement with online materials on Canvas prior to class. Practicals: HIVE Superlab (3h) x 10 Practicals will take place for 3h in the HIVE each week for 10 weeks. You will plan, conduct and record experiments as a group, collaborating to complete a cell-based research project together. Assessments : The assessments will be developed over a number of weeks through laboratory-based work, inquiry-based learning, critical literature appraisal and application of learnt concepts. These assessments will empower you to think creatively and solve a clinical problem, apply findings or address knowledge gap. The findings will be communicated through oral and written scientific reports suitable for a range of audiences. Feedback will be provided verbally during workshops from both peers and facilitators. Written feedback will also be provided in relation to the assessments submitted.
learning_outcomes: Compare and describe clinical applications of different biotechnologies and methodologies in the medical field.
Critically analyse and effectively communicate experimental findings in the context of existing literature on the topic.
Develop laboratory-based and research skills in cell culture and in vitro models of disease.
Develop experimental plans to interrogate research questions based on ethical considerations and critical evaluation of relevant literature.
Foster creative thinking to identify knowledge gaps and meet clinical needs.

title: Medical Biotechnology Thesis 1
syllabus_overview:
The Master of Philosophy course provides advanced research training in life and environmental sciences, enhancing your skills and knowledge for a research career. Centred around a research project spanning two 24-credit-point sessions, you'll work closely with an academic supervisor to conduct research in your chosen area. You'll learn to formulate hypotheses, set objectives, manage time and resources, employ appropriate research methods, evaluate evidence critically, and construct detailed arguments. Under supervision, you'll analyse and interpret scientific data from your project. Your science communication skills will be honed through written works and oral presentations. The culmination of your work is a thesis, which is the primary assessment component of the course.

Teaching Strategies:
In the Master of Philosophy program, teaching and learning are anchored in each student’s individual research project. Early stages emphasise guided practice, with students supported to: Acquire essential laboratory and/or practical field-based skills through structured training with academics, research staff, and senior postgraduate mentors. Develop core research practices including risk management planning, project design, experimental methods, and ethical engagement. Strengthen academic communication by receiving and actioning constructive feedback on written and oral assessments, building competence in scientific writing, literature critique, and presentation. Engage in regular one‑on‑one meetings with supervisor to monitor progress, troubleshoot challenges, and refine approaches. Participate in targeted workshops that scaffold assessment completion and develop professional capabilities. As expertise grows, students are expected to assume greater ownership of their learning and progressively take increased responsibility for the direction and outcomes of their research. Independent Learning The program cultivates independence by encouraging students to: Submit drafts for timely feedback in line with negotiated deadlines. Provide regular updates on project progress and outcomes. Leverage online resources - scientific literature, webinars, tutorials - to solve project challenges, deepen disciplinary understanding, and select appropriate data analysis methods. Engage with CANVAS support materials, including the Honours/MPhil Program Manual, workshop resources, which complement supervisory mentorship on writing critical literature reviews, oral presentations, preparing a thesis, and broader research practices. Through these practices, students transition from guided learners to self‑directed researchers capable of critical inquiry and professional judgement. Research Group Participation and Collaborative Learning Master of Philosophy students are active contributors to their research groups, where collegiality and collaboration are central skills. This involves: Attending research team meetings to share updates, receive feedback, and engage in scholarly dialogue to enhance knowledge of the research area and troubleshoot experimental issues. Attending seminars and workshops to refine scientific communication and presentation skills, and to develop professional capabilities. Overall, the Master of Philosophy program is designed as a developmental journey - guiding students from structured mentorship to independent research, while embedding professional capabilities, critical thinking, and collaborative practice.
learning_outcomes: Develop a research plan and design suitable experiments to address an existing gap in disciplinary knowledge based on a review of existing literature.
Conduct independent research to generate new knowledge relating to a medical, environmental or biotechnology problem.
Critically situate research and professional capabilities within the current state of the field, articulating how the work contributes to, extends, or challenges existing knowledge.
Communicate research findings effectively in diverse contexts.
Collaborate effectively within a research team.

title: Medical Classics and the History of Chinese Medicine
syllabus_overview:
This subject delves into the history and classical texts of Chinese medicine, enhancing your understanding of its foundational theories and principles and their application in modern clinical practice. You'll examine the historical and geographical contexts of these seminal works, their place within the broader Chinese medicine literature, and their influence on contemporary therapeutic approaches.

Teaching Strategies:
This is an online subject with CANVAS as the primary platform for learning. The subject will consist of course notes to guide students in their study but also facilitate reading and self learning in the subject. Additionally a variety of multimedia materials is also provided to support study, including some lecture recordings and Ted-talk style topical presentations. The subject is split into two modules Module A: history and philosophy of Chinese Medicine as well as Module B: the study of specific classics, their history, impact and relevance today. Whilst these modules are separate, they do interconnect through their specific cultural and historical junctions. Feedback within this subject will come from a variety of forms. Topical quizzes which are low stakes individually, are embedded within the online learning and will provide students with immediate feedback regarding their learning as they progress through the material. Feedback will also be provided for their essay assessment. Discussion board will also allow for students to communicate with fellow students about concepts and material learnt, as well as receive and give feedback from peers and assessors.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the classical texts of Chinese medicine within the context of the evidence based practice framework.
Effectively communicate the theories and principles contained in the Chinese medical classics with reference to their historical placement.
Understand, interpret and discuss the key principles and theories within the primary classical texts of Chinese medicine and acupuncture.
Apply research skills to examine key features of the classical Chinese medicine literature and appraise them based on their historical context.
Critically appraise the relevance of classic Chinese medicine texts and their applications for contemporary clinical practice.

title: Medical Devices and Diagnostics
syllabus_overview: This postgraduate subject focuses on medical devices, delving into the scientific principles that underpin their use in medical practice. You will explore emerging technologies poised to influence the future of medical diagnosis and treatment. You'll cover diverse topics such as biomaterials, biomedical implants, technology for oligonucleotide detection, portable and microfluidic devices in medicine, point-of-care devices, clinical trials, and regulatory aspects including standards and ethical considerations. You will also examine the integration of devices into medical practice and their ethical, legal, social, cultural, and economic implications. You'll learn about the regulatory frameworks and classification systems for medical devices, alongside challenges in designing and conducting clinical trials.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the scope and role of medical devices and medical device industry in our health care system.
Assess the significance of regulatory processes for medical devices on a national and international level.
Synthesise and communicate complex scientific, technical and regulatory information in the medical device sector, including ethical, social, cultural and economic considerations.
Investigate the principal components of medical devices used in monitoring of physiological function, diagnosis and treatment.
Contextualise scientific principles related to physiological measurement and implantable technologies in industry scenarios.

title: Medical Devices: Regulatory and Quality Systems Requirements
syllabus_overview:
This subject equips you with an industry focused foundation in the growing Medical Device industry to broaden your skill base. Regulatory pathways and quality management systems for medical devices in the major global markets including US, EU and Australia will be studied using ISO 13485:2016 Medical Devices - Quality Management Systems, FDA 21 CFR Part 820 - Quality System Regulation and ISO 14971 Medical Devices - Application of Risk Management as the basis for the development of practical skills. You will test your developing skills by engaging in challenging assessments based on industry scenarios.

Teaching Strategies:
On campus (standard) mode: This subject will be delivered on the City campus and requires attendance for three hours of face-to-face contact per week, as well as approximately 1-3 hours of personal study pre-work before each class. The format and content of online classes (should they be required) will be equivalent to face to face on-campus classes and the same attendance requirements apply. Online (distance) mode: This subject is delivered online via Canvas. Students are required to contribute to weekly discussions as well as participate in occasional online meetings via zoom when required. Students should dedicate approximately 3-6 hours of time to this subject per week. Students will learn in this Subject through online content comprising videos, set reading, directed research, activities, online discussions and self-check quizzes. This independent learning will be supported by group learning experiences, in which ideas and concepts can be tested and refined Strategy 1: Student directed learning: Students read articles and use online resources, such as online course material, videos, directed research, activities, self-check quizzes and case studies, provided via Canvas. This learning prepares students for their participation in activities that may include facilitated discussion of fundamental concepts drawn from course materials and solutions to industry case studies, assessable quizzes or activities as well as collaborative and interactive learning experiences. Strategy 2: Collaborative and interactive learning experiences: Provide the students with the opportunity to engage with Peers and Academics to discuss and clarify concepts for a deeper understanding of online course materials. On campus students - engage in a weekly 3 hour workshop. Each workshop aims to apply online course materials to real life pharmaceutical industry scenarios through discussions and problem solving in collaboration with fellow students. Online students – engage in weekly discussion forums. Each online discussion aims to apply course material in real life pharmaceutical industry scenarios and collaboration with fellow students is required by posting and responding to other students posts in the discussion forum. Students participate in the online discussions by writing their comments in the Canvas platform in their own time and also read and respond to posts from peers. Each discussion has an end time designated by which students must have contributed. Strategy 3: Early and consistent feedback: Early feedback is provided prior to the census date. On campus students – receive feedback in workshops or via the Canvas platform for activities. Feedback regarding the quizzes is provided following each quiz, via provision of answers and/or in-class review. The collaborative learning approach utilised in class will enable ongoing feedback to be provided in class, as areas of learning need are identified through class discussions. Online students – receive feedback during ‘open office’ hours and discussion forums. Feedback regarding the self-check quizzes is provided via Canvas immediately upon submission of each quiz. The collaborative learning approach will enable ongoing feedback to be provided to students, via teacher responses to posts, as areas of learning need are identified through online discussions. Strategy 4: Group work: students work in groups during collaborative and interactive experiences. Students will need to coordinate group work, fostering negotiation, team building and teamwork skills. Students will need to demonstrate the ability to respond respectfully and constructively to their peers, fostering communication, constructive criticism and and respect for diverse ways of working. Strategy 5: Students are encouraged to critically reflect on their learning throughout the subject to identify areas where they may improve their performance and develop lifelong learning skills.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate compliance with regulatory requirements and recommend improvements.
Apply regulatory and risk management standards in medical device development and manufacturing.
Generate ideas and contributions within a group dynamic, demonstrating effective communication, feedback and collaboration.
Devise a comprehensive risk assessment for a medical device.

title: Medical Genetics and Genomics in Practice
syllabus_overview:
This subject equips you with the medical literacy needed to effectively convey complex genetic information, a vital skill for genetic counsellors. You'll gain a solid grasp of genetic concepts, inheritance patterns, genomics, and variant interpretation, alongside human development and genetic conditions. Through case studies, you'll learn to navigate medical assessments and diagnostic tools essential for genetic counselling. Additionally, you'll explore biomedical ethics and the delivery of genetic services, laying the groundwork for your clinical placement.

Teaching Strategies:
Preparation for Learning : Pre-work is undertaken on Canvas prior to weekly live and online workshops. Students will be provided with preparation activities each week, including readings, discussions, reflection questions, case studies and videos that prepare them for the live and online sessions. Please ensure that prep work is carried out prior to the live and online session so that you have spent time accessing and making sense of ideas. Attending the live and online workshops will allow you to test these ideas and get feedback from the academic staff and peers which will further consolidate your learning. Live and online workshops: Weekly live and online workshops provide students with opportunities to participate in discussion and problem-based learning activities. Guest lectures by experts in specific areas will occur during the weekly live and online workshops. The activities in the weekly workshops build on the prep work. Students will work in pairs, small groups and as a class during the workshops. Group discussions will often involve case-based learning activities. Students will participate in role play and learning activities to assist with the development of explanations of core concepts in preparation for clinical placement. Feedback will be provided by the teacher and by peers, using feedback models that will be provided. Block workshops: Students will attend a block, during which they will participate in workshops that will include problem-based learning activities, practice of core skills for genetic counsellors, and class and group discussions. When core skills are practised, the teacher will provide guidance on how feedback should be provided, so that students receive immediate feedback from peers and from the teacher. Research Integrated Learning: Taking an evidence-based approach to work with clients is an essential skill. Current research is integrated into content provided in prep work and workshops. Students are encouraged to seek out, read, discuss and utilise current research in medical genetics and genomics in the context of providing evidence-based care. Reflective Learning: Students are encouraged to critically reflect on their learning and their skill development throughout the subject, to identify areas where they may improve their performance, and to assist in the development of lifelong learning. Opportunities for reflection include the weekly reflective practice supervision groups that are part of 96105 Clinical and Community Placement 1. Ongoing feedback: Verbal feedback will be provided throughout the subject during block and live and online workshops. Opportunities for verbal formative feedback on assessment tasks are available prior to the due date and summative feedback is provided following final submission. Peer and staff feedback on the video assessment tasks will be provided.
learning_outcomes: Identify and apply ethical considerations in genetic counselling.
Interpret genetic information and pathology reports for use in genetic risk assessment and genetic counselling practice.
Use relevant databases and the genetics/genomics literature to inform practice.
Evaluate client comprehension and facilitate their understanding of genetic concepts in genetic counselling practice.

title: Medical Devices and Diagnostics
syllabus_overview: This subject looks at the science underlying medical devices used in clinical settings, as well as cutting-edge technologies poised to shape the future of medical diagnosis and treatment. You will explore a wide array of topics, including biomedical implants, diagnostic devices, biomaterials and biocompatibility within the body, microfluidic devices for medical applications, conducting clinical trials for medical devices, 3D bioprinting in healthcare, detecting oligonucleotides, portable and point-of-care devices, and the regulatory standards governing medical devices. Additionally, you'll examine the ethical, legal, social, cultural, and economic impacts of integrating these devices into medical practice. The course also introduces you to medical device regulatory frameworks and classification systems, while addressing challenges related to designing and executing clinical trials.
learning_outcomes: Identify the role of medical devices within the healthcare system and explain the regulatory environment.
Investigate the scientific principles behind implantable medical technologies.
Critically analyse and communicate complex scientific, technical and regulatory information in the medical device sector, including ethical, social, cultural and economic considerations.
Describe the key components and scientific principles of medical devices used in physiological function, diagnosis and treatment.

title: Medical Microbiology
syllabus_overview:
In this subject, you'll delve into medical microbiology, beginning with an overview of microbe classification and progressing to the role of microbiology in epidemiology and public health. The latter modules focus on bacteria and viruses, examining contemporary diagnostic tests and best practices for clinical disease identification.

Teaching Strategies:
This course is completed via the online learning environment of UTS CANVAS. Throughout the session, students will work their way through four independent, self-directed learning modules. All subject material will be delivered online. There are no practical classes or on-campus activities associated with this subject. Learning content will be delivered in dynamic formats and may include expert interviews, interactive activities, videos, lecture recordings, readings (including scientific research and technical literature), library tutorials, and other online media. There will be multiple small progress quizzes associated with each module and two assessment items to submit. There will be a scheduled time for all students to meet and converse with classmates and the subject facilitator via a weekly Zoom session. This is not a tutorial and will not automatically be recorded. Occasionally, guest speakers may be invited to give a talk at this time. It is an opportunity to touch base and participate in a collegiate scientific environment. Feedback will be provided to students through small formative self-guided tests and activities throughout each module and through the end of module quizzes. Students can also discuss their learning and assignment progress in live ZOOM classes and in discussion board in CANVAS.
learning_outcomes: Engage in critical thinking, research, and reflective practices to advance new understanding of microbiology.
Apply knowledge of microorganisms to evaluate diagnostic tests and inform health outcomes.
Communicate complex microbiology topics effectively to diverse audiences.
Demonstrate specialised knowledge related to microorganisms.
Articulate independent judgements across a range of microbiology related functions and contexts.

title: Medicinal Chemistry
syllabus_overview:
You will cover the drug discovery process, from lead compounds to clinical trials, highlighting the interdisciplinary essence of medicinal chemistry. You'll explore the chemical, pharmacological, and biological principles of drug development, learn about macromolecules involved in disease, and study drug synthesis, design, and the body's influence on drug efficacy. This will equip you with knowledge crucial for practicing medicinal chemistry.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject will be delivered through online and on-campus lectures, tutorials, and practical laboratory sessions Online lectures and resource material: 12 x 1 hour. Each week students will need to view online material in the form of recorded lectures or other online content (youtube videos etc). The material delivered here will be built upon during the on-campus activities. Integrated lectures and workshops: 12 x 2 hours on-campus with recordings available on Canvas. In these sessions there will be a mixture of lectures covering key concepts and problem solving exercises. Students will be expected to engage with pre-lecture material in Canvas. Questions and lectures will consolidate concepts learnt in the online material. Students will receive on-going feedback during the classes in the form of discussion of the solutions to quiz and tutorial questions both as a full class and in small student-led groups. Laboratory: 8 x 3 hour. Students will conduct a laboratory research project in groups that runs over 8 weeks. To successfully complete the research project students must familiarise themselves with the assigned pre-lab reading- this material will be used to design the first series of compounds. Consideration of ‘real-world’ issues such as price and commercial availability of regents is included in the project to give students an authentic experience of medicinal chemistry research. Throughout the project students will keep records in their laboratory notebooks that will be assessed at regular intervals during the lab sessions via written and verbal feedback. Students can incorporate this feedback into their final written report. In the laboratory sessions students are required to work in groups. Team work is a vital skill for a medicinal chemist, as all drug discovery requires a team of researchers. If you cannot attend a scheduled practical class, please contact your subject coordinator as soon as possible to discuss your situation.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate effectively within a team to manage and execute projects.
Demonstrate practical laboratory skills and record-keeping in medicinal chemistry.
Communicate scientific research effectively through various formats.
Apply fundamental principles of drug pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and computational molecular modelling to drug design.
Explain the role of clinical trials and intellectual property in drug development.

title: Medicine and Law
syllabus_overview:
This subject deals with the aspects of law relevant to healthcare, with a focus on the patient-practitioner relationship. You will consider intersecting legal, ethical and policy issues in the contemporary Australian context, with some international comparisons. Topics include: • legal foundations of the health care system; • health practitioner regulation; • negligence; • consent to treatment; • privacy and confidentiality of health information; •and law, ethical issues and the beginning and end of life. Discussions and collaboration provide an opportunity for you to critically explore and reflect on various perspectives on key concepts. You will also undertake independent research to create logical, justifiable and persuasive written and oral arguments.

Teaching Strategies:
Strategy 1: Student preparation . Students complete assigned readings and other preparatory activities prior to attending seminars. Students come to class ready to participate and engage in informed discussions. Strategy 2: Discussion and collaboration . Discussions and collaboration provide an opportunity for students to critically explore, analyse and reflect on the subject topics. Discussions include oral and written contributions. Strategy 3: Research . Students undertake independent research relevant to class discussion and assessment tasks. Students develop and refine skills in identifying and synthesising relevant material and deploy it to make reasoned, logical, justifiable and persuasive written and oral arguments. Strategy 4: Feedback . Students receive early and ongoing feedback on their preparation, discussion and collaboration. Students also receive individual feedback on formal assessment tasks.
learning_outcomes: Initiate and complete self-directed learning through engagement with materials to prepare for class discussion and activities.
Assess different legal and policy approaches to health law problems.
Apply legal principles to a range of health law problems, including elaborating on legal concepts learned in previous subjects;
Communicate effectively in writing and orally, demonstrating an ability to inform, analyse, report and persuade.
Conduct research on health law topics, including locating and critically analysing legal and health sources;

title: Memory and the Image
syllabus_overview:
You will explore how visual culture influences memory through image-based practices. This subject examines the complex yet contributory role of images in shaping personal and political narratives, storytelling, and autobiography. You'll delve into photographic theory, memory philosophies, and historiography, analysing diverse sources from family albums to public archives and manipulated photographs. The course also reveals techniques used by creatives to manipulate the interplay between image and memory, including photographic montage, archive remixing, the interplay of image and text, synthetic media, and interviews.

Teaching Strategies:
A weekly three-hour tutorial/workshop combining historical, theoretical and technical instruction to guide students in producing new written and photographic work that explores photography's relationship to memory. Each week students will be asked to familiarise themselves with a range of resources that relate to the topic; these are included in the program descriptions. They will then attend tutorials and workshops and must be prepared to ask questions, raise ideas and apply their understanding of the topic in a collaborative learning environment. Preparation in advance of workshops is crucial. Workshops will give students the opportunity to work with peers and tutor/mentors, to collaborate on projects directly relevant to the assessment items, and develop photographic skills in a practical context. Studio tutorials will provide students with the opportunity to take ownership of the ideas encountered in preparatory research. Tutor/mentors will help facilitate discussion and offer expert insight and direction where needed, but students are primarily responsible for the collaborative and participatory nature of the tutorial. They are also responsible for taking notes that record feedback. Outside of class time, students are expected to extend the enquiries made in the collaborative learning session with the independent development of their assessment projects. Students are supported in these projects by access to level 2 photo media facilities. Grades, marks and feedback on submitted tasks will be provided through Canvas. Semester-long subject, delivered through weekly lectures and tutorials, studio classes, group discussion and portfolio presentations.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a practical and conceptual strategies for working with photography in the field of memory studies.
Communicate ideas effectively in a variety of ways, including visual, written and oral.
Initiate and execute self-critique, critical thinking and design responses to memory related photographic work.
Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between photography and memory in current image based practice and photographic history and theory

title: Mergers and Acquisitions Law
syllabus_overview:
This subject examines the law relating to takeovers of public companies and publicly listed trusts. You’ll consider key issues relating to regulated acquisitions, acquiring a relevant interest prior to a takeover, disclosure of substantial shareholdings and defensive tactics. You will explore regulated industries such as telecommunications, broadcasting and financial services, as well as foreign investment rules relating to mergers and acquisitions. Your classes will be taught weekly through a combination of recorded lectures, seminars and discussions and small class group assignments. The assessment will culminate in an analysis of a current merger/acquisition from a number of facets. Mergers and acquisitions are inherently multi faceted and it is important to understand the processes and input by lawyers and non lawyer parties who take part in the process. Each class will involve both small and large group discussions analysing a range of hypothetical problem scenarios. You’ll present one case study to the class involving either a decided case or a practical case study based on a recent M&A transaction. The focus of this subject is to be as practical and real world focused as possible. Mergers and acquisitions are taking place regularly, providing us with many real life case studies to learn from.

Teaching Strategies:
Strategy 1 Class discussion on assigned topics Each class will involve both small and large group discussions and will be facilitated by the teacher. Topics will be set in advance and require students to read in advance of each class. There will be no formal lectures, but rather a seminar style discussion involving all members of the class. The classes will be taken weekly and we will build on our knowledge from previous weeks making advanced preparation by the students a key part of the subject. Strategy 2 Legal problem solving Each class will have a range of hypothetical problem scenarios for analysis and discussion. Strategy 3 Case study evaluations Students will be expected to present one case study to the class during the semester. This will involve either a decided case or a practical case study based on a recent M&A transaction. Strategy 4 Guest speaker presentations We will arrange for a guest presentation from a practicing lawyer who will share his experiences with you on a large scale acquisition, restructure and sale.
learning_outcomes: demonstrate an appreciation of the range of legal and commercial issues that shape the form and outcomes in mergers and acquisitions;
demonstrate the ability to apply the appropriate legal rules to a range of issues that commonly arise in mergers and acquisitions transactions;
apply appropriate research techniques to identify relevant legal and equitable rules to assist with advising on undertaking mergers and acquisitions.
demonstrate a sound understanding of the legal position of key participants in common mergers and acquisitions transactions;

title: Mentoring in the Workplace
syllabus_overview:
This subject enhances your ability to design and implement workplace mentoring a key organisational learning strategy.Engaging with contemporary research literature on mentoring in the workplace in a range of contexts, you will explore the issues involved in designing effective workplace mentoring programs. You will participate in a peer mentoring process throughout the subject, and have the opportunity to design a workplace mentoring program relevant to your own professional context

Teaching Strategies:
Students are guided through a series of six online modules using a process of practice-based learning. Each module contains rich content that is organised around a series of topics and includes activities that help students actively engage with the content and undertake the practice–based tasks. Students engage interactively through online discussion boards, embedded comments, and concept-based activities and are scaffolded to carry out the design of a mentoring program and to identify factors impacting on its implementation. This subject employs an authentic learning approach in which students design and develop a mentoring program based on their workplace, using models and practices introduced throughout the subject that students are encouraged to use in their own contexts. Students participate in collaborative activities and share observations and insights with peers from different professional contexts to expand their understanding of the concepts and practices used in this course. Students also engage in a peer mentoring process throughout the subject, in which they experience mentoring in a realistic setting. Synchronous online seminars provide an opportunity to revise key concepts, further develop connections with other students, and to prepare for assessments. Students receive formative feedback on assignment tasks both from their lecturers and peers, including early formative feedback. To ensure practice-relevant and authentic outcomes, teaching and learning strategies for this subject involve students customising learning to suit their professional practice context. This occurs through the ‘Capability Wrap’ process. Students develop a ‘Subject Learning Plan’ for each subject, as a way of customising assessments and their learning in the subject to their professional context. As a first step in this process, students must complete their ‘Course Learning Plan’ and Portfolio (Part A – (if this is the student’s first subject in the course) and their ‘subject learning plan’ (Part B), which are compulsory (non-graded) tasks and constitute minimum requirements for this subject. Students also complete a ‘subject wrap-up’ on conclusion of the subject by reflecting on their learning in relation to their course and subject learning plans. This also contributes to the ongoing ‘capability wrap’ process.
learning_outcomes: Identify key issues in designing and implementing workplace mentoring programs
Reflect on their practice as a workplace mentor
Design workplace mentoring programs
Analyse professional contexts with a focus on how particular issues and challenges, shape mentoring programs
Communicate using genres and technologies appropriate to the purpose

title: Mental Health Conditions and Psychological Wellbeing
syllabus_overview:
This subject is for students seeking to understand mental health conditions and interventions. You will critically evaluate historical perspectives and contemporary models of the development, classification, diagnosis, and treatment of mental health conditions, considering the influence of socio-cultural factors and scientific developments. Applying knowledge to case studies, you'll evaluate theoretical models and the evidence supporting various approaches to mental health and wellbeing, intervention, and service delivery.

Teaching Strategies:
Orientation activities Preparation for the session - You may be expected to undertake activities during orientation week. These activities are designed to introduce you to the subject and your peers and will assist you to prepare for the subject's assessment tasks. Lectures Each week, watch the lecture before attending the tutorial. Prep work Prep work is undertaken prior to tutorials. Prep work includes attending or viewing lectures. It can also include watching other videos, reading a blog entry/website/textbook chapter/journal article/magazine article and/or listening to a podcast/video/interview. Questions often accompany the prep work so students read with intent which encourages deep reading. Content covered in prep work is strongly linked to the content covered in lectures and tutorials. Please ensure prep work is carried out so that you have spent some time accessing and making sense of ideas. Attending the tutorials will allow you to test these ideas and get feedback from your teachers and peers which will further consolidate your learning. Your knowledge and understanding of the lectures and prep work will be tested and applied using quizzes, group discussions and practical activities in tutorials. Tutorials Tutorials are conducted in groups of up to 30. Content in classes often includes the practice of practical skills and further consolidation of information gained in the prep work. Activities are varied and require students to work alone, work in pairs or work in groups of 3 or more. Examples of these activities include short quizzes, short student-led presentations, group discussions where students reflect on what they have learnt in class and share this with the class. Group discussions often involve solving a problem or answering a question based on case studies or the content topic. All activities are facilitated by the teacher. Feedback is provided by the teacher where there is discrepancy in the knowledge and understanding of the content or disagreement in opinions between groups. Feedback can also be provided by peers. Teaching Much of the material that will be assessed is discussed during lectures and tutorials. Therefore, regular viewing of lectures and attendance at tutorials is necessary for optimal learning outcomes, and to ensure adequate preparation for assessment tasks. Failure to view lectures or attend tutorials is very likely to jeopardise your chances of passing or doing well in the subject. For this reason, attendance records will be kept. Students are regarded as responsible adult learners. Therefore, if you cannot attend a particular tutorial, it is your responsibility to catch up on material that you may have missed (e.g., by requesting to attend another tutorial, or organising to access a friend’s notes). Tutorials will not be conducted outside of scheduled times. For this reason, it is a good idea to set up a “buddy-system” with one or more other students in your tutorial, so that you can assist each other with notes and debriefing for missed tutorials. Independent learning activities Relevant readings, videos and activities will be made available online relevant to the topic of the week. This will support your ability to progress successfully throughout the subject and complete assessment items effectively. The online material aims to enhance your understanding of the topic or delve deeper into a more specific area, compare experiences and ideas with others and gain feedback. Information and links to all these learning activities can be accessed via Canvas as well as the subject outline. Feedback Feedback in this subject takes several forms including self-assessment, peer review, automatic feedback from interactive activities and from the teaching team. Formative feedback throughout the subject aims to increase your performance in summative assessments. Feedback and changes from previous subject offering We will be collecting feedback from you in several forms to evaluate the design and depth of the content and its delivery. We appreciate you taking part in this process to ensure we are delivering subjects that are contemporary and meet your needs.
learning_outcomes: Communicate ethical and/or social issues relevant to theoretical models of psychology.
Justify evidence-based mental health treatment options and/or service delivery.
Critique professional practice issues associated with the evolving discipline of psychology.
Apply knowledge and skills that are responsive to cultural diversity, including Indigenous Australians and Indigenous Australian contexts.
Demonstrate comprehensive knowledge of mental health conditions and interventions.

title: Method and Discovery
syllabus_overview:
Research is an active process with a defined method. In this research training subject students plan-out the research method and program for their thesis. They explore a range of research methods relevant to their topic. Students draw on peer insights and expertise, across disciplines and genres, to allow cross-fertilisation and re-conceptualisation. Research questions, aims and objectives direct the researcher to specific 'approaches' to research discovery, and entail associated ethical assumptions, including for Indigenous research, normative aims, collaborative possibilities and social and creative impact. The research process may centre on collecting and analysing information, or involve a creative intervention or initiative, or be focused on designing or producing new 'ways of doing'. Engagement with specific methods in the subject is shaped by their priorities and interests and is led by specialist academics in 'masterclass' format.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject uses both participatory and independent learning modes. These may involve sustained small-group and whole-class discussions, peer-led critique, scaffolded learning to develop independent project management skills, formal presentation of research to peers and advanced digital library research skills. Students meet face-to-face at the start of the subject and then participate in a weekly online workshop to explore theoretical concerns. Topic choice is driven by student interest and discussion is led by student presentations. In the second half of the subject students participate in a second more extended face-to-face workshop centred on Assignment 2. Students are required to engage actively with literature in preparation for seminars and as part of the assessment process. While there is an emphasis on independent work and inquiry, active student learning will be supported by early and ongoing feedback from both peers and instructors on performance in weekly class activities and through workshopping of assessment tasks. This is a pass/fail research training subject.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate relevant research skills necessary for developing a research plan
Design a feasible research plan
Evaluate and incorporate ethical dimensions of research practice into the research plan.
Identify and address methodological challenges;

title: Meta-Analysis Methods
syllabus_overview:
This subject provides an introduction to systematic reviews and meta-analysis. You will learn the statistical techniques for performing meta-analysis and address the common challenges that may arise with the methodology. By the end of the course, you will be equipped to carry out your own meta-analyses and effectively interpret the results from published studies using statistical computational software.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject is taught via interactive workshops comprising in-depth case discussions, exercises involving analysis of datasets, and group work collaboration. You are expected to engage with the materials provided on the UTS Learning Management System (e.g., cases, other readings) before each of the workshops. The workshops will include time where you will work together in peer-led discussions of the cases and exercises with the provision of teacher and peer feedback. To allow in-depth discussion and work with the class materials, the course will be delivered in a block-mode format.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on the applicability of systematic reviews and meta-analysis methodology to a marketing context
Evaluate and adapt different statistical techniques used in meta-analysis to specific applications
Develop and implement meta-analysis research methods using statistical computational software

title: Metabolic and Other Clinical Conditions
syllabus_overview:
In this subject, you will consolidate and advance your knowledge of the anatomy and physiology of the endocrine and immune systems as well as normal and abnormal renal (kidney) and liver function. Here, you will also develop clinical, epidemiological, pathophysiological, and pathomechanical knowledge of metabolic, renal, and other clinical conditions (such as diabetes, obesity, metabolic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, and liver disease). You will also learn about gender-based conditions, autoimmune diseases, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Importantly, you will expand your practical skills in clinical assessment, exercise selection, prescription, delivery, progression, monitoring, modification, and case management, by adopting evidenced-informed practice and applying scientific knowledge as it pertains to these diverse range of clinical conditions. You will also gain an understanding of common barriers to exercise in these populations while developing evidence-based strategies to overcome these barriers.

Teaching Strategies:
Learning in this subject is designed to place you at the centre of the learning experience, in part through the use of a range of modes and activities. Four online modules will form the foundation of the subject, which will be complimented by adjacent face-to-face classes (tutorials and practicals) that will allow you to put your learnings into practice. The subject content will be delivered in the online platform Canvas. This will include discussion forums and other activities, allowing you to engage with the content and your peers, throughout the learning. These activities and discussions will also foster the development of self-discovery/self-directed learning skills, as well as critical thinking skills. They will challenge you to consider how you can apply learnt concepts to real world environments. In order to be prepared for the planned face-to-face-to-face classes, you are encouraged to engage with the content on at least a weekly basis. Content will remain available past the specific delivery week; however you will be expected to cover each module on a week-to-week basis. You will be required to communicate information and demonstrate your understanding in a variety of formats, including written and verbal forms. Assessment tasks are designed to enable you to demonstrate application of what you have learned, with individual feedback provided following each of the three assessment tasks.
learning_outcomes: Effectively and respectively communicate with clients and other relevant professionals that results in shared decision-making through collaborative and interprofessional practice for people with metabolic and other clinical conditions.

Apply, integrate, and adapt knowledge and skills of anatomy, pathophysiology, and pathomechanics of metabolic and other clinical conditions including the endocrine and immune systems, renal (kidney) function and liver function, as well as human immunodeficiency virus and autoimmune diseases.

Apply appropriate screening, risk management strategies, and behaviour change principles to safely create, prescribe, implement, and evaluate effective interventions for people with metabolic and other clinical conditions to optimise health outcomes.
Engage with ongoing personal and professional self-development and reflective practice as it pertains to metabolic and other clinical conditions.
Apply evidence-informed practice and professional decision-making to optimise person-centred care across metabolic and other clinical conditions.

title: Metabolic Biochemistry
syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces you to cellular metabolism and energy transfer mechanisms. It provides an overview of the main carbohydrate catabolic and anabolic pathways including glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, oxidative phosphorylation. It provides an understanding of nitrogen and fatty acid metabolism, and the metabolic specialisation of tissues. Additionally, you'll study cell signalling and hormonal regulation of homeostasis. This knowledge underpins further studies in biological and biomedical sciences, focusing on the principles of cellular reactions and their relevance to various cell types. The subject will also introduce you to the basic tools and methods of enzymatic biochemical experimentation.

Teaching Strategies:
Autumn: 11 x 1.5 hour online lectures Summer: 5 x 3 hour online lectures The lectures will provide you with the background knowledge necessary for understanding the biochemistry that underpins how our bodies convert the food we eat into energy and chemical compounds to maintain the thousands of processes that keep our bodies working. All lectures will be online. For lectures that are live/recorded, students will need to use their UTS login to access the Zoom lecture. All lectures will be recorded and posted on Canvas. 8 x 3-hour face to face laboratory practicals Practicals give you a chance to learn many of the techniques used that have helped us discover what we know of our bodies' chemistry. The techniques you will learn are commonly used in laboratories around the world, so it is important to get a good understanding through hands-on experience and practice. Practical demonstrators are available to provide feedback and to assist with laboratory skill development. All practical sessions will be held in the HIVE Building 2.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and report on laboratory data.
Apply logical thought, critical thinking and problem solving skills in a scientific context.
Demonstrate excellence in written scientific communication.
Evaluate and use information from different sources such as research and review articles, textbooks, catalogues and technical references.
Explain the major biochemical pathways in nature whereby organisms store and use energy.

title: Method and Discovery
school: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview:
Research is an active process with a defined method. In this research training subject you plan-out the research method and program for your thesis. You explore a range of research methods relevant to your topic. You draw on peer insights and expertise, across disciplines and genres, to allow cross-fertilisation and re-conceptualisation. Research questions, aims and objectives direct the researcher to specific 'approaches' to research discovery, and entail associated ethical assumptions, including for Indigenous research, normative aims, collaborative possibilities and social and creative impact. The research process may centre on collecting and analysing information, or involve a creative intervention or initiative, or be focused on designing or producing new 'ways of doing'. Engagement with specific methods in the subject is shaped by your priorities and interests and is led by specialist academics in 'masterclass' format.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject uses both participatory and independent learning modes. These may involve sustained small-group and whole-class discussions, peer-led critique, scaffolded learning to develop independent project management skills, formal presentation of research to peers and advanced digital library research skills. Students meet face-to-face at the start of the subject and then participate in a weekly online workshop to explore theoretical concerns. Topic choice is driven by student interest and discussion is led by student presentations. In the second half of the subject students participate in a second more extended face-to-face workshop centred on Assignment 2. Students are required to engage actively with literature in preparation for seminars and as part of the assessment process. While there is an emphasis on independent work and inquiry, active student learning will be supported by early and ongoing feedback from both peers and instructors on performance in weekly class activities and through workshopping of assessment tasks. This is a pass/fail research training subject.
learning_outcomes: Identify and address methodological challenges
Design a feasible research plan
Demonstrate relevant research skills necessary for developing a research plan
Evaluate and incorporate ethical dimensions of research practice into the research plan

title: Methods in Quantum Computing
syllabus_overview: This subject offers a structured introduction to quantum computing, a revolutionary technology poised to surpass traditional computing capabilities. You'll learn the fundamental principles, discover quantum algorithms, and acquire programming skills to develop software that leverages the extraordinary potential of quantum computers, preparing you for advancements expected in the near future.
learning_outcomes: Explain the advantages of quantum computing over classical computing. (D.1)
Evaluate the application of quantum computing technologies to known and unknown contexts. (D.1)
Analyse efficiency and complexity of quantum technologies. (D.1)

title: Microbiology Diagnosis
syllabus_overview:
Microbiology Diagnosis develops your ability to swiftly and accurately identify pathogens and determine effective treatments, crucial for preventing serious health outcomes and curbing infection spread. The subject offers hands-on diagnostic lab experience, utilising the latest technologies to diagnose infectious diseases and select appropriate antimicrobial therapies. Through interactive workshops and practical sessions in the HIVE Superlab, you'll engage in critical analysis and interpretation of real case studies, honing professional skills such as quality assurance and laboratory safety. These competencies are vital for careers in diagnostic labs and infectious disease research.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject will run over 12 weeks. The subject will be organised in modules and will be a mix of online workshops and face-to-face practicals and workshops. The schedule for each week will vary depending on the activities offered. A detailed timetable will be available in CANVAS. You will be expected to follow closely communication via CANVAS and UTS emails to ensure you know your weekly activities. Week 1: You will attend a 2h face-to-face Introductory activities session that will include revisions, laboratory safety and introduction to new tools. Details will be posted on CANVAS. During this session, the teaching staff will introduce you to the subject and its different modules. You will work in groups to use your prior knowledge to start acquiring essential information necessary for the successful completion of the subject. These activities will set the foundation of your learning in this subject. To complete this session, you will have access to online material on CANVAS. Online content There are no scheduled lectures. Part of the disciplinary knowledge is acquired through modules, including case studies and knowledge checks available in CANVAS. Each module is directly related to a practical session and a workshop. Your learning will involve studying this content on your own, at your own pace as the modules will be open ahead of time and will stay for the duration of the session; however, to help with your studies, it is recommended that you keep your learning synchronised between the CANVAS content, the workshops and the practicals within a module. Workshops : You will attend 2 types of workshops: 5x1h of online workshops in weeks 2, 3, 4, 9 and 11 and 5x2h of on campus workshops in weeks 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 . These sessions will prepare you for the practical sessions but will also be in the format of a Q&A session about content, review of case studies or presentations of topics such as automation in microbiology laboratories, the importance of quality controls or laboratory accreditation. You will learn about various pathogens and the diseases they cause at different sites of infection. You will discuss clinical cases obtained from real-life patients. You will have access to clinical and biological data and you will identify the pathogen and propose treatments. This will allow you to obtain immediate feedback during the discussions. You will also have the opportunity to learn about pathogens and diseases from experts in microbiology who will give you an up-to-date, enthusiastic and passionate overview of their work. During the 5x2h face-to-face workshops, you will work in collaborative spaces with the same group of students as in your practical classes. Practicals : Practicals will be delivered in the HIVE. You will work in groups of 6. In order to provide you with a diagnostic laboratory experience that mimics how a specimen is processed in the microbiology section of a pathology laboratory, your practicals will run for 2.5h over 3 consecutive days unless specified otherwise. Practicals will run in weeks 1, 3, 5, 9 and 11. The final practical exam will run during the final exam period. The final date will be published in CANVAS later in the session. You will learn about identification techniques and antimicrobial testing within a specific specimen obtained from various body sites (blood, sputum, stool, urine, genital etc), together with patient history. As part of your laboratory training, you will use an online practical manual (Class Notebook) to describe in detail the different methodologies to use and you will have access to online learning material to study before and after the class in the form of slides to read and online quizzes to perform. Before the census date, you will be given a formative quiz that will be corrected during the next class. At that time you will receive feedback. Independent learning activities: To help you understand key concepts, you will complete CANVAS formative quizzes at your own pace, but we recommend they are attempted outside prior to or after practical classes. You will have the opportunity to take these quizzes as many times as you want. These quizzes will be available on CANVAS and answers will be provided at a later time.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the decision-making process for conducting rapid identification tests on isolates and perform basic reading of results.

Distinguish among the different groups of anti-microbials (Indigenous knowledges, traditional methods and modern techniques), their methods of action and mechanisms of resistance, and interpret susceptibility tests.
Apply results from diagnostic laboratory testing to identify organisms and communicate results effectively to relevant stakeholders.
Comply with safety regulations and quality control processes to work effectively in a diagnostic laboratory setting.
Identify the major groups of microbes pathogenic to humans.

title: Microelectronics
syllabus_overview:
This subject will equip you to analyse and design microelectronic circuits and appreciate their application in communication systems and consumer electronics. You will learn about semiconductor physics, device characteristics of transistor and diodes, and apply this knowledge to circuit design. Through labs and projects, this subject will prepare you for advanced study or a career in the field of microelectronics.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is scheduled for 4 hours per week involving different types of activities to help students develop both their theoretical and practical knowledge through active and collaborative learning. Students build their technical knowledge and capability through a series of lecture videos/recordings, which are viewed before class so that related in-class quizzes and lab work can be successfully completed. A weekly online workshop supports students in understanding the technical content. Alongside the workshop, students attend weekly lab classes to engage with the practical development of microelectronics, and complete design project work. Students are strongly encouraged to attend workshops and lab sessions which are designed to complement each other in helping students develop both their theoretical knowledge and practical skills. Tutors provide feedback and guidance in these interactive sessions to help students improve and learn throughout the session. Assessment in this subject is very practical and hands-on, and is based around a series of circuit design projects of increasing difficulty that students complete throughout the subject. Formal assessments are predominantly based on lab activities, where students work according to detailed design specifications that are provided. Short quizzes are also conducted at stages throughout the subject to help students self-evaluate their own learning and identify areas where they can improve, which in turn will help improve their circuit design projects.
learning_outcomes: Design and simulate low-noise amplifiers using commercial semiconductor processes. (C.1)
Analyse passive and active circuits using circuit theories. (D.1)
Design and simulate passive filters, including both narrowband and wideband designs. (C.1)
Apply circuit theories to guide integrated circuit design. (D.1)

title: Microeconomics for Property
syllabus_overview:
In this core first-year subject for the Bachelor of Property Economics, you'll learn microeconomic principles and methods to analyse property markets. You'll study the fundamentals of demand, supply, pricing, elasticity, production, and costs, and their impact on the property industry. The course also examines market structures, competition, and market failures.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject is structured so that you will have access to weekly online lectures that guide you through the key concepts, leading you to complete self-paced guided activities such as practice quizzes and exercises. This preparation work will help you to participate in class, where the key concepts will be reviewed via tutorial activities. Completing the weekly online activities and undertaking class tasks will give you feedback on your learning at key points, and support your successful completion of the assessments. The set text for this subject is an ebook, Economics for Today, by Layton
learning_outcomes: Understand the essential principles of Microeconomics and their significance in the property industry.
Use Microeconomic theory to explain the pricing , output and efficiency outcomes across different market structures.

title: Microbudget Production
school: MAP and Sound and Music Design
syllabus_overview:
In this subject, you are introduced to the creative practices of microbudget screen production. Through historical and contemporary lenses, you will gain an understanding of the ways in which microbudget screen creators have pursued bold visions, critiqued industrial norms, and revitalised screen production. Following this example, you will explore the ethos and practices of microbudget production using fast, agile and flexible models, including for online and social media contexts. Throughout this subject you will be required to engage with innovative models of writing/producing, shooting and editing for a diverse range of platforms.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is delivered through live lectures, engagement with online content, practical studio sessions and technical workshops. Lectures and online materials contextualise the key concepts investigated in each of the studios and their corresponding modules. Studios are focused on techniques for microbudget screen content production. Workshops – both online and in-person – enable access to facilities and provide structured development of technical skills and capabilities. Microbudget screen content work in progress is presented in studio sessions, with formative feedback provided by peers and teaching staff. In the final weeks, you present iterative microbudget screen content for feedback before submitting final projects.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse microbudget practices and the resulting screen content projects
Perform micro crew roles for microbudget screen production
Collaboratively produce microbudget content that demonstrates technical proficiencies

title: Midwifery as Primary Healthcare: a Public Health Strategy
syllabus_overview:
This subject will contribute to your understanding of midwifery as a public health strategy situated in a woman-centred and primary healthcare framework. You will explore midwifery within a broad social context influenced by particular social, cultural, political, and economic environments. As a midwifery student you will be supported to appreciate the impact that social disadvantage and other vulnerabilities have on women and their families. The subject encourages critical examination of systems and practices designed to support and promote optimal health outcomes within the context of maternal and newborn health.

Teaching Strategies:
In this subject, students will participate in a range of teaching and learning strategies that are designed to encourage students to develop the necessary knowledge and skills to practice midwifery in a primary health care framework as part of a public health strategy ONLINE LEARNING ACTIVITIES Students access online learning resources including pre-class activities, podcasts, videos, professional and grey literature prior to attending face-to-face sessions. Online activities are then reviewed and discussed in class to share learning, experiences and reflections. STORIES AND SCENARIOS Stories and scenarios are used to help students explore health and wellbeing-related scenarios. Cases depict women and their families in a primary health care setting. Students use these scenarios to learn concepts, interpret information, form judgments and develop creative solutions. Students develop critical thinking through analysis, interpretation of and reflection on issues or situations. SIMULATED ROLE PLAYS Role play enables students to practise new skills learnt through theory and knowledge development. Scenarios from relevant situations are used to depict real life experiences in midwifery. Students interact, observe and provide feedback within the facilitated debriefing, and reflect on their own skills, values and experiences. COLLABORATIVE LEARNING ACTIVITIES The majority of the face-to-face time in this subject involves collaborative group activities and workshops. Staff support students to engage in content prior to attending class, and class time focuses on group learning and mentored activities to support learning. Small group activities develop students’ understanding of public health campaigns. PERSONAL, PROFESSIONAL AND EXPERT NARRATIVES Guest speakers provide students with personal and professional stories in relation to the subject content. Hearing stories from both a professional and personal perspective supports students to relate learning to real world situations.
learning_outcomes: In a simulated environment, demonstrate skills in specific aspects of midwifery as public health practice including smoking cessation, limiting weight gain, promotion of breastfeeding and health promotion.
Appraise midwifery as a public health strategy and identify aspects of practice that relate to public health.
Explain how the Australian health care system facilitates a framework of primary health care in relation to the provision of and access to midwifery care.
Illustrate the impact that social disadvantage and other vulnerabilities have on women’s ability to access safe and appropriate maternity care.

title: Microfluidics in Biology and Medicine
syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces you to Microfluidics, the precise control of fluids at a micro-scale, revolutionising point-of-care diagnostics and cell biology. You'll learn to manipulate biological materials and chemicals on this scale, constructing miniaturised devices like Lab-on-a-chips for applications such as cell separation and single cell analysis. Through educational videos and interactive virtual labs, you'll learn how to build functional microfluidic devices and explore the use of microfluidics in real-world medical and biological scenarios, preparing you for cutting-edge research and diagnostic work.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject will offer several different modes of curricular activities to enhance the student’s learning experience both individually and in groups. This will include face-to-face (or via Zoom) classes (~2 hr lecture), which will be complemented by independent learning activities (~2-4 hrs per week) including lab-based works, and interactive tutorial sessions (group activity). The subject will provide an interactive and hands-on learning experience: Interactive lecture tutorial components Computer-based laboratory sessions (instructor guided) Tutorial questions and laboratory projects designed to give further practice in the application of microfluidics theories and procedures
learning_outcomes: Formulate and apply prototyping and design methodologies to design and develop microfluidic technologies. (D.1)
Critically analyse and communicate disciplinary knowledge and practices to a wide range of audiences. (E.1)
Identify, and understand microfluidic principles in the context of the medical industry and current research problems. (C.1)
