title: Reading the Law: Language, Power and Ideology
syllabus_overview:
This subject critically examines the relationship between law and language. The legal profession recognises the importance of language, particularly oratory skills, legal argument and reasoning. In many legal cases, there are issues of interpretation and ambiguity, such as in relation to the words in a conversation, a term in a contract or a provision in a statute. You will examine how legal players construct important concepts, such as consent, provocation, intention and 'the reasonable person'. You’ll compare key linguistic theories including sociolinguistics, critical discourse analysis and narrative theory to actively assess and critique legal texts. You will apply a nuanced understanding of each linguistic theory to explain how the law uses language to exercise power and create meaning. In seminar discussions you will engage with how the law is structured by class, gender, race and culture. You’ll explore how poor English-language skills may lead to disadvantage in the legal system and evaluate how language affects issues of justice, fairness and equality.

Teaching Strategies:
Strategy 1 Student preparation and self-directed learning Students will be required to read and critically evaluate prescribed texts prior to class, available in the subject folder via Canvas. Set readings may be accompanied by additional online materials that students will access before the seminars. Students’ preparatory reading will be guided by a series of critical discussion questions, available via Canvas, which will allow students to develop critical reading skills by reflecting on how a text is argued, what evidence is used to support the argument and how it reaches a conclusion. Students will receive feedback from the seminar leader, available in class or via Canvas, on their responses to discussion questions for the seminars. This will assist them in preparation for the research essay assessment item. Strategy 2 Seminar participation and facilitation In each seminar, students will be required to actively lead and contribute to class discussion. Seminars will be based on a series of prior questions, which students will be required to reflect upon and answer before class. Students will share their reflections on seminar topics and questions, and be required to respond to and debate with their peers’ views and interpretations either in small groups or in class discussion. Each student will be required to ‘co-facilitate’ one class seminar, together with another student and the seminar leader. This will involve initiating class discussion in relation to each discussion question, offering critical reflections on prescribed texts, and attempting to identify the themes addressed in that week’s seminar. Students will be required to conduct research to identify and synthesise at least one additional text relevant to their topic. This will assist them in developing research skills in preparation for the research essay assessment item. Students will be provided with feedback, available in class or via Canvas, on their seminar facilitation, communication skills and critical analysis in class and as part of their seminar participation mark. Students will be encouraged to take responsibility for their own learning by orally presenting and defending their own views and interpretations of the linguistic theories and methods discussed. Strategy 3 Collaborative learning Students will engage in collaborative learning throughout the semester. They will be expected to participate in class discussions about the key concepts, ask questions and demonstrate their understanding, critical analysis and oral communication skills in relation to the set readings. Each student will be required to ‘co-facilitate’ one seminar together with another student. This will involve communicating with the other student to prepare approaches to initiating class discussion in relation to each discussion question, offering critical reflections on the prescribed texts and attempting to identify the themes addressed in the reading. In small groups, students will also critically discuss and review a range of texts. Students will work in pairs to practice plain legal language drafting, using an existing statute or jury direction and will learn and practice key legal oratory skills. This will involve students working collaboratively to prepare and perform a piece of short script demonstrating legal oratory techniques and skills. Formative feedback will be provided during class on students’ ability to work together on legal strategy and use of legal oratory techniques. Strategy 4 Developing legal research skills Legal research skills are essential for developing an understanding of theoretical approaches to law. Through preparing for seminars, participating in seminar discussion and facilitation, and planning their research and essay, students will practice their legal research skills. Students will be exposed to research methodology choices, interdisciplinary research and importance of being able to articulate a research process. In the process of preparing for their final essay, students will be required to generate a draft abstract and a bibliography that is appropriate to their chosen essay question. Students will submit this prior to submitting the final essay and the seminar leader will provide feedback on the research topic, research strategy and bibliographic sources ahead of the final writing task. In the research essay workshop, students will present their research essay outline to the class. During this presentation they will be given the opportunity to explain and discuss their choice of research question, research strategy and essay plan. Strategy 5 Early Feedback In addition to the feedback opportunities outlined above, students will submit assessment item 2 early in the program. The seminar leader will assess the work, with attention to clarity of writing style and clarity of argument. This task will facilitate low-stakes but directed feedback from the lecturer prior to the census date. The feedback provided on students’ writing style and articulation of argument will develop skills ahead of the final written essay task. Subject Delivery: This subject will be delivered in three-hour seminars over 8 weeks.
learning_outcomes: Conduct effective legal research by identifying and synthesising primary and secondary legal and interdisciplinary texts in order to investigate the relationship between law, language, power and ideology
Investigate, synthesise and evaluate a range of linguistic theories and articulate their relevance to the analysis of law, language, power and ideology
Express, debate and justify their interpretation of law and language theories and scholarship

title: Reading, Writing and Spelling
syllabus_overview:
You will examine evidence-based literacy instruction tailored to meet the diverse abilities of students across the full range of abilities in inclusive primary classrooms. You will study cognitive processes involved in learning to read and write, emphasising phonemic awareness, phonological knowledge, decoding strategies, vocabulary development, fluency, and comprehension. And you will be taught to use assessment strategies to identify instructional priorities. The subject highlights explicit, systematic approaches to teaching literacy, equipping you with practical strategies to support primary school learners who are not meeting expected literacy outcomes.

Teaching Strategies:
You will experience learning in this subject through prescribed readings, videos and podcasts and online lectures, followed by workshops that facilitate collaborative practice and application of concepts. The subject is practice-based, and engages you in learning activities based on realistic scenarios from school settings where you will collaborate with your peers in analysing school students’ literacy performance, considering solutions that are inclusive and conducive to all students’ learning. The readings and input from lecturers and tutors provide you with the scholarly basis from which you will develop your responses to the diverse scenarios that you may encounter as classroom teachers. You will receive early formative feedback on your understanding of key principles and concepts during your learning activities.
learning_outcomes: Design and implement formal and informal assessment techniques to identify instructional priorities for learners not achieving expected literacy outcomes.
Analyse the cognitive processes involved in learning to read, spell and write and strategies to support learning.
Develop strategies to support learners who are not achieving vocabulary, fluency, and comprehension outcomes.
Collaborate with peers to evaluate existing programs and create and share inclusive literacy teaching resources and strategies.
Apply explicit, systematic approaches to literacy teaching that address the needs of students who are not meeting expected literacy outcomes.

This subject equips you with the skills to analyse real estate investments across various asset types, including residential, commercial, and specialised sectors like student accommodation. You'll learn to appreciate the nuances between property funds and going concerns, understand the value drivers, and assess risk and return for different property classes. The course examines the real asset lifecycle, due diligence in real asset decisions, and the environmental, social, and governance (ESG) implications for each asset type. You'll also explore the role of green finance in property investment, enhancing your financial analysis skills within the real estate market.

Teaching Strategies:

The subject will be delivered through a blend of interactive lectures on key concepts and project-based learning relating to the financial and market characteristics of real estate asset class. The subject deliverables will include generating and assessing real estate data and information to inform investment decisions. There will be collaborative problem-solving exercises, involving current property markets and case studies, to strengthen key concepts discussed in class. Students are required to conduct real-life property market research on what to invest in and discuss the sustainability considerations of a chosen investment asset. There will be two separate guest speakers to share their expertise or perspectives about the subject to enhance learning outcomes. Online resource materials are also provided throughout the semester via Canvas to encourage flipped learning. Demonstration of learning is undertaken using a variety of assessment techniques that include group activities and presentations in class, evaluation of property data and information, property investment report writing, and a report on the green features of property assets. An aim of this subject is to help you develop academic and professional language and communication skills to succeed at university and in the workplace. During this subject, you will complete a milestone assessment task that will, in addition to assessing your subject-specific learning objectives, assess your English language proficiency.

title: Real Analysis
syllabus_overview:
Real Analysis rigorously establishes calculus foundations, starting with real numbers and the least upper bound principle, progressing through limits, continuity, derivatives, and their applications, including Taylor series. After becoming well-versed in these fundamental topics, you will learn more advanced topics such as Riemann sums, Riemann integration, uniform convergence and convergence of Riemann integrals. You will also be taught rigorous real analysis definitions of important mathematical functions. A key aim is to teach you how to construct and present precise and rigorous mathematical proofs.

Teaching Strategies:
Interactive workshops and tutorials on campus. The material will be developed with the students in interactive workshops. Students will have several exercise sheets on which they will work through outside of class. In the tutorials students will be expected to work with their peers on particular questions from the subject's exercise sheets and may be asked to present them to the class on a whiteboard. All exercise sheet solutions will be made available at later dates. A key skill in mathematics is the ability to communicate with one's peers in clear mathematical language. Constructing a proof is one of the most challenging aspets of mathematics. There are however various proof strategies and the students will be shown several of these. Students will see how mathematicians formulate theorems and write proofs, with each step laid out clearly and precisely. Each part of a proof must follow logically from the previous parts. Students will have a chance to write their own proofs in the various assessment tasks. They will be required to set them out in a clear logical order with every part of the proof fully justified. This is the essence of communication in mathematics. They will receive feedback on their work in assessment tasks 1 and 2, which are returned to the students after marking with helpful comments, as well as in the tutorials. This will help them to see how their work can be improved. They will also, eventually, be given worked solutions to the exercise sheets so that they can compare their own work and privately reflect on how they can improve.
learning_outcomes: Develop skills in constructing rigorous mathematical arguments and presenting them using clear language and mathematical notation.
Apply the skills learnt to solve problems in areas where mathematical analysis is used.
Be able to understand the proofs of the major results in the topic of real analysis.
Develop the ability to prove mathematical results that the student has not previously seen.
Develop skills concerning the use of computer coding and computing to understand, check and validate mathematical results.

title: Real Estate Economics
syllabus_overview:
This subject applies economic principles to real estate markets, helping you understand and predict price trends, supply, and demand. You'll learn to analyse market fundamentals, forecast trends, and examine investor behaviour using the latest economic research. The course introduces you to land economics, microeconomics, macroeconomics, behavioural economics, corporate finance, and industry economics as they relate to the residential, commercial, industrial, retail, and mixed-use property markets. Students also examine how broader macroeconomic conditions shape Australian property markets, including the impact of monetary policy, fiscal policy (how federal, state, and local government decisions influence property market outcomes), housing and business cycles, lending conditions, inflation, immigration, population growth, and regional economic change.

Teaching Strategies:
Real Estate Economics is structured and delivered through eight Modules in Canvas. The Program has the Module topics and required reading. The first Module is an introduction and explanation of the subject, then there are eight with recorded PowerPoint lectures on the Module’s topics. We are basically substituting two Modules for a block day, replacing two hours of class lecture time with a lecture of narrated PowerPoint slides around 45 minutes and an hour or two of reading time. The reality of distance learning is self-directed study and more reading, You are expected to organize your own time over the semester. The subject can be done weekly over the semester allowing a couple of weeks for the assignments, or, if you are organising around the block structure, done two modules at a time. You should allow two to four hours for each Module. Modules have set readings and supplementary readings. Set readings for five Modules are from a free online economics textbook by CORE Economics called The Economy, used as the subject’s set text. You register and get access to their web page here http://www.core-econ.org/ . This is a widely used introductory text and is suitable for students without any prior studies in economics. For students who have done some Economics, the examples and explanatory boxes will be useful. Modules also have supplementary reading, links for extended research, and sources for further study. Library ebook and ddr links and pdfs for other set readings are provided. The Introduction Module has a 30-minute recorded lecture on the subject content and assessment. Students are asked to watch that and introduce themselves to the class by posting a short 200-word biography on the Discussion board in Canvas at the beginning of the semester.
learning_outcomes: Apply concepts and approaches relevant to real estate from macroeconomics, microeconomics, transaction cost economics, behavioural economics and industry economics.

title: Real Estate Initial Public Offer Methodology
syllabus_overview:
This subject equips you with the skills to create a comprehensive IPO document for real estate, suitable for listed or unlisted offerings. You'll study managed investment scheme legislation, real estate IPO research methods, and explore equity and debt as capital funding sources. You'll learn to determine suitable debt levels based on earnings risks of the asset(s) and examine different debt-to-equity scenarios and their impact on returns. The course also covers forecasting income growth, considering factors like lease expiry profiles and tenant quality, as well as assessing various debt structures. You'll learn to project substantiated revenue forecasts for the initial two years of the IPO.

title: Real Property
syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces you to the law and practice of real property. You’ll examine the underlying principles and interests in land that underpin property transactions in New South Wales. You’ll explore the connections between the doctrines of real property law and the bureaucratic practices associated with transacting property within the Torrens Title system. This subject has a strong practice-oriented focus on solving realistic real property law problems, alongside building your understanding of the relationship between the law of real property and other legal domains; such as contract law, equity and trusts. You’ll learn through scaffolded, self-paced learning exercises to develop your knowledge of real property law and your problem-solving skills. You will also improve your critical analysis and communication skills through participating in problem-solving focused tutorials where you’ll collaborate to apply your new knowledge to practice-based scenarios.

Teaching Strategies:
Strategy 1 Preparation: Students will be encouraged and supported to undertake independent study. This will aid with the acquisition of core knowledge and the key graduate attribute of self-management. Students will be expected to engage in a range of activities before classes which will assist them to engage more deeply with the core knowledge in the subject, and to apply it in practice-based scenarios. Preparation activities include: Engage with the set topic materials prior to attending class, in particular reading and analysing the identified cases. Prepare tutorial questions including legal problems before tutorials in order to facilitate understanding of the issues. Students are required to prepare their answers to all tutorial problems on each topic prior to the tutorial and to demonstrate this by the quality through the quality of the pre-prepared answers (see Assessment Task 2) and the quality of their participation in class discussion of the problems. Scaffolded, self-paced learning exercises, including a video/quiz module which aids students to understand the connection between basic doctrines of real property and the practice of property law. A study guide that incorporates topic materials (readings and links to other on-line resources), tutorial questions and legal problems is available to students on Canvas Strategy 2 Active Learning: Students will interact with lecturers and other students on campus during lectures and tutorials. In both of these formats students will be provided with opportunities to improve their skills of critical analysis and problem solving through the use of scaffolded activities, flipped exercises, ‘breakout sessions’ and group problem solving sessions. These enable students to practice Assessment items encourage students to undertake both independent and group study and to applying their analytical and doctrinal skills to the practice-orientated problems they will encounter in assessments. Strategy 3 Collaborative learning: Students will engage in learning with their peers through a number of fora: tutorials buzz groups and breakout sessions. Students collaborate to develop their critical thinking and core legal skills of primary source analysis, and to apply these skills to practice-based scenarios. Strategy 4 Feedback: Feedback is given for assessment items (except the final exam) by means of a combination of generic class and student specific feedback. Feedback focuses not only on the right answer but also on the ways in which student could have better approached the various tasks and strategies for improvement on future tasks. We also offer formative, no-stakes tasks designed to provide ongoing feedback to students on their own performance. This takes place though pre-prepared questions, and by means of self-paced quizzes. Subject Delivery This subject is taught in mixed mode with a blend of online and face to face learning. There will be pre-recorded lectures available to students as per the program in Canvas. Students have the option of enrolling in either a face to face or an online tutorial. Recorded Lectures on Canvas Lecture recordings will be made available for download from Canvas. Students may use these audio-tapes for private student purposes, and to avoid legal action, permission must be obtained from the Subject Coordinator for any other usage.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the framework of contemporary real property law; its key legal doctrines and the implications of the relationships between them.
Relate the basic doctrines of real property to the ways in which property is identified and transacted in practice.
Evaluate the relative merits of different legal doctrines and strategies in assessing, advising and responding to simulated ‘real world’ legal scenarios.
Analyse and monitor their own performance and implement strategies for developing their self-management, particularly time-management.
Reflect, evaluate and improve their core skills in real property case analysis.

title: Real-time Creation and Collaborative Production
school: MAP and Sound and Music Design
syllabus_overview:
In this subject you will use improvisatory and real-time processes to generate and respond to sound and musical material. You will form part of a small team of peers with complementary skills, tasked with collaborating on a short music/sound work from start to final realisation. As real-time generation of music and sound material is the basis for professional practice across diverse contexts this subject will harness and hone your skills in listening, improvised musical and sound-based performance, live sound capture, manipulation, and production. Through interaction with others in a studio environment, you may engage your practice as a sound designer, instrumentalist, vocalist, laptop performer, DJ, spoken word artist, emcee, producer, live sound or mixing engineer, curator, or any combination of these. Material generated in real-time will then be edited and produced, tailored to different applications based on industry and artistic models of practice. Outputs will be catalogued and offered for use (subject to IP) on interdisciplinary collaborations that might include works by designers, architects, journalists, game designers, video artists, filmmakers, animators, or record labels.

Teaching Strategies:
You will prepare for weekly studio sessions by engaging with your creative practice at home, and with lectures, readings, videos, recordings and discussion threads online. You will select an area of practice you wish to explore throughout the semester and focus on readings and online material that are relevant to that practice. These references may be sourced from the subject reading list initially, but you will also be required to source your own references specific to the niche of your own work. You will engage in supervised work within small teams through practical sessions led by the lecturer. You will also engage in-studio within your team to work towards assessment. Opportunities for formative and summative feedback on learning will be offered prior to Census date, in mid-term Stuvac and in Week 12. All students are expected to demonstrate high levels of active, collaborative learning supported by engagement with their peers in positive creative processes, in completing assigned tasks, in being an active and supportive group member, through timely attention to required collaborative input, and through online engagement with prepared content.
learning_outcomes: Utilise improvisatory and real-time processes to generate original sound and musical material
Apply skills in listening, live sound creation, capture, manipulation, and production
Investigate and present the context of your practice
Collaborate in small teams to realise short music and sound works
Reflect on and write about your practice and its context

title: Realtime Animation and VFX
school: MAP and Sound and Music Design
syllabus_overview:
In this subject, you will explore and apply the knowledge, skills and resources required to develop and execute real-time animation and visual effects projects. The term ‘real-time animation’ refers to the use of 3D game engines in the creation of animations for the screen and/or games. Apart from the film and television industry, animation and games, real-time animation tools and techniques are being applied in an increasingly diverse range of creative and other industries such as theatre and live events, installations, architecture and construction, digital fashion, data visualisation, manufacturing and health sciences and beyond. In this subject, you will use industry-standard real-time game engines and associated technologies and tools, including AI, to create animations and visual effects. You will develop original content alongside preexisting digital assets such as environments, props, and characters and apply processes such as modelling, rigging, blocking, layout, motion and facial capture, animation, and post-production.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject, delivered via online learning, face-to-face lectures, and studio teaching, mirrors a professional production environment. You will actively engage with real-time animation and compositing through project-based group learning, applying theoretical knowledge and technical skills to develop creative projects. Formative feedback from tutors is provided pre-census date through engagement in weekly classes. Feedback is also given on summative tasks, in-class, before submission. The subject integrates industry-standard software, workflows, and collaborative practices, fostering creative and technical proficiency. You are encouraged to think critically, reflect on their work, and respond and adapt to emerging technologies, preparing them for successful careers in the ever-evolving media landscape.

Develop effective teamwork, problem-solving, critical thinking and communication skills in a collaborative production setting.

Gain proficiency in industry-standard tools and techniques for 3D modelling, texturing, rigging, animation, lighting, camera work, visual effects, and post-production, addressing technical and creative challenges throughout the production pipeline.
Develop a solid understanding of real-time animation and VFX's core principles and workflows.
Learn how to plan, stage, and composite scenes for optimal audiovisual storytelling and character performance.

title: Real-time Operating Systems
syllabus_overview:
This subject provides an understanding of computer operating systems for embedded systems, PCs, and servers. It focuses on their roles in a conventional computing environment and addresses how operating systems support real-time computing requirements, such as managing operating for programming on PC and server. You'll explore process management, scheduling, inter-process communication, memory, and I/O device management through case studies on OS adaptations. Practical work includes programming in POSIX-compliant C, using the Linux kernel as a UNIX example, and studying real-time systems, real-time kernels, and CPU scheduling.

Teaching Strategies:
Students will learn in this subject by reading the uploaded lecture notes and the recommended sections of the readings and textbook, and by attending interactive tutorials that build on these materials. Students are required to participate in group Q&A discussions and complete one individual quiz during laboratory sessions to demonstrate their understanding of the subject content. For the lab-based Q&A discussions, students will form groups of four to five members and engage in collaborative question-and-answer activities. These group discussions are designed to enhance teaching and learning (T&L) outcomes through peer interaction and active learning. Two projects will be assigned to enable students to demonstrate and/or implement key concepts from the subject in practical applications. The first project will be completed in pairs, while the second project will be undertaken individually. Students are required to submit all assessments by the specified due dates and to prepare for the final examination. Students are expected to spend approximately eight hours per week on this subject, including class time, assuming they are average students aiming to achieve a pass grade. Class sessions will primarily be used for interactive tutorials, individual quizzes, and group discussions.
learning_outcomes: Solve quantitative and qualitative problems related to understand operating system design and use. (C.1)
Identify the basic principles of real-time systems analysis to understand Linux systems. (D.1)
Show competence in using and writing application programs in POSIX compliant C that is applied on a Unix operating system. (D.1)
Illustrate the basic principles of the design and implementation of an operating system to create an experimental analysis report. (C.1)

title: Recognising and Responding to Acute Deterioration
syllabus_overview:
This subject is designed to enhance your knowledge and understanding, of how to promptly recognise and appropriately escalate and manage a patient's acute deterioration in physiological, cognitive, and/or mental state, to improve patient safety and outcomes. A particular emphasis is placed on the importance of using a person-centred approach, when caring for acutely ill patients and their significant others. Orientation activities will introduce you to the subject and peers, aiding in assessment preparation. Engage with weekly online resources to deepen your understanding and participate in Zoom meetings for collaborative learning and feedback, which is crucial for your professional growth. Feedback is varied and continuous, aimed at improving your performance. The subject content and assessments are regularly updated to ensure alignment with learning objectives and clinical relevance.

Teaching Strategies:
Orientation activities Preparation for the session - You are expected to undertake activities during orientation week. These activities are designed to introduce you to the subject and your peers, and will assist you to prepare for the subject's assessment tasks. Independent learning activities Relevant readings, videos and activities will be made available online relevant to the topic of the week. This will support your ability to progress successfully throughout the subject and complete assessment items effectively. The online material aims to enhance your understanding of the topic or delve deeper into a more specific area, compare experiences and ideas with others and gain feedback. Information and links to all these learning activities can be accessed via Canvas as well as the subject outline. Zoom meetings You are strongly encouraged to attend all scheduled Zoom meetings as they will prepare you for the subject’s assessment tasks. Additionally, they provide opportunities for group activities, discussion, self-assessment, peer review and formative feedback from the subject coordinator and your teaching team. The schedule for this subject’s zoom meetings is below in the program section. Feedback Feedback in this subject takes several forms including self-assessment, peer review, automatic feedback from interactive activities and from the teaching team. Formative feedback throughout the subject aims to increase your performance in summative assessments. Feedback and changes from previous subject offering Feedback from the previous offering was positive and subject has been revised to align more with the subject learning objectives. Several resources and readings have been updated and/or refined to maintain subject quality, accuracy and relevance.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate how a patient's acute deterioration in physiological, cognitive, and/or mental state, is recognised promptly, and escalated appropriately.
Explore appropriate activation of Rapid Response Systems for patients for whom resuscitation measures cannot achieve acceptable outcomes or preserve dignity.
Analyse the importance of self-care, personal and team well-being when working in complex and stressful situations.
Critically compare current systems, technology and processes that are used to support and promote detection and recognition of acute deterioration.

title: Reflective Academic Practice
syllabus_overview:
This subject helps university teachers to better understand their learning styles and optimise professional development opportunities. You will reflect on your learning preferences, strengths, and workplace factors affecting your professional growth. The subject offers a choice of topics, such as research supervision and technology-enhanced learning, to tailor your development. You can earn credit by engaging in university-provided activities like Mental Health First Aid or entrepreneurship modules. By reviewing these experiences, you will learn to navigate unforeseen challenges and adapt your learning strategies for practical outcomes in your future practice.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject entails participants undertaking a professional learning activity that may focus on any aspect of the subject participant’s academic work. The professional learning activity is negotiated with a project adviser. Activities could include on-the-job training, including online courses, taking on additional responsibilities in order to build skills, shadowing a co-worker to see how they do their job, a secondment to another unit to broaden their experience or being mentored or mentoring a colleague. Early feedback is provided on initial reflections on practice with suggestions for changes occurring through independent reflection and negotiation with a Faculty advisor. Participants develop their understanding of how they may prepare for the future world of academic work by reflecting critically on what you have learned as a participant in a professional learning activity.
learning_outcomes: revise learning from previous subjects
identify meaningful dimensions of academic work related to their own work
justify the practical significance of learning to their own practice
relate learning to the higher education, university and/or academic contexts in which they work
reflect on an aspect of their scholarly academic work

title: Recovery and Nutrition for High Performance Sport
syllabus_overview:
This subject is designed for individuals to advance knowledge in recovery and nutrition in high-performance sports. You will gain robust understanding of fatigue management, recovery techniques, and nutritional strategies to enhance athletic performance. You will learn to address recovery challenges and nutritional issues, tailoring solutions to the high-performance sports context. Teaching methods include interactive lectures, case studies, and problem-solving exercises, ensuring you can apply your knowledge to real-world scenarios and influence positive behavioural change in athletes

Teaching Strategies:
This subject incorporates a range of learning activities to engage students. The student learning journey will take place online, in Canvas. Modules will give students the opportunity to view content at a time and location that suits their busy schedules. They will also provide an equivalent learning outcome to the traditional face-to-face lectures, whilst giving students added flexibility with their learning. They will focus on understanding recovery and nutrition concepts, characteristics of effective interventions and operating and succeeding in high performance environments. Students will develop expertise and synthesise contemporary evidence to prescribe recovery and nutrition techniques and employ those relevant to high performance sport practice. They will also learn ways to positively affect behaviour change. These activities will require collaboration with others, preparation work and various interactive mediums (e.g. Zoom). Feedback will be provided to students throughout the session via several mediums. Each week students will complete online tasks and peer feedback will be central to the review of this content in the module activities. The subject coordinator will also provide feedback and discussion about these formative tasks where appropriate, and they will lead debriefing discussions within online forums on Canvas. The tutorial activities and these forums provide the opportunity for students to receive low-stakes feedback. There will be a high concentration of low-stakes feedback in the early weeks of each module to enable students to understand the foundation concepts of the subject, and equip them with the knowledge and confidence to approach the more complex cases covered in the second half of each module. The assessment items will be marked using a rubric which will be provided to students, along with written feedback about their work.

title: Reframing International Political Economy
syllabus_overview:
This subject offers an interdisciplinary view of International Political Economy, valuable for careers across business, government, diplomacy, and the NGO sphere. You will focus on the interplay between politics and economics rather than economic technicalities or maths. You'll examine the influence of states, international organisations, and transnational corporations, applying both traditional and critical theories to understand power dynamics. Through case studies like economic crises, international development, and climate finance, you will analyse and propose solutions to transnational challenges. The subject integrates diverse theories and empirical data, equipping you with a comprehensive understanding of the global economy and possible directions for the future of global governance.

Teaching Strategies:
Students are guided through a series of six online modules framed around active learning. Each module draws on a wide range of contemporary and historical empirical and theoretical content. Students engage interactively through online discussion boards, embedded comments, and are scaffolded towards conducting their own critical analysis to address key challenges in international politics. This subject uses an authentic learning approach with students developing a policy brief to communicate their analysis to key audiences. Students practice and refine the application of core theories within International Political Economy to key contemporary challenges. Synchronous online seminars provide an opportunity to revise key concepts, further develop connections with other students, and to prepare for assessments. Students receive formative feedback on assignment tasks both from their lecturers and peers, including early formative feedback.
learning_outcomes: Analyse real-world case studies and complex global issues using key theories within International Political Economy.
Apply core theories to interpret the actors that shape the global political economy.
Critically analyse historical and contemporary challenges faced by the global economy.
Effectively communicate evidence-based solutions to complex issues within the global political economy.

title: Refugee Law and Practice
syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces you to the legal principles and procedures of international refugee law and their application within a domestic context. You’ll learn about the historical development of refugee law and evaluate the key features and limitations of the current refugee determination system in Australia. You will explore the practical realities of refugee law and practice through a clinical experience, working on 'real-life' refugee law cases and current legal issues. This practical work is supervised by UTS Law staff in conjunction with a local refugee legal organisation. You will apply your academic learning to a professional context by undertaking research and drafting submissions informing real-life refugee casework. This will deepen your understanding of refugee law and policy and provide a critical understanding of refugee status determination processes. By working on real-life refugee cases, you’ll gain practice-based, cross-cultural skills and insights necessary for work as a refugee lawyer.

Strategy 1 Preparing for professional practice in Refugee Law Strategy 2 Exposure to the professional practice of refugee lawyering through working in conjunction with a refugee legal organisation Strategy 3 Active learning through interactive seminars and class discussion in a small group format Strategy 4 Ongoing feedback to encourage critical reflection and self-improvement Subject Delivery The subject will be delivered in an intensive mode via online podcasts and resources, collaborative seminars and clinical workshops. It will be co-run with 78013 Refugee Law and Practice.

title: Real-time Visualisation for Architectural Design
syllabus_overview: Stundets explore and represent architectural and spatial design from both cinematic and human perspectives via contemporary visualisation software, Unreal Engine 4. Real-time visualisation is an emerging tool in architectural practice. Through the use of software like Unreal Engine 4, architects can produce project flythroughs, rendering, interactive apps and VR experiences to support design and its communication. Real-time visualisation affords minimal setup, reducing the time and cost associated with the use of dedicated 3D visualisers. Importantly, it enables architectural experimentation throughout the design process, from concept development through to construction. Student of this course learn the fundamentals of Unreal Engine 4, using the software to leverage existing digital models to produce visualisations alongside design changes. They also create their own 3D model and use it to study the effects of lighting and materials, cinematic cameras and movement through space, and interaction as they relate to architectural real time visualisation. By completing this course, participants are eligible to participate in the course ‘Advanced Virtual Reality for Architectural Design'.

title: Regulating Technologies
syllabus_overview:
This subject provides you with the knowledge and skills needed to examine the question of how to best regulate new and rapidly changing technologies. This is one of the most important and difficult problems confronting governments, regulators and policymakers in Australia and worldwide today. You’ll examine the ‘fundamentals’ of regulation including rationales for market intervention. You will consider matters relating to enforcement and compliance and how a regulatory system can be designed to overcome the limits of rules. You’ll learn through critically assessing key concepts, theories, tools and strategies and applying them to case studies drawn from the communications and technology sectors. Legal and regulatory practitioners working in these sectors may also give guest presentations. The subject is useful if you are enrolled in the Legal Futures and Technology major, but also if you are interested in public law or intend to work for a regulatory body following graduation. No prior knowledge of technology or regulation is required.

Teaching Strategies:
Strategy 1 Class Preparation: In advance of each class, students are expected to prepare by reading set materials and attempting answers to a series of discussion questions. Strategy 2 Class Engagement: Class discussions will provide students with opportunities to explore, analyse and reflect critically on set materials. During class, students will also be provided with opportunities to apply concepts and principles from those materials to case studies drawn predominantly from the communications and technology sectors. Legal and regulatory practitioners working in these sectors may also give guest presentations. Strategy 3 Independent research: Students will be able to extend and deepen their knowledge and understanding of material discussed in class by engaging in independent research. Students will be expected to find and reflect on academic literature relevant to a topical regulatory issue in the technology sector, deploying arguments and information they've found to support their position in a policy submission. Strategy 4 Simulated practice as a regulatory advisor: Students will prepare a policy submission in response to a 'live' policy debate. This will require students to draw on material covered in the subject and other relevant sources, using reasoned argumentation. Strategy 5 Feedback: Informal feedback from teaching staff and peers will be provided throughout seminars in response to contributions made, and questions asked, by students. Students may also request informal feedback regarding their seminar participation by completing and submitting an Interim Seminar Participation Self-Evaluation Sheet. Subject Delivery The subject will be delivered in block mode by way of face-to-face seminars and online lectures.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and evaluate the strengths and limitations of the theories, tools and strategies that inform regulatory policy and design.
Be able to assess proposals to address current and emerging regulatory issues in the technology sector.
Identify, reflect on and apply ideas from relevant research materials that inform contemporary regulatory debates in the technology sector.
Demonstrate an understanding of, and a capacity to apply, key concepts, ideas, theories, tools and strategies that inform regulatory policy and design.

title: Regression and Linear Models
syllabus_overview:
This subject teaches regression analysis, a method for modelling relationships between a response variable and multiple explanatory variables. Regression analysis is widely used in fields such as science, engineering, medicine, and business. The subject covers the development and testing of multivariable models and techniques for deciding which set of variables gives the best model.

Teaching Strategies:
Materials are available on Canvas to help you prepare for the subject. These include an introduction to R, as well as short video clips to help reinforce your prerequisite statistical knowledge. During session, the subject is four hours of classes each session (weekly for Autumn/Spring), consisting of lectures, laboratory work, tutorials and discussions. Students are expected to support each hour of class time with an hour of private study, be it in groups or as individuals. Each lecture will be two hours that will involve review of the previous session's content and the presentation of new material. The practical application of this material will then occur in that session's computer lab. After completing the two-hour computer lab, full solutions will be made available and students are encouraged to review the lab output prior to attending the following lab session. The subject makes extensive use of Canvas. Lecture materials are posted prior to the lectures and students are encouraged to review prior to the lecture as interaction during the lectures is encouraged. All lab solutions, discussion of the R assignment, and solutions to a previous exam will also be available as the course progresses. The main R assignment MUST be undertaken as a group assignment. General feedback covering the solutions to the assignment will be given during the review lecture and made available online. Marks will be available prior to the final exam.

title: Renewable Energy Systems Studio A

Power electronics is a crucial technology that enables the efficient management and conversion of electrical power in various applications, including motor drives, renewable energy systems, data centers, and HVDC networks. This studio provides an engaging learning experience, equipping you with the skills to understand and control power electronic converters, particularly in renewable energy contexts such as solar PV-battery systems. Throughout this subject, you will explore the details of circuitry and control challenges inherent in power electronic systems. You will gain practical experience using commercial software for thorough circuit analysis and development, allowing you to design circuits that meet industry standards and custom specifications. title: Reinforcement Learning
syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces you to reinforcement learning, the study of how machines learn from interactions with their environment. A subset of machine learning, it's essential for automated decision-making and AI, teaching programs to predict and act optimally through experience. You'll explore its applications in control systems, gaming, and inventory management. The subject covers both theory and practice, including Markov Decision Processes, classic and modern algorithms, and hands-on agent training using cutting-edge software tools. By the end, you'll understand value functions, explore exploration versus exploitation, and be able to deploy an AI system to solve real-world problems in your final project.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject includes a 1.5-hour face-to-face lecture each week for 12 weeks. During each lecture, the lecturer or guest lecturer will introduce a key topic in Reinforcement Learning (RL). This will be followed by a Q&A discussion and a tutorial activity related to the topic. In the 2-hour tutorial session, students will work on practical tasks that involve implementing state-of-the-art RL algorithms. Each week’s task is designed to develop a key component needed to complete the subject project. The subject also includes a group project (group and individually assessed), which helps students develop skills in implementing RL algorithms, reviewing relevant research literature, and presenting experimental results. Through the project, reflective activities, and an online formative quiz, students will explore RL topics in both breadth and depth and demonstrate a strong understanding of the selected concepts/topics.

title: Remedies
syllabus_overview:
This subject considers the various court-ordered remedies sought for private law wrongs, such as torts, breach of contract and restitution. You’ll also learn about statutory remedies for misleading and deceptive conduct. You will compare and evaluate the causes of action and the remedial choices available. You will discover how a particular interest may be protected by the law in several ways. Through weekly videos you will develop your knowledge of the key concepts. You will then work collaboratively in tutorials to advise clients in hypothetical scenarios on the legal remedies available to them. You will learn to identify alternative causes of actions and remedies arising from factual scenarios and critically evaluate which are the most desirable for the client.

Teaching Strategies:
Strategy 1: Doctrinal learning in videos, readings and other self-directed learning Recorded weekly videos provide some of the legal knowledge (GA 1) that students must understand to pass this course. They act as an overview by providing an entry into the relevant principles and by signposting key areas of interest. Students are expected to develop and fill in the details of their legal knowledge with recommended readings, self-directed learning and tutorial participation. Strategy 2: Comparative analysis & evaluation in tutorials Students will develop their legal knowledge (GA 1) and critical analysis and evaluation skills (GA 3) by attending and participating in tutorials. Students will work collaboratively to advise clients in hypothetical scenarios on the legal remedies available to them. Students will learn to identify alternative causes of actions and remedies arising from factual scenarios and critically evaluate which are the most desirable for the client. The skills practiced in tutorials will be applied in the formal summative assessments. Strategy 3: Summative research and written assessments Students will apply their research (GA 4) and written communication skills (GA 5) to produce written, formally assessed responses to legal questions involving hypothetical scenarios. In doing so, they will also draw on their legal knowledge and critical analysis skills practiced in tutorials. Students’ research skills will be tested by setting questions on legal principles not directly covered in lectures or tutorials thus requiring them to research the appropriate responses. Strategy 4: Formal and informal feedback Both formal and informal feedback will be provided consistently throughout the semester. Formal feedback will consist of results and comments provided on summative assessments, and advice provided at the cohort level on assessments. Topic-based practice quizzes will provide students with immediate formative feedback after each video in a module. Students can, therefore, quickly identify gaps in their knowledge and confirm their understanding. Informal feedback will also be provided in tutorials where students can test their understanding of the readings and their legal knowledge. It is important to recognise that feedback is more than comments by an academic written on an assessment. Feedback occurs informally by participating in discussions with teaching staff and your peers. For example, if you offer an opinion on a problem question with a peer and your peer agrees with your opinion or suggests an alternative, then you have just received feedback. If you then offer that opinion in a class discussion and the teaching staff comments on it, then you have received feedback. If you do not attend tutorials, then you significantly reduce the amount of feedback you receive during the teaching session. Subject Delivery: Videos : The weekly videos cover the doctrinal foundations of remedies for tort, contract, deceptive trade practices and restitution. Tutorials : The weekly tutorials run as interactive discussion groups, based around set questions. Students must complete the required preparation (readings, tutorial questions) before the tutorial. Recommended readings : Readings provide further detail on the principles covered in the videos. Students are encouraged to read cases in full for a deeper understanding of the principles.

title: Research and Evaluation in Indigenous Health

This subject introduces you to the foundations of research and evaluation with Indigenous peoples in Australia and worldwide. You will explore the philosophical, empirical, scientific, cultural, methodological, analytical, writing, ethics, and cultural safety aspects of research and evaluation. Grounded in Indigenous research methodologies, you will develop core research and evaluation skills, including generating research questions, managing literature reviews, engaging with First Nations Peoples, and writing journal articles. You will learn how to design culturally safe research that is co-designed with, and beneficial for, First Nations participants. By the end of this subject, you will have the knowledge and skills to support culturally safe and respectful practice in research and evaluation with Indigenous peoples worldwide, helping you build your graduate cultural capabilities.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is delivered implementing Indigenous teaching and learning strategies which incorporates and respects Indigenous Allied Health Australia’s Cultural Responsiveness in Action Framework (Indigenous Allied Health Australia, 2019), the National Health and Medical Research Council guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health research (NH&MRC, 2018) and current Indigenous led research in learning and teaching. The explicit teaching and learning strategies from these sources include; Utilising imagery to visualising and understanding processes Working collaboratively, embedding stories and experiences into learning Learning in the local context Applying learning to professional contexts, innovating, problem solving and thinking laterally Working with community Reflective practice including self-awareness, critical reflection and accountability Woven within all teaching and learning activities is Indigenous ways of knowing, being and doing; Being, through giving and receiving, and carrying out all actions in relationships with others Doing, based on diverse information and tools, and principled and reflective action Knowing, from best available types of evidence, guidance of Elders and community, and respect for the learning journey

title: Research Critique and Literature Review
syllabus_overview:
This subject prepares you for your first assessment as a higher doctorate research or Honours student by teaching you to critically analyse texts and craft a literature review. You'll learn to effectively summarise, paraphrase, search for, evaluate, and synthesise literature, culminating in a draft of your review chapter. You're expected to engage with four research papers weekly, developing the ability to spot gaps and underscore your research question's significance. Through this, you'll gain the skills necessary to articulate a compelling literature review.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is taught online or face-to-face workshop at the City Campus. It is a requirement that students undertake a minimum of 80% of activities online and attend the workshop. Each week students will be asked to familiarise themselves with a range of different online written and visual resources that relate to the topic which are included in the program descriptions. Students are expected to use the online tools to ask questions, initiate student discussions with other students, and regularly respond to Canvas postings that clarify questions. Students will also work closely with their supervisors throughout the semester to guide their literature search, but articles should be searched and critiqued by students. Students will be assessed on their critical evaluation of literature reviews published in academic journals and their peer-assessment of critical assessments completed by other students throughout the semester. Students will be required to offer constructive feedback verbally and will have several opportunities to receive feedback during the subject. The feedback provided will vary in form, purpose and in its degree of formality: Formative feedback will be provided during the learning process, typically provided verbally by the subject's teaching staff. It will address the content of work and a student's approach to learning, both in general and more specific ‘assessment orientated’ terms. It is designed to help students improve their performance in time for the submission of an assessment item. For this to occur students need to respond constructively to the feedback provided. This involves critically reflecting on advice given and in response altering the approach taken to a given assessment. Formative feedback may also, on occasion, be provided by other students. It is delivered informally, either in conversation during a tutorial or in the course of discussion at the scale of the whole class. title: Research Critique and Literature Review
syllabus_overview:
This subject prepares higher doctorate research students in the School of Built Environment to master critical analysis and literature review composition, essential for their first candidature assessment. You'll learn to critically assess texts, draft a literature review chapter, and maintain a steady pace of reviewing four papers weekly. Key skills developed include summarising, paraphrasing, literature searching, critical evaluation, synthesising sources into a cohesive argument, and identifying research gaps to underscore your research question's relevance and contribution.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is taught online with a two-day face-to-face workshop at the City Campus. It is a requirement that students undertake a minimum of 80% of activities online and attend the workshop. Each week students will be asked to familiarise themselves with a range of different online written and visual resources that relate to the topic which are included in the program descriptions. Students are expected to use the online tools to ask questions, initiate student discussions with other students, and regularly respond to UTS online postings that clarify questions. Students will also work closely with their supervisors throughout the semester to guide their literature search, but articles should be searched and critiqued by students. Students will be assessed on their critical evaluation of literature reviews published in academic journals and their peer-assessment of critical assessments completed by other students throughout the semester. Students will be required to offer constructive feedback verbally and will have several opportunities to receive feedback during the subject. The feedback provided will vary in form, purpose and in its degree of formality: Formative feedback will be provided during the learning process, typically provided verbally by the subject's teaching staff. It will address the content of work and a student's approach to learning, both in general and more specific ‘assessment orientated’ terms. It is designed to help students improve their performance in time for the submission of an assessment item. For this to occur students need to respond constructively to the feedback provided. title: Research Design and Methods in International Relations
syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces you to research design, methods, and methodologies in International Relations. You will learn about the foundations of International Relations research, and the skills and techniques required to conduct ethical and independent research for careers in global politics. The subject covers topics such as decolonising methodologies and Indigenous research, qualitative and quantitative methods, developing research questions, choosing data sources, and analysis techniques. You will also learn how to navigate the ethical and practical challenges of international research, and how to apply research methods in the international arena.

Teaching Strategies:
You will be guided through a series of six online modules. You will be supported to develop skills in research design and ethical research practices as a core workplace skill in the International Relations profession, as well as to an academic audience through assessments that encourage engagement with methods and scholarly literature. You will participate in collaborative and independent activities to share insights and observations with peers from various professional contexts. You will engage interactively through online discussion boards and embedded comments. The subject will be scaffolded towards the development of a research design in the final assessment, that will apply your learning of research methods, techniques, and approaches to an International Relations topic. To ensure professionally relevant outcomes, this subject uses authentic activities and assessments. In Assessment 1 and specific modules, you will be supported to identify and analyse ethical Indigenous research practices as central to conducting research in the International Relations profession, both in domestic and international contexts. Teaching and learning strategies to support this include engaging with Indigenous scholarship within and beyond International Relations. You will also learn about research methods through the modelling of exemplary International Relations research design in academic publications. Synchronous online seminars provide an opportunity to consolidate key learning material, further develop connections with other students, and to prepare for assessments. You will receive formative feedback on assessment tasks from your instructors throughout your learning in the subject.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate research methods and their relevance within particular contexts in International Relations.

Critically reflect on and apply Indigenous ethical principles and practices in International Relations research, to inform capabilities to work with and for Indigenous Australians and other Indigenous peoples in domestic and international settings.
Communicate the impact of research and the importance of ethical research practices within professional contexts in International Relations.
Demonstrate knowledge of key concepts and research design in International Relations, including Indigenous ways of knowing, being, and doing.

These activities are designed to introduce you to the subject and your peers and will assist you to prepare for the subject's assessment tasks. Lectures Each week, watch the lecture before attending the tutorial. Prep work Prep work is undertaken prior to tutorials. Prep work can include watching videos, reading a blog entry/website/textbook chapter/journal article/magazine article and/or listening to a podcast/video/interview. Questions often accompany the prep work so students read with intent which encourages deep reading. Content covered in prep work is strongly linked to the content covered in lectures and tutorials. title: Research Design in Physiotherapy
syllabus_overview:
This subject equips you with the skills to critically consume research literature and undertake a research project, enhancing your clinical practice. You will learn effective search strategies and appraisal techniques, understand the research process, including design, methodology, ethics, and statistical analysis, and explore key research methodologies for evidence-based practice. Working in groups with a supervisor, you will formulate a research question, conduct a literature review, and present a research proposal. Some projects may necessitate specialised training beyond scheduled hours.

Teaching Strategies:
Prep work Prep work is undertaken prior to masterclasses and workshops. Prep work can include watching a video, reading a blog entry/website/textbook chapter/journal article/magazine article and/or listening to a podcast/video/interview. Questions often accompany the prep work so students read with intent which encourage deep reading. Content covered in prep work is strongly linked to content covered in masterclasses and workshops. Please ensure prep work is carried out so that you have spent some time accessing and making sense of ideas. Attending the masterclasses and workshops will allow you to test these ideas and get feedback from your teachers and peers which will further consolidate your learning. Your knowledge and understanding of the prep work will be tested and applied using quizzes, group discussions and practical activities in masterclasses and workshops. Masterclasses Masterclasses are conducted in groups of 60 or more. There is usually a presentation of content by the teacher followed by activities which build on the prep work and the content presented. These activities are varied and require students to work alone, work in pairs or work in groups of 3 or more. Examples of these activities include short quizzes, group discussions, and using critical appraisal tools. Group discussions often involve comparing and contrasting an issue or answering a question based on case studies or the content topic. All activities are facilitated by the teacher. Feedback is provided by the teacher where there is discrepancy in the knowledge and understanding of the content or disagreement in opinions between groups. Feedback can also be provided by peers. Workshops Workshops are conducted in groups of 15-35. Workshop activities are varied and often require students to work in pairs or work in their research project groups. Workshops may provide an opportunity to work on aspects of the research project while under academic supervision (e.g. completing sections of the ethics application, writing literature review), facilitating immediate feedback.

title: Research Design in Speech Pathology
syllabus_overview:
You will learn about diverse research paradigms and designs used in the field of speech pathology. This includes qualitative, quantitative, mixed methods, and Indigenous approaches. You will develop skills in critiquing clinical research methods and results as well as designing ethical and rigorous studies. This subject also covers implementation science and knowledge translation. It will prepare you for your future literature reviews, clinical practice, and ongoing professional growth in speech pathology.

Teaching Strategies:
Preparation for Learning Students prepare for learning by completing learning activities before attending face-to-face classes. These activities may include reading recommended materials, watching a video or listening to audio podcasts, completing a quiz, or exploring online materials relating to the subject. Students take part in discussions online and answer questions online that relate to the readings and class activities. Activities before class, during class, and after class are outlined on the Canvas site for the subject. Active Lectures / workshops Active lectures and workshops briefly introduce topic content each week and guest lecturers are invited to share their professional expertise on particular topic areas at relevant times throughout the session or through video-based mediums. Workshops are active and require students to engage and participate in class through analysis of research, quizzes, class discussion and debate and other active and collaborative learning methods. Feedback Students have several opportunities to request and receive feedback from learning and teaching staff in class and online contexts. Lecturers provide feedback in a variety of formats and at various times throughout the subject to enable students to understand how they are progressing with their learning and where to focus their efforts. Students also receive feedback from lecturers specifically relating to assessment tasks. Students also provide peer feedback in learning activities and assessment tasks to enhance their learning at that of their peers. Research-integrated Learning Students actively engage with the research appraisal and design process. Students apply research appraisal and design knowledge to available research studies and problems. Collaborative Learning Clinical decision-making and research both require a team-based approach. Collaborative online and face-to-face learning activities and assessment tasks provide students opportunity to develop collaborative team skills.
learning_outcomes: Explain both qualitative and quantitative paradigms of research using examples from the field of speech pathology.
Source, appraise and report on selected research in terms of rigour and confidence in the study results.
Conduct and interpret statistical analyses in speech pathology research.
Appropriately resolve problems relating to the ethical conduct of human research.

title: Research Foundations
syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces higher degree research students to the fundamentals of research, fostered through the initiation of their own studies. You will learn about the research ecosystem, including academic publishing, presentations, research integrity, assessing research literature, creating data management plans and ethical considerations. The subject also explores the broader impact of research through your attendance at intensive workshops geared to engage in skill development, core understanding and attitudinal expectations required for this level of study. This subject is a pre-requisite for the second subject in this series of research subjects and together they create the foundational knowledge needed for you to succeed as a researcher in your field of expertise.

Teaching Strategies:
Research Foundations is delivered to Higher Degree Students commencing either PhD and MScRes research projects. Students will contribute to a series of teaching modules aimed at developing a foundational understanding of research skills, structure and environment. The modules offer students a range of opportunities to explore different aspects of the research endeavor. The primary focus of Research Foundations is for the student to consider how to form a meaningful research question that they will pursue during the rest of their HDR candidature. Student will join a workshop navigating the sources of information (including library resources) required to present a justified case for pursuing the research question. Further sessions will guide the students on how to establish well managed, inclusive and ethically viable investigations. The teaching modules will also consider how students communicate and defend their research projects through written reports and publications as well as oral presentations. Students are asked to examine the role of data in their research project and will complete a short assignment outlining their data management plan. Students will also work on substantive writing tasks to demonstrate their understanding of the research literature associated with their research project. The subject is primarily delivered during a single week of classes. The 'Intensive Teaching Week', is split into a series of 6 teaching modules, covering the areas listed below. In addition to the Intensive Teaching Week, 3 Drop-In sessions will be run during the semester to allow student to ask the subject Coordinator questions related to the course work and the assignments. This course feeds into the 42069 Research Methods where the students will consider how they will answer the research question considered during Research Foundations.
learning_outcomes: Communicate research outcomes effectively. (E.1)
Demonstrate social responsibility in academic research. (B.1)
Critically evaluate relevant academic literature. (C.1)
Develop a research data management plan. (D.1)

title: Research in Health

You'll craft an original research question informed by literature and practice issues, evaluate various research designs and methods, and select the most suitable approach. With an ethical lens, you will justify the potential risks and benefits of your proposed research to the study population, healthcare practice and policy as you develop and refine a feasible design that reflects methodological quality and rigor. Orientation activities will introduce you to the subject and peers, preparing you for assessments. Weekly online materials will support your progress and understanding. Participation in Zoom meetings is crucial for collaborative learning and receiving feedback, essential for your development. Feedback is diverse and ongoing, aimed at enhancing your performance. The subject content is regularly reviewed and updated to ensure its quality and relevance.

This will support your ability to progress successfully throughout the subject and complete assessment items effectively. The online materials aim to enhance your understanding of the topic or delve deeper into a more specific area, compare experiences and ideas with others and gain feedback. Several resources and readings have been updated and/or refined to maintain subject quality, accuracy and relevance.

title: Research in International Studies
syllabus_overview:
The subject is designed to equip students for independent, creative and ethical research through the development of the critical, analytical and methodological skills required to complete the planning and proposal stages for a small-scale piece of original research within an international context. It introduces students to qualitative and quantitative social science and humanities research data-gathering methods (field work and archival) appropriate to international studies research.

Teaching Strategies:
Research in International Studies is conducted as a seminar/workshop, which means that students are expected to be active participants in every class and the teacher will act principally as a facilitator to guide discussion, highlight key concepts and provide additional information. Classes will combine group work, discussions, student presentations, hands-on workshops and plenary sessions, some of which may be conducted by guest lecturers. In preparation for each class, students should complete the required readings or other assignments and be ready to contribute to class learning, for instance by having some notes or questions prepared about the readings. This subject is based on Problem Based Learning, which means that students will be presented with a problem to be solved in the form of a real-life research scenario. They will solve it (i.e. design a research project to answer the questions asked in the scenario) by assessing the tools and knowledge they already have and outlining what they still require or need to learn. They will in turn build their skills/knowledge base in these areas and apply them to the problem before developing a comprehensive response.
learning_outcomes: Design and communicate an ethical qualitative research plan for building knowledge about societies and cultures other than one’s own
Evaluate the outcomes of original humanities and social science research within an international context
