title: Science Thesis (Life Sciences) 1
syllabus_overview:
The Master of Philosophy course provides advanced research training in life and environmental sciences, enhancing your skills and knowledge for a research career. Centred around a research project spanning two 24-credit-point sessions, you'll work closely with an academic supervisor to conduct research in your chosen area. You'll learn to formulate hypotheses, set objectives, manage time and resources, employ appropriate research methods, evaluate evidence critically, and construct detailed arguments. Under supervision, you'll analyse and interpret scientific data from your project. Your science communication skills will be honed through written works and oral presentations. The culmination of your work is a thesis, which is the primary assessment component of the course.

Teaching Strategies:
In the Master of Philosophy program, teaching and learning are anchored in each student’s individual research project. Early stages emphasise guided practice, with students supported to: Acquire essential laboratory and/or practical field-based skills through structured training with academics, research staff, and senior postgraduate mentors. Develop core research practices including risk management planning, project design, experimental methods, and ethical engagement. Strengthen academic communication by receiving and actioning constructive feedback on written and oral assessments, building competence in scientific writing, literature critique, and presentation. Engage in regular one‑on‑one meetings with supervisor to monitor progress, troubleshoot challenges, and refine approaches. Participate in targeted workshops that scaffold assessment completion and develop professional capabilities. As expertise grows, students are expected to assume greater ownership of their learning and progressively take increased responsibility for the direction and outcomes of their research. Independent Learning The program cultivates independence by encouraging students to: Submit drafts for timely feedback in line with negotiated deadlines. Provide regular updates on project progress and outcomes. Leverage online resources - scientific literature, webinars, tutorials - to solve project challenges, deepen disciplinary understanding, and select appropriate data analysis methods. Engage with CANVAS support materials, including the Honours/MPhil Program Manual, workshop resources, which complement supervisory mentorship on writing critical literature reviews, oral presentations, preparing a thesis, and broader research practices. Through these practices, students transition from guided learners to self‑directed researchers capable of critical inquiry and professional judgement. Research Group Participation and Collaborative Learning Master of Philosophy students are active contributors to their research groups, where collegiality and collaboration are central skills. This involves: Attending research team meetings to share updates, receive feedback, and engage in scholarly dialogue to enhance knowledge of the research area and troubleshoot experimental issues. Attending seminars and workshops to refine scientific communication and presentation skills, and to develop professional capabilities. Overall, the Master of Philosophy program is designed as a developmental journey - guiding students from structured mentorship to independent research, while embedding professional capabilities, critical thinking, and collaborative practice.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate effectively within a research team.
Develop a research plan and design suitable experiments to address an existing gap in disciplinary knowledge based on a review of existing literature.
Communicate research findings effectively in diverse contexts.
Conduct independent research to generate new knowledge relating to a medical, environmental or biotechnology problem.
Critically situate research and professional capabilities within the current state of the field, articulating how the work contributes to, extends, or challenges existing knowledge.
prerequisites: Admission requisite: Admission into C04267 Master of Philosophy in Science

title: Scientific Perspectives for Global Issues
syllabus_overview:
Our planet is undergoing significant change at multiple scales. This subject equips you with the skills to investigate current and future global challenges through scientific inquiry. You’ll explore the importance and application of scientific thinking and diverse knowledge systems, focusing on those of Indigenous peoples of Australia, in addressing complex global issues and sustainability. You will examine how knowledge is produced through scientific processes, and learn to evaluate and synthesise scientific information from multiple sources. You’ll develop critical thinking, communication skills, professional and ethical attributes essential for a successful scientific career.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is delivered using a blended learning approach, with a series of complementary interactive online activities, collaborative workshops and online workshops to explore science as a knowledge system and current scientific thinking and practices used to address global issues facing society. Collaborative Workshops (2h, on campus): The collaborative workshops are held on campus. In preparation for the collaborative workshop activities and discussions with your peers, you complete pre-workshop online activities, which are designed to introduce you to the topics using articles, videos and real-world examples. The pre-workshop online activities are available via Canvas and are completed before attending your workshop. During the collaborative workshops, you engage with your peers in small group and class discussions and collaborate through guided inquiry case studies about science as a system of knowledge, how scientific knowledge is gathered, organised and shared ethically and responsibly, and applications of scientific thinking and practices to address current global issues. The workshops are designed to help you develop critical thinking, inquiry, collaboration and communication skills in a supportive learning environment. You are strongly encouraged to attend all scheduled workshops to maximise learning opportunities. The readings and worksheets used in workshops will be available on Canvas. After the workshops, you complete post-workshop exercises to consolidate and critically reflect on your workshop learning experience, scientific thinking and skills development. Online Workshops (1h, online): During certain weeks, you attend a timetabled online workshop in addition to the on campus collaborative workshop. The online workshops are held via Zoom and are dedicated time for you to develop academic and scientific writing skills and receive detailed information about the major assessment tasks. You will have the opportunity to ask questions about the subject material. The workshops are not recorded and you are strongly encouraged to attend to maximise your learning. Refer to the information on Canvas and subject announcements for the weeks, Zoom links and topics covered. Feedback: Feedback on your progress and opportunities to check your understanding are available while completing the online activities and during workshops from your peers and Teaching Associates. Criteria-based rubrics provide guidance and feedback for the written assessment tasks. Academic Language Proficiency: An aim of this subject is to help you develop academic and professional language and communication skills in order to succeed at university and in the workplace. To determine your current academic language proficiency, you are required to complete an online language screening task, OPELA (information available at About OPELA for Students ).If you receive a Basic grade for OPELA, you will be directed to a language development intensive during Stuvac. If you do not complete OPELA you will receive a sanction preventing access to view your subject results and transcript in My Student Admin . Assessment Task 3 will be assessed for English language proficiency. You will be directed to further language support after the completion of this subject if your language is below the required standard.
learning_outcomes: Explain the process of scientific knowledge production, and evaluate and synthesise scientific information from multiple sources.
Critically examine the process, responsibilities and limitations of science in addressing global challenges.
Explain ethical communication strategies and considerations to engage with Indigenous peoples and communities in scientific research.
Critically reflect on and communicate new scientific perspectives on global issues and sustainability.
Analyse and summarise major global challenges within Australian and sustainability contexts.

title: Screen Ideas

syllabus_overview:
This subject immerses you in diverse screenwriting practices for short drama, hybrid, animation, and immersive media. You'll develop creative screen ideas, drawing from industry standards, independent, micro-budget, and emerging media models. You'll enhance your understanding of narrative structure, character development, and refine your script-editing skills. Students are expected to regularly check and engage with subject materials on the online subject site in order to effectively manage their learning experience.

By reading and analysing contemporary screenplays you'll explore how literary concepts have adapted to various screen formats and their unique demands. Seminar activities include student presentations, discussions of in-class screenings and creative practice exercises. From the start of session students complete a range of in-class exercises, receiving formative feedback from their tutor and peers. This feedback scaffolds the assessments.

syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces you to the core principles of screenwriting. By reading and analysing contemporary screenplays, and engaging with relevant theory, you will gain an understanding of how common literary concepts have been adapted for the purpose of telling stories on screen. As you craft your own short screenplay, we will ask you to consider the ethical questions surrounding narrative ownership and who gets to tell what stories. Your understanding of screen story will deepen through practical exercises, enriched by feedback from tutors and peers, developing your skills as a cinematic storyteller.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is delivered through engagement with online content and face to face lectures and seminars. The online content and lectures contextualise key concepts (theoretical and practical) that have shaped the way we craft stories for the screen. Seminars are the venue for activities that will help you apply this knowledge and develop your craft. Seminar activities include student presentations, discussions of in-class screenings and creative practice exercises that will be rolled out from the first week of session. You will be given formative feedback from your tutor and peers on these exercises, scaffolding the delivery of your assessment tasks.
learning_outcomes: Explore and analyse a range of screen story theories and formats
Demonstrate an introductory knowledge of the contribution of Indigenous screen storytellers to Australian culture and an understanding of their self-determination practices
Consider and apply ethical frameworks to screen story development
Analyse and write about screen story in a scholarly way
Apply audio-visual storytelling techniques

title: Secure Programming and Penetration Testing
syllabus_overview:
This subject will equip you with the knowledge and skills necessary to develop secure software and assess the security of systems through source code analysis and penetration testing techniques. There will be coverage of the principles and practices of secure coding, the identification and mitigation of vulnerabilities, software verification, and the methodologies used in penetration testing. You will learn how to approach and develop automatic auditing systems, identifying vulnerabilities and developing security analysis and testing methods to protect systems against cyber-attacks. Additionally, you'll have the chance to engage in national and international security challenges, with assessments on secure programming, software analysis, and your communication skills in speaking and writing.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject uses active learning strategies, which involves a series of on-campus workshops and tutorials to support a hands-on and lab-focused collaborative learning activities. Students will build up their professional experience in secure programming and penetration testing throughout each workshop accomplishment. Outside class, students will be required to review online materials, pre-readings and open education resources before taking the on-campus workshops. Students will also conduct an authentic ethical hacking project in small teams through multi-staged assessments, which mainly composed of information gathering and enumeration plan report, and performance and analysis report in real testing. Students will have experiences in reflecting on and identifying how they may improve both group and individual activities through Canvas discussions boards as required to communicate ideas and questions with peers when studying the subject. Feedback for assessment tasks will be given to students two weeks after submission. Students will also receive in-class feedback for their workshops and tutorial exercises on weekly basis.
learning_outcomes: Automate the analysis of a software project using source code analysis on top of compilers to defend against real‐world attacks from malicious entities. (D.1)
Classify software security vulnerabilities in the source code of systems, applications, and services. (D.1)
Communicate effectively individually and as a team to describe plans for countering changing security threats. (E.1)
prerequisites: Academic requisite: 31251 Data Structures and Algorithms
Academic requisite: 41012 Programming for Mechatronic Systems

title: Self and Society
syllabus_overview:
How are we shaped by the societies in which we live? This subject introduces students to key ideas in social and political thought which enable us to understand social life. It focuses on concepts such as class, race and gender and explores how these structures shape society and the life-paths of individuals and groups. As a core activity of the subject, students learn how to conduct a life history interview, in order to build their own social analysis of one individual's life story. A close examination of an individual life history enables students to understand how self and society are powerfully intertwined.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject consists of lectures, tutorials and large collaborative studios, with independent student reading the basis for active, collaborative learning supported by online resources. Face-to-face classes incorporate a range of teaching and learning strategies including short presentations, videos, discussion of readings and case studies and student group work. Tutorials and assignments provide opportunities for students to deepen their knowledge through critical analysis, creative, self-directed, and collaborative inquiry, library and digital research, and through giving and receiving constructive feedback. Formative feedback is provided during the first half of the session, via informal class quizzes and other activities. Tutorials and assignments enhance students’ capacity to apply their knowledge and to advocate and intervene ethically in public debates and global civil society, by developing professional skills in communication, responsible leadership and teamwork, project management, and problem solving.
learning_outcomes: Organise and present information from scholarly literature and empirical data
Explain key concepts of the social sciences
Apply theory and mobilise empirical data for social analysis
Appreciate different standpoints, viewpoints and frameworks for understanding the social world

title: Sense Studio: Mark/Make
syllabus_overview:
You'll choose from various studios to enhance your conceptual, formal, analytical, and critical skills from prior studies or work. Each studio offers a space to experiment with design, encouraging innovation through creative material and process combinations, with an emphasis on craftsmanship. You must be self-motivated and independent. Activities vary by discipline, including generating and testing ideas, developing propositions, or crafting well-designed objects and experiences.

Teaching Strategies:
This studio aims to develop your skills in independent/self directed/negotiated research and practice. It provides an opportunity to develop and integrate conceptual and practical skill sets, and focuses on the completion of a self-determined and self-generated project. The studio prioritises learning outcomes in: research, critical thinking, creativity, judgment, technical mastery, problem solving and conceptual thinking. The emphasis is on independent/self directed/negotiated projects which are supported by tutorials and group critiques. Work will be evaluated based on aesthetic and conceptual qualities, innovative approaches to the medium, and overall effort. Each week, in class, you will present design project work to your studio leader and peers. In class you will participate in discussion of all the work presented. Your role in providing feedback to your peers, and in opening yourself to feedback on your own project, will help you to develop good judgment in relation to design development, as well as prepare you to work effectively in design teams in professional practice. During the week, between classes, you will need to significantly develop your project for further presentation, drawing upon ongoing research as well as on the feedback provided in class. There is an expectation of approx 10 hrs of self-directed project development outside class hours each week.
learning_outcomes: Evidence of self-direction and autonomy in the research, design development, production and commercialisation processes.
Appreciate the importance of experimentation in new product design.
Develop appropriately considered and well resolved design outcomes.
Demonstrate the skill and knowledge required to develop designs for small or limited batch production.
Demonstrated sensitivity in selection, use and application of design media.
Ability to reflect upon and explain your own learning, thoughts and ideas.
Demonstrate the ability to develop broad reaching conceptual project ideas.
prerequisites: Admission requisite: Admission into C04243 Master of Design

title: Sensors and Control for Mechatronic Systems
syllabus_overview:
This subject aims to enhance your theoretical knowledge and practical skills in sensing, estimation, as well as feedback control techniques for mechatronic and robotic systems. You'll learn to select and evaluate sensors, process sensor data, and implement computer-aided tools for designing estimation and control systems that leverage sensory information. Key topics include visual and depth sensing, time-of-flight measurements, detection, tracking, state-space modelling, estimation (Kalman filter) and advanced control strategies like linear quadratic control. Real-world engineering case studies will contextualise and examine these concepts.

Teaching Strategies:
Modern teaching techniques will be used in this subject to facilitate active learning through interactive lectures and practical exercises in a clearly defined and real-life context. The students will further enhance the competencies in sensing, data processing, estimation and control required to develop intelligent mechatronic systems. Students will have the opportunity to review learning materials, participate in in-class discussions and to follow guided exercises to further strengthen their knowledge. Students will personalise their learning experience and methods through an open project on close-loop sensing and control system development and delivery. Regular attendance is expected during the teaching sessions.
learning_outcomes: Explain the fundamental working principles of sensors and demonstrate data acquisition from these sensors for use in mechatronic system applications. (D.1)
Design sensor, signal processing and control solutions to solve practical problems. (C.1)
Apply knowledge of image processing and active sensor processing for using the data to guide mechatronic systems. (D.1)
Apply knowledge of advanced control techniques to control mechatronic systems. (D.1)
prerequisites: Academic requisite: 48622 Embedded Mechatronics Systems

title: Serious Games and Gamification Studio
syllabus_overview:
This subject focuses on creating serious games and gamified experiences, designed for purposes beyond entertainment such as education or training. You'll learn cutting-edge design frameworks and techniques for tailoring games to specific audiences and objectives. Working with end-users, you'll engage in co-design workshops, prototype development, playtesting, and evaluation to ensure impactful outcomes. Additionally, you'll consider the ethical implications inherent in game design.

Teaching Strategies:
In the first half of the semester, students will be presented with the theoretical foundation for designing and developing a serious game. Each lesson will include a case study focusing on the successes, challenges and lessons learnt from real-life research projects that used serious games for various purposes (including health, language preservation, rehabilitation, education, among others). As new concepts and topics are introduced, students will be expected to reflect on how these could be incorporated in their own semester project. The second half of the teaching session focuses on putting in practice all the skills learned up to this point. Students will design and develop a game-like prototype that helps a specific audience achieve a meaningful real-world outcome. For this, they will work closely with the audience they are designing for and will receive guidance from the subject coordinator/tutor. Students will be exposed to a mix of user-centred design methodologies that will help them understand the needs and preferences of a target audience, including participatory design, small focus groups, and workshops, to name a few. Also, students will follow a series of agile game development principles to efficiently build rapid game prototypes that illustrate core game mechanics and formal elements chosen for their games. This includes sprint planning meetings, SCRUM meetings and review meetings. Formative feedback will be provided by the subject/coordinator during such meetings (in class). At the end of the session, students will demonstrate their game prototypes to the UTS community in the form of a showcase.
learning_outcomes: Design a game-like prototype that serves a specific purpose for a specific audience. (C.1)
Critically reflect on one’s own designs and iteratively propose alternate game-like solutions that fit a purpose and benefit an audience. (F.1)
Evaluate ethical, cultural, and societal considerations when designing a bespoke serious game or gamified experience. (B.1)
Apply professional standards relating to Indigenous Australian contexts when designing games and serious games. (A.1)
prerequisites: Academic requisite: 31262 Game Design Methodologies

title: Service Design Communication - Beyond Journey Maps
syllabus_overview:
Services are considered difficult to market because they have been described, famously, as things you cannot drop on your foot. This subject explores ways in which the quality of a service can be made tangible, to designers and their participants, to employees who must perform them, and to customers in order that they learn how to engage with the services appropriately. Services, as interactions between people over time, are designed in industry at the moment primarily through ‘Service Design Blueprints,’ a variation of ‘Customer Journey Maps.’ These are useful for baseline sketches of linear sequences of activities so that organisations can plan how to resource customer experiences. To comprehensively design and implement a service requires a more diverse set of richer communication design strategies. Students in this subject learn new ways of depicting service interactions that allow all involved to anticipate more complex and adaptive services.

Teaching Strategies:
Seminar and Studio
learning_outcomes: Visually plan for service delivery variability
Understand the place of Service Blueprints in the history of process and value management
Communicate service designs in diverse and creative ways

title: Service Design Foundations
syllabus_overview:
You will learn Service Design, which enhances interactions between those seeking change and those providing assistance. Service Designers streamline these interactions and prepare for unexpected events. Unlike other design disciplines that focus on materials, Service Design directly shapes the behaviour of all participants, including customers and community members. Recognising services as value-creating and inherently political, the course starts with the history of services and the emergence of the service economy, identifying design principles for effective service design. It then critically examines contemporary service design tools, and finally addresses service management challenges.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject is structured as a seminar with applied research exercises. You will be discussing readings and listening to lectures on a range of Service Design concepts, and the evaluating their validity by observing services you engage with, and developing insights into other ways in which services can be designed. As a result of participating in this subject, you will be develop more sophisticated ways of designing services that ensure the dignity of both those who need help and those prepared to help them. In addition, students will need to complete guided research into live services that they can access. The subject assessments involve writing up case studies of research into services that exemplify the concepts examined in the modules. Evaluation and feedback on submitted tasks will be provided through the ReView system following self-evaluations by the students.
learning_outcomes: Clearly describe the history of services and the more recent history of the service economy as the backdrop for the rise of the practice of Service Design
Demonstrate a familiarity with the language of the management of services and service workers and customer relations
Understand the limits of, by modifying the use of, commonly used Service Design tools such as Service Blueprints and Customer Journeys
Critically evaluate a service, on the basis of interviews and observations, in terms of the dignified co-creation of value.
Translate the service design principles values of maximising autonomy and minimising role stress for all involved in a service interaction to a wide range of service contexts

title: Service Design Research
syllabus_overview: Service designing means developing not only a new service system, but also devising the service of implementing that service. This subject introduces different tools and techniques for establishing a new or modified service design. Students will learn how to research the organizational cultural changes needed to establish new social practices of service, motivating the adoption of new service habits and values by service providers and recipients.

title: Service Design: Advanced Research
syllabus_overview: This subject focuses on designing services in extreme or challenging social contexts. In this subject we draw on the history of work undertaken by social and service designers in the School of Design for over a decade, for example in Designing Out Crime, to engage with designing services for diverse experiences and in complex social scenarios.
prerequisites: Academic corequisite: 81533 Service Design Foundations

title: Service Design: Communication
syllabus_overview: There are a range of maps, canvases, blueprints and tools for understanding and communicating service journeys that are very dominant in the industry now and tend to convey uniformity. In this workshop-based subject, students develop innovative ways of communicating the service experiences they are designing. Students learn techniques of rich storytelling and how to engage a range of different scenarios.
prerequisites: Academic corequisite: 85808 Service Design: Implementation

title: Service Design: Implementation
syllabus_overview: In this studio, students learn how to ensure their service designs get realised. A design for service implementation is a crucial but underdeveloped aspect of service designing. Students learn to develop protocols and techniques for clients or partners to carry service designs through to fruition, including the evaluation of the service. Often, this means service designers embedding themselves with their clients in organisations to make sure the design gets realised.
prerequisites: Academic corequisite: 89107 Service Design: Communication

title: Service Supply Chain Design and Innovation
syllabus_overview:
Service supply chains are complex, adaptive networks requiring dynamic processes and real-time decision-making. This subject equips you with an understanding of service characteristics and the management of service supply chain networks. You'll learn the importance of collaboration, information sharing, and visibility across the service value network. It emphasises service strategies, customer co-creation, and collaborative value creation, alongside frameworks and models for service design, network operations, and configurations. The subject also highlights the critical role of human and technology-centric approaches in people-embedded service networks. You'll gain insights into the value of data, innovative data analysis techniques, and develop the technical knowledge necessary for managing end-to-end service value networks effectively.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is delivered online using a range of resources, self-directed study and live interactive sessions with the academic. Learners engage in the essential content through a variety of formats (lecture slides, notes, webinars, videos, articles, real case studies) online and learner-led dialogue through online discussions and posts, and interactions via Canvas. The teaching and learning strategies have been designed to enable learners to make progress in their achievement and maximise their accomplishment of the learning outcomes. Various teaching and learning strategies adopted are as follows: Learners will be expected to read all the assigned readings and media articles, research and identify innovative models and effective techniques applicable to service supply chain design and innovation that result in enhanced performance management. By conducting self-paced study, learners contribute to the discussions on the influence of service supply chain/service value networks on firm performance. This will enhance learners’ ability to progress successfully throughout the subject and complete all assessment items effectively. The online sessions will provide opportunities for group activities and discussion, selfassessment, peer review and formative feedback from the subject facilitator. Online collaborative sessions with the facilitator will be conducted at a set time. Formative and summative feedback will be provided to all learners and will take several forms, including quizzes during the independent learning activities and online collaborative sessions to support and enhance learner performance outcomes via assessments.
learning_outcomes: Develop and understand the role of data, information, and technology-centric approaches for value creation in service value networks
Understand fundamentals of service characteristics to design and manage cross-cultural processes
Analyse service design, delivery, and operations to innovate, co-create value through collaboration with stakeholders, and devise new business models
Apply frameworks and models for service supply chain design and delivery, including customer journey orchestration

title: Services and Network Productivity with Data Analytics
syllabus_overview:
This subject focuses on designing and managing service operations and supply chains through data analytics. You'll learn service strategies involving customer engagement and value creation, alongside models for service design that integrate human and technological elements. The subject develops your skills in using analytics for decision-making and measuring productivity in service and supply chain networks. You'll gain the ability to operate service value networks effectively using data analytics tools in complex business settings.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject is taught using flipped leaming, along with a combination of lectures, case studies, video material and experiential exercises to assess students' understanding theory and its application across the subject through real service and supply chain network problems. Lectures and tutorials allow students to engage with real-world problems using interactive, group-based leaming activities, where students collaborate to solve service and value network problems. These classes are supplemented with both print and electronic leaming materials which students must access in advance of class, in order to be fully prepared to engage with in-class activities. The learning management system is used to facilitate learning. All students will be provided with the opportunity to receive formative feedback on their performance during the sessions. Other forms of formative and summative assessments and feedback include the use of quizzes, peer review activities and opportunities for self-assessment and reflection. Further feedback will be provided specifically on the progression of technical and professional skills during sessions and in relation to the completion of each of the worksheets and submitted assessment tasks.
learning_outcomes: Apply and interpret results using different methodologies used to analyse business performance
Discuss the challenges of managing different types of service network configurations and how customers and other stakeholders facilitate value co-creation in service value networks
Explain the nature of and service specific attributes, concepts around service strategy, service concepts, new service development and the service eco- system
Describe the human-mediated and computational connected services available and the toolkits that can be applied in service and supply chain network environments

title: Services Marketing
syllabus_overview:
This subject enables you to broaden your understanding of marketing by focusing on the marketing of services. Services dominate the global economy and are becoming critical for competitive advantage in organisations across the world and in all industry sectors. Services require a distinctive approach to marketing strategy, both in its development and execution. In this subject, you will explore the foundations of services marketing, including how to create, promise, and deliver a successful, interactive customer experience.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject is based on dynamic and interactive lecture and tutorial sessions. It is taught through a combination of lectures and tutorials. The lectures involve critical debate and case deliberations; and the tutorials are built around in-class exercises, case discussions and presentations. These classes will be supplemented with both printed and electronic learning materials and resources. The UTS Learning Management System will be used to share information and encourage interaction between staff and students. Students will also use appropriate computer software such as spreadsheets and word processors to complete assigned tasks.
learning_outcomes: Produce and justify practical solutions to complex services marketing problems
Apply analytical perspectives and decision tools, which underlie creative services marketing

title: Servicescape and Venue: design, operations and management
syllabus_overview:
This subject focuses on the management of servicescapes and venue design, encompassing planning, operation, evaluation, and maintenance. You'll learn about various venues, including stadia, tourist attractions, performing arts centres, museums, multipurpose arenas, and convention centres. Key issues such as outsourcing, traffic flow, and security are addressed. Featuring guest speakers and incorporating current trends and case studies, the subject prepares you to adeptly manage venues in line with future developments.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject involves a variety of teaching and learning activities, which may include: lectures, case study presentations; expert panel discussions; student presentations; and directed readings. This subject adopts aspects of flipped and collaborative learning that requires students to accept learning responsibility of pre-preparing for workshops through engagement with pre-class exercises/readings readings and pre-class tests or contributing to online pre-class exercises. Key concepts from pre-class activities will be reviewed in an interactive approach to lectures together with weekly case studies. The workshop environment will involve understanding key concepts and case studies through collaborative learning based on video reviews, experiential learning and field trips. Students have a learning responsibility to not only prepare for class but to actively participate in collaborative exercises and report on the outcomes of such exercises. In addition to the lecturing staff, selected practitioners with direct experience in one or more areas related to venue management will present on particular topics. The underlying learning strategy employed in this subject is one of linking theory, concepts, ideas and techniques associated with venue and facility management to actual practice. Students receive informal feedback based on the workshop exercises, class quizzes and reflective case study/field trip activities; and formal feedback on group venue selection approval form, individual report and poster/video presentation.
learning_outcomes: Describe processes associated with the design, planning, management and operations of servicescapes and venues
Demonstrate an understanding of the main components of servicescape and venues and the development and management in both local and global environments
Critically evaluate servicescapes and venues in terms of their management and operation practices
Identify and discuss key operational practices in servicescape and venue design and management

title: Sexing Power
syllabus_overview:
This subject examines in depth how social and political institutions function to regulate sex, gender and sexuality, how gender analysis helps us understand contemporary social and political issues, and how gender and sexual identities are embodied and performed in everyday life. In this subject, you undertake a rigorous and detailed analysis of the notions of sex, gender and sexuality in a wide variety of cultural and social contexts.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject includes interactive lectures and class discussions based on in-class student presentations using various multimedia/ open education resources; Intense student-initiated small-group tutorial ‘theme-explorations’ and online discussions sustaining collaborative investigations and debates. Students receive formative/diagnostic feedback on their assignments through the provision of “benchmarking”, discussion of criteria, feedback from tutors and peers, self-assessment and reflection.
learning_outcomes: Examine in depth how social and political institutions function to regulate sex, gender and sexuality
Analyse theories and social/cultural practices relating to gender and identity within a transnational context
Examine gender from a critical theoretical, interdisciplinary and cross-cultural framework
Explain theories of gender, culture and power through contemporary issue-centred debates
Reflect on students’ own practice

title: Shaping Meaningful Worlds: Language Texts and Context
syllabus_overview:
This subject hones your ability to use language with precision, creativity, and appropriateness across various purposes, contexts, and audiences. You will engage in writing for different audiences, responding to and crafting a range of texts with growing confidence and skill. The course focuses on structuring texts effectively, enhancing the flow of ideas, paragraphing, sentence construction, and vocabulary. You'll also critically read and discuss texts to evaluate their purpose and features, aiding your own text composition. Additionally, you'll refine your listening, speaking, and visual representation skills through active engagement with texts and peer interactions.

Teaching Strategies:
Face-to-face classes will incorporate a range of teaching and learning strategies including short presentations, videos, simulations, discussion of readings and student groupwork. Independent student reading, writing and reflection will complement these strategies. Students will be be expected to demonstrate high levels of active and collaborative interaction and independent research into examples of writing appropriate for their own learning and relevant to the subject.
learning_outcomes: Respond to a diverse range of texts reflectively and with growing expertise, insight and confidence;
Critique a range of language forms, features and texts to express ideas, information and emotions clearly, effectively and appropriately;
Use language skilfully, appropriately, imaginatively and with precision in a range of forms and contexts for different purposes and audiences;
Work collaboratively with others in pairs and small groups;
Apply appropriate academic writing and referencing conventions

title: Shaping Policies for the Future
syllabus_overview:
This subject equips you with a critical understanding of how public policy, shaped by scientific, economic, social, and political factors, affects health, wellbeing and sustainability. You'll study the creation of evidence-based science policies, including climate action and vaccination programs, and learn about the regulatory frameworks and authorities that govern science in Australia and internationally. You’ll develop a critical understanding of the theories and practices behind developing some of the most influential evidence-based science policies. You will also develop an appreciation of the complexity of decision-making processes in the public sphere, where the formulation of public policies depends on a variety of scientific, economic, social, and political forces.

Teaching Strategies:
Shaping Policies for the Future is designed as a completely online educational experience that students can take at their own pace. Students explore real-world public policy development through a range of rich interactive content and media. Students will examine real-world policy development through relevant case studies in peer-connected learning activities, including discussion boards, aimed at building the required skills and knowledge in a collaborative online environment. This will include pre-recorded video presentations, interviews and pre-set readings. Assessments are designed to complement student learning and provides students with the opportunity to apply and track their skills development as well as their understanding of key concepts. Students will receive formative feedback on their work throughout the session.
learning_outcomes: Appreciate the influence public policy has on the health and wellbeing of people and the environment.
Critically analyse the established scientific theories and practices that underpin evidence-based policies.
Develop an integrated understanding of how science interplays with economic, social, environmental, and political influences during policy development
Identify relevant regulatory frameworks and governing bodies in Australian and global contexts

title: Show and Tell: Francophone Cultures on Display
syllabus_overview:
This subject is designed to provide students who are proficient in reading, listening, speaking and writing in French with opportunities to engage with francophone culture. It corresponds to Level B2/C1 (independent/proficient user) of the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) for Languages. You’ll examine and engage with the sociocultural contexts in which the language is used, specifically with regard to its role in visual and performative communication in the francophone world. Via written, oral and aural assessments that demonstrate continuing mastery of the French language, your learning will involve a communicative approach, engaging in interactive tasks and using a variety of resources to enhance language proficiency. You'll be expected to prepare for classes through various exercises and analyse a variety of authentic sources in a manner that considers their cultural provenance and role. You’ll explore subject materials and concepts through independent research, creative outputs and/or close textual analysis. The language learning approach will focus on linguistic and cultural practices across the francophone world. You’ll be expected to commit to approximately 12 hours of weekly study, including class time, and immerse yourself in French both inside and outside the classroom to build confidence and fluency.

Teaching Strategies:
Class time is used for interactive practice and advancement of skills through work in pairs, small and large groups and/or presentations, as well as clarification of subject content. Students will spend a substantial portion of each lesson in dialogue with their peers and their teacher. Preparation for these activities requires students to complete exercises and reading/listening/viewing activities prior to coming to class and for them to make effective use of subject materials (including UTS Online), community and peer resources available to them to support their learning. As this is an 8 credit point subject, the approximate time commitment expected from students is 12 hours per week, including class time. Students will customise their learning experience as per the Global French approach to promote their engagement with francophone peoples and societies. This entails keeping in mind one's goals for the use of French (for instance studying abroad or travel in a particular country or region) and tailoring one's practice and learning to maximise exposure to local variants of the language, relevant cultural norms and authentic materials from the area. As part of an immersive approach to language education, students are expected to use only French when communicating with each other or with their teacher in class. Students are encouraged to explore subject materials and concepts through independent research, creative outputs and/or close textual analysis.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical cultural awareness of multiple francophone peoples and societies.

Communicate effectively in oral and written form, in French, on a wide range of topics, as set out in the subject program. This roughly corresponds to the skill set for students at the B2/C1 level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages.
Effectively employ strategies and resources for independent learning as relevant to the subject program.
Evidence competence in critical engagement with the specific topics discussed in the subject program.

title: Signals and Systems
syllabus_overview:
This subject lays the theoretical groundwork for system analysis and equips you with skills for designing components within control and communication systems. You will learn to derive models from actual devices, compare predictions with experimental outcomes, and apply your knowledge through a group project focused on a real-world control or communication challenge. Core topics include signal representation, system modelling with equations and transforms, signal processing, the interplay between discrete and continuous data, feedback effects, system performance, stability, and control design principles. Through various learning activities, you will also improve your academic literacy and gain insight into engineering's diverse practice areas. The subject incorporates lectures, tutorials, lab work, and project assignments. Lab sessions, integrated with MATLAB simulations, reinforce theoretical concepts and allow you to engage with practical applications directly.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject uses a problem-based learning strategy that allows students to research and develop their own solutions to complex design challenges. There are a number of formal laboratory sessions. Students then undertake a substantial group project that reinforces the theoretical content and culminates in a formal written presentation of their work. Class class time occurs in two 2 hour sessions per week. The first 2 hour session is used to conduct class activities, such as collaborative problem solving. The second 2 hour session is used to conduct hands-on activities. 1. Prior to each class session, students will be required to study the Notes and associated readings and prepare questions relating to the weekly content and the assesment tasks they are working on. 2. At the beginning of the class session, academic staff will discuss with the entire group the challenges they are facing. Students faced with similar challenges will be prompted to come together to facilitate collaborative discussions and work on tutorial exercises in a group setting. 3. Prior to each lab session, students will be required to complete pre-lab work. 4. In the lab session, students will work in groups of 2 on their tasks. Academic staff are available in each lab to review work and provide immediate feedback. 5. For the final project, lab time will be used for one-on-one consultations on particular aspects of a student's work.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, design, simulate and test parts of a communication system and a control system in both the time-domain and frequency-domain. (D.1)
Measure time and frequency characteristics of signals and systems using appropriate laboratory equipment. (D.1)
Communicate technical ideas, decisions, calculations and experimental results in a written document. (E.1)
Apply the mathematical tools associated with transform theory to the analysis and design of continuous-time and discrete-time systems. (D.1)
Model real and complex systems using a hierarchical approach, and be able to simplify them with appropriate assumptions. (D.1)

title: Site Establishment and Management
syllabus_overview:
This subject explores construction site establishment, operation, and surveying, addressing the dynamic nature of sites as projects progress. You'll delve into excavation issues, including shoring and piling, and the design and erection of temporary structures. You'll also develop advanced site surveying skills, using theodolites and mastering building marking out techniques, with a continuous focus on safety and legal liabilities. Through individual and group work, you'll create operational plans for site efficiency and safety, select temporary facilities, determine excavation stabilisation methods, optimise earthmoving productivity, manage site traffic, and conduct precise surveying and setting out. As a construction manager, you're expected to master these principles and practices, combining theoretical knowledge with practical application of manual and technological tools.

Teaching Strategies:
Classes will incorporate a range of teaching and learning strategies including lectures, videos, discussion of readings and case studies, online quizzes, and student group work. Materials related to each strategy, including lecture notes, exercises, tutorial instructions, tasks' briefs, questions and answers, and videos will be provided on UTS Canvas. This subject involves field exercises including surveying exercises and potentially site visits. The site visits aim to enable students collect information of a case project to be used in developing a site establishment plan. Both formative and summative feedback will be provided to assist students in achieving the intended learning outcomes. The formative feedback is typically delivered informally during lectures or tutorials at the scale of the whole class and students are responsible to record any feedback given. The summative feedback focuses on assessment outcomes of a certain task and will be provided in writing along with grades on UTS Canvas.
learning_outcomes: Survey and set out buildings.
Methodically examine a project site environment and conditions in order to effectively establish a site.
Investigate and describe the sub-strata conditions of a site.
Develop site and environmental plans.

title: Skill Acquisition
syllabus_overview:
This subject is for those aiming to deepen their understanding of motor control and skill acquisition. You will extend your knowledge of neuromotor functions and implement this into the evaluation and design of effective motor training programs. Emphasizing the principles of motor learning, this subject offers valuable insights into the prescription of skills in sport and exercise. Interactive sessions will help you apply theoretical concepts in practical settings. Your learning will be facilitated through a blend of pre-class activities, online engagement, and hands-on laboratory work, focused on applying theory to real-world scenarios.

Teaching Strategies:
The following teaching and learning strategies will be utilised to achieve student learning outcomes: Before class activities (online) Information activities (online) Application activities (face to face & online) Before class activities will be provided through Canvas. Students will be encouraged to engage in these activities prior to participating in any tutorial/laboratory sessions. This will aid students in gaining a basic understanding of the week's content before attending. The Before class activities will be reflected upon in the Information and Application activities. Content will be delivered each week online in a series of recorded presentations. Information activities will be recorded in real time using screen capture software and uploaded to Canvas. Students may access these recordings at any time following the release of the presentations until the completion of the subject. During laboratory sessions, students will engage with instructors and peers to undertake Application activities and solve workbook questions. Students are strongly encouraged to familiarise themselves with the key learning outcomes that are listed in the laboratory handbook for each practical session and examine online material prior to class to improve their chance for success in this subject. In addition, students will be able to register their interest in weekly Question and Answer sessions. These sessions will be conducted online and students will have the opportunity to raise questions, explore topics further or seek clarification on assessment details via this forum. Finally, students will also have the opportunity to undertake a number of online quizzes before the census date for enrolment. Students are strongly encouraged to complete this assessment as they will be provided with in-class, informal feedback on their performance during the following lecture and/or laboratory.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the different stages involved in motor learning
Apply knowledge from biomechanics, anatomy, physiology, and sport psychology to motor learning
Classify and measure motor skill performance
Implement common theoretical models explaining the motor learning processes
Design and discuss a motor learning protocol / environment to maximise motor learning in a sport, exercise and health contexts

title: Skills and Wills Practice
syllabus_overview:
This subject covers the skills, practice areas and values you will require to be admitted to practise law as prescribed by the ‘competency standards’ set out in the Legal Profession Uniform Admission Rules 2015. This subject is part of the Practical Legal Training (PLT) program. You will develop and apply your legal skills and understanding of the ethical responsibilities of legal practitioners, including obligations relating to legal costs and the trust and office accounts. Participation in drafting, interviewing and negotiation workshops and in the practice area of wills and estate administration will enable you to practise essential skills in a client- focused environment. You will also develop a capacity for building professionalism and resilience as a legal practitioner

Teaching Strategies:
Strategy 1: Preparation for Professional Practice Students are introduced to learning for professional practice through their preparation for lectures and assessment tasks using specific resources and materials. Students build on their preparatory learning in face-to-face workshops and online activities based on the work of an entry-level lawyer. Preparation for lectures and activities includes reading lectures slides, articles and engaging with instructional video and other online resources. Students collaborate in groups, distributing tasks, providing feedback comments to peers about their contribution to the documents and completing activities together. Teachers provide feedback on workshop tasks completed. In this preparation, students are also required to draw on their knowledge of the law in their academic study in order to understand its application. Strategy 2: Lectures Lectures given by clinical practitioners and guest lecturers from the profession provide students with real-world knowledge, skills and values relevant to legal practice. To assist students, lectures are recorded and complemented by additional resources on CANVAS. Students are provided with practical scenarios demonstrating the application of knowledge and skills in legal practice. The lectures form the basis for work undertaken in on-campus workshops and on CANVAS. Strategy 3: Workshop activities – face-to-face Face-to-face workshop activities are planned to enable students to achieve the Competencies required by the Legal Profession Admission Board (LPAB). These activities, based on the work of lawyers in practice, are designed to scaffold student learning in the academic degree through to the development of professional skills and an ethical framework. Students are encouraged to discuss the professional tasks undertaken in the workshops and on CANVAS. Structured opportunities are provided to allow students to practise professional skills and to receive peer and clinical practitioner feedback prior to undertaking practical assessments, including a simulated negotiation applying the principled bargaining approach and simulated client interviews. Workshop activities are the platform for assessment tasks, engaging students to think, reflect and apply legal knowledge from their learning in core and elective subjects to a practical application. Students have the opportunity to experience the role as an advocate in a court, utilising the mock trial courts with video equipment enabling students to observe and reflect on their and fellow students’ experience. Strategy 4: Online learning All students access material and resources on CANVAS. Students engage in student-led discussion. All students have access to an online Discussion Board forum on CANVAS providing students with resources to assist in their understanding and in collaboration of tasks. Students are encouraged to share their questions, experience and helpful information on the Discussion Board with prompt guidance and support from the Subject Coordinator. Strategy 5: Ongoing feedback Ongoing formative feedback is provided to students individually and in groups throughout the subject on practice-based activities; and on CANVAS discussion forums, as well as giving written feedback on marked assignments. This formative feedback is provided on activities from Day 1 providing students with multiple early opportunities to gauge their learning and progress. Students are encouraged to conduct themselves as a professional and to produce work of a standard expected of an entry-level lawyer. In order to achieve this, students practise, refine and receive feedback on their oral and written communications and their ability to receive and apply feedback. Students have the opportunity to reflect on how to give feedback to peers that is considered and measured. Students are able to engage with resources in relation to resilience in order to recognise the duty to self as well as others and to develop as self-directed and autonomous professionals within a practice of work/life balance. The ongoing provision of feedback enables students to develop the capacity to work effectively in a team, to mentor peers and to understand the value of professional development. Strategy 6: Communication and Collaboration Activities for developing advanced oral communication skills are practised by students in a professional context through negotiation and interview simulations. These activities simulate legal practice which will assist students in their legal and professional careers. Tasks for developing advanced written communication skills are practised by students through drafting letters and file notes. Peer and clinical practitioner feedback is given during the practice activities to enable students to reflect on and apply feedback to assessed tasks. Students learn collaboratively in the workshops through peer feedback and discussion. In workshops, students prepare in small groups for practice-based tasks, including negotiations and communications with clients. Students give feedback to each other prior to discussing the tasks as a workshop group. Subject Delivery This subject is delivered as follows: Recorded lectures and resources and materials on CANVAS. In the Skills component, on-campus workshops as set out in the university timetable. Some assessments will be undertaken as part of the on-campus days. In the Wills component, on-campus workshops as set out in the university timetable.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of ethical and professional and personal frameworks to solve challenges and manage risk in legal practice.
Demonstrate the skills required to effectively engage with legal work, including will drafting, client interviews, dispute resolution with a focus on principled based negotiation and advocacy.
Demonstrate effective communication and collaboration skills to solve problems in legal contexts, including in the practice area of wills and administration of estates.
Demonstrate an understanding of financial principles in legal practice including cost disclosure, trust and general accounting.
Demonstrate an understanding on how to build resilience in a professional context and strategies to manage such conduct.

title: Small Business Management and Accounting
syllabus_overview:
This subject equips you with the skills to harness financial data for decision-making in small business. You will master management accounting systems, performance measurement, and the impact of information technology on small business management and accounting. Your learning experience includes engaging lectures and practical workshops/sessions. You will engage in hands-on exercises, case study analysis, and real world projects to solidify your grasp of accounting and finance's role in small business. You will explore small business through a mix of self-guided online materials and collaborative workshops, applying theory to real-world scenarios. Prepare for workshops by reviewing online content and pre-class materials. Workshops end with a homework online quiz (with multiple attepmts), assessing your weekly learning. Bring a Wi-Fi-enabled device to participate in class activities or use the desktop in the lab. Additional support includes online quizzes, a free text book and staff consultations. The subject also focuses on enhancing your academic and professional language skills, with milestone assessments evaluating both subject knowledge and small business proficiency.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject is presented as a “flipped class”. Before each week’s lecture, students are required to download and review documents from the UTS Learning Management System including, Lecture Notes and support files for each lecture. For each lecture topic, students will be required to undertake pre-reading and review the resource materials provided on the learning management system. After the coverage of each week’s lecture topic, the students will be required to work individually and collaboratively, in small groups on selected small business case studies that simulate real world decision scenarios. For all in-class activities, students will receive immediate feedback either from the lecturer and/or group members for collaborative exercises. The Class contact comprises large group three-hour workshops per week which include lecture time and demonstrations for 1 to 1.5 hours per week and student collaboration activities for 1.5 to 2.0 hours per week. As most class activities require access to a computer, students will need to have access to a laptop computer during lectures. (If you do not own a laptop computer, you may borrow one from UTS Library). The subject emphasises the importance of the use of accounting processes supplemented by information technology productivity tools to support the information requirements for decision activity in the small business sector. title: Smart Design
syllabus_overview:
This subject prepares you to thrive amidst rapid technological and social shifts by developing 'smart' and innovative products, systems, and environments. Leveraging skills and design thinking from earlier studies, you'll delve into the functionality of products and their sociocultural impact. You'll gain a deep understanding of the technologies that power products and facilitate human interaction and control, equipping you to create solutions that resonate with contemporary societal needs.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject includes active and collaborative learning experiences where ongoing feedback is provided weekly in all on-campus engagements. It is therefore imperative that students prepare for and attend all on campus engagements according to the Program. The subject combines a weekly recorded lecture, a design studio (3hrs) and a build workshop (3hrs) per week. Lectures provide information around the effects changing technology has on human behaviour and how technology can find meaningful integration into everyday life. Students are expected to demonstrate an understanding of the knowledge gained from the lectures and build workshops by applying that knowledge in the context of product design challenges worked through in the design studio sessions. This subject uses an enquiry-based learning strategy that involves students researching and developing their own solutions to complex design challenges. The subject uses design professionals as studio leaders to ensure that all content and tasks are relevant to current professional practice in a global context. Learning resources will be provided in forms such as videos, book chapters and academic papers. Prior to each design studio students will be required to review the learning material and reflect on how the material will be applied to their project, and discuss it with their studio leaders each week. The knowledge provided is information relevant to topics such as research methods, the prototyping of human-product interaction and product experience. Where to find or how to access resource materials is listed in the Program. In studio students will work collaboratively with their peers and studio leaders on their design projects. At the beginning of each studio the studio leader and the group will discuss the challenges they are facing with their projects in connection to the weekly studio topic. The studio leaders will be reviewing the work weekly and will provide feedback verbally. It is the student's responsibility to record any feedback provided both in studio and after presentations. Students will be expected to actively participate in collaborative peer review feedback exercises. Students will also be supported by the level 2, Faculty Workshop in the construction of models and experience prototypes. Grades, marks and feedback on final design submissions will be provided through Re.View.
learning_outcomes: Understand appropriate integration of micro-controller and sensor technologies in the development of functional experience prototypes.
Identify opportunities within socio-cultural and technological contexts through design thinking.
Manage complex design projects through commitment to studio and design iteration.
Apply design methods and translate them into a Product Design outcome.
Demonstrate a rudimentary understanding of electronics and microprocessor programming in relation to Product Design.
Develop design proposals iteratively through exploratory and experimental design development methods relevant to Product Design.

title: Social and Environmental Education 1

This subject equips you with an understanding of the NSW primary History and Geography curricula, enhancing your skills in planning, delivering, assessing, and evaluating K–6 learning experiences in line with current syllabus approaches. You are also prompted to critically consider the broader task of preparing Australian children for local, national, and global citizenship. title: Social and Environmental Education 2
syllabus_overview:
This subject focuses on planning and delivering the NSW History K–10 and Geography K–10 Syllabus for stages 2 and 3, with a special emphasis on sustainability and key learning areas such as civics and citizenship. You'll learn to extend teaching beyond the classroom by leading action-oriented campaigns that connect historical and geographical knowledge to real-world issues. Topics include Australia Day celebrations, refugee support, the environmental effects of single-use plastics and meat consumption, and government influence on religious freedom. External experts and campaigners will support your learning experience.

Teaching Strategies:
Each week there will be a face-to-face seminar or workshop. Each workshop will include a range of teaching and learning strategies including short lectures, discussion of readings and curriculum planning exercises. Occasional guest speakers from potential school-community partner organisations (e.g. Australian Electoral Commission) will also deliver short lectures and lead simulations of teaching and learning activities. These guest-led workshops may be hosted by the external organisation and delivered off-campus. An important feature of most weekly workshops will also be formative assessment where students will be supported to pitch ideas for various aspects of the two assignments and feedback will be provided by teaching staff and fellow students. The face to face teaching will be supported by a range of online activities, including discussions and quizzes, that will need to be completed before and after each workshop.

title: Social and Information Network Analysis
syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces you to the fundamentals of social and information networks, including core concepts, network characterisation metrics, generative models, and analysis methods. You'll learn to use software tools to visualise and analyse real-world network data. The subject also covers practical applications such as user recommendations and web search, equipping you to interpret the increasingly interconnected data of our social and economic activities.

Teaching Strategies:
The material will be presented weekly over 1.5 hour lecture and 1.5 hour laboratory. Students will need to undertake preparation using material on UTSOnline to make effective use of their class time. There will also be assignments and a group project which will present aspects of the subject which depend on the material presented in seminars. The subject takes an active learning approach in this subject and will receive feedback on their progress by completing zero-mark quizzes. Students will engage in collaborative learning activities in the laboratories as well as in the group project. Other assessments will be individual work.
learning_outcomes: Analyse social and information networks with software tools to visualize real-life network data. (D.1)
Apply concepts in social and information networks with software tools to visualize real-life network data. (D.1)

Collaboratively work as a team to produce design solution to complex problem. (E.1)

title: Social Innovation Project A
syllabus_overview: This subject involves exploring and framing a real-world problem to form the basis of a student’s major project. Students will select from complex problem areas presented by research and industry partners and work in a project collective with other students to undertake participatory design research. This may include problem mapping, site visits, observations, interviews and co-design workshops with project stakeholders; reflecting collaborative design practice that would occur in a professional studio environment working in social, service or strategic design. Students identify an individual focus area within the problem space and begin developing a socially impactful design response utilising their disciplinary expertise. This subject operates in connection with 85812 Design Methods and 85810 Research Paper A. It lays the foundation for realising the major project in 85817 Social Innovation Project B.

title: Social Innovation Project B
syllabus_overview: This subject involves the development and testing of design concepts that respond to the exploration and framing of the real-world problem undertaken in 85816 Social Innovation Project A. In this subject, students draw on their existing disciplinary expertise (including product design, visual communication and fashion and textiles) to iteratively design and test their solution ideas to establish a creative and feasible concept that generates value for the project stakeholders. Students design a series of prototypes and creative activities to test their design assumptions, consider the broader systemic implications of their designs, and articulate how their designs generates value. Deliverables of this subject comprise of a prototype or series of materialised concepts, co-design activities, presentations, and process documentation. This subject operates in connection with 85811 Research Paper B and 85813 Design Advocacy. It can be thought of as the second and final phase of the Honours project.

title: Social Media Cultures
syllabus_overview:
This subject explores the profound impact of the internet and social media on society, examining how they've redefined presence and interaction. You'll critically analyse these platforms as networks of power and technology, learning to craft impactful design interventions. The course focuses on interaction designs that enable digital connectivity and cultural responses to these designs. Your personal experiences with social media will enrich our collective understanding of online cultures. Combining desk and design research, you'll engage reflectively in the environments you're studying. Your assessments will include designed responses reflecting your research insights.

Teaching Strategies:
You will prepare for each studio by following the learning guide for your studio. Preparation required may include reading, preparing drawings and concepts, individual and group research and using online resources. Studios incorporate a range of teaching and learning strategies including forums, discussions, thinking and making exercises and student presentations. These are complemented by guided student reading and research, reflection on studio work, and group and individual project work.
learning_outcomes: Identify critical perspectives on the cultural impacts of social media platforms
Explain the histories behind the design of current social media platforms
Develop design interventions into social media platforms that enhance collective well-being
Articulate the nature of a situated context through sensitive experimental design research

title: Social Perspectives in Public Health
syllabus_overview:
This subject equips you with an understanding of social science concepts to tackle health issues, focusing on the human experience of illness and the societal structuring of health. You'll learn how social processes affect health and contribute to inequity, and how to address health challenges amid technological and social changes. You'll develop skills in qualitative research, critical analysis, and applying theoretical perspectives to public health problems. Learning is interactive and online, comprising weekly activities, discussions, and case studies over six weeks. You're expected to work independently, engage with peers and instructors, and attend weekly Zoom sessions for collaborative problem-solving. Assessments are practical, allowing you to apply your knowledge and receive feedback to enhance your understanding of qualitative research in health care.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is delivered through weekly online learning activities distributed over a period of six weeks. There is an expectation that students complete all online activities to get the most out of the subject. Students will be provided with engaging learning activities to deepen their understanding of qualitative research approaches, concepts and processes and their application relevant to health care and public health. Online activities will offer students with the opportunity to gain knowledge using a range of material, including case studies, and apply their knowledge to real-world contemporary public health issues. Students are expected to work independently and to engage with other students and teachers online through discussion forums and other interactive activities such as weekly Zoom meetings. During weekly Zoom meetings students will engage in discussions to analyse, reflect and develop ideas to address contemporary public health issues using qualitative research methods and theory. Assessments are designed to complement the learning by providing students with the opportunity to practically apply and track their understanding of fundamental concepts and techniques relevant to qualitative research enquiry. Students will receive feedback from teaching staff in online discussion and activities and on assessment tasks.
learning_outcomes: Define key concepts in health inequalities

Examine the impact of social norms and behaviour on access to health services, care and information and health policy and practice examples in health care in a range of Australian Indigenous, national and global settings
Evaluate explanations for socially determined health inequalities in relation to selected public health issues
Critically appraise research findings relevant to social determinants and health inequalities
Apply theoretical perspectives on health inequalities to policy options for public health
