title: Sustainability and Information Systems
syllabus_overview:
Sustainability and Information Systems encourages you to actively consider the impact of sustainability on organisational leadership within complex systems. It takes a holistic approach, covering environmental, technological, social, and economic facets. The subject highlights the importance of stakeholder engagement through information technologies and collaborative media, addressing the challenges faced by traditional operations and the opportunities for innovation. You'll engage in a learning environment that focuses on these dynamic possibilities for sustainable organisational growth.

Teaching Strategies:
Sustainability and Information Systems is a weekly three-hour combination of classes, discussions, and group activities based on case studies. The core objective of this course is to encourage the students to develop their critical and analytical skills in using IS tools in a sustainability context. Students will consider various real and hypothetical case-based scenarios, where they identify and evaluate challenges to sustainability, and recommend informed, innovative, collaborative, and rigorously supported arguments and policy initiatives from an IS perspective. To achieve this, students will focus on various activities including in-class discussions, individual literature review, group-based analytical report, presentation, culminating in an in-class debate. Students will have two weeks to rehearse debating skills to use the gathered information to effect. The class materials are provided on UTSOnline (Canvas) before each weekly session with exercises attached for students to pose questions and reflect on their understanding and to bring this to class. In the class, the lecturer explains the complex background for each topic based on these UTSOnline (Canvas) materials and students use their sense-making to clarify their interpretations through dialogic feedback. Group discussions follow classes, in which students are given a question based on a case study. They use design thinking to define the problem and to come up with solution ideas that they present to the whole class. Students critique and evaluate each other’s responses.
learning_outcomes: Apply computational tools to characterize and explore a relevant sustainability issue. (D.1)
Demonstrate personal understanding of critical sustainability problems and the role of information systems in alleviating them. (F.1)
Work collaboratively to understand and resolve sustainability challenges. (E.1)
Research, create, discuss, and defend recommendations for complex and multidimensional sustainability problems from an IS perspective. (C.1)

Describe the historical and cultural origins and current state of a complex sustainability challenge and the roles that information systems play in identifying, characterising and solving such sustainability challenges. (B.1)

title: Sustainability in Public Health
syllabus_overview:
This subject is designed for individuals aiming to create sustainable public health systems. Building upon foundational knowledge in public health and related disciplines such as biostatistics, health promotion, epidemiology, and health psychology, this subject provides practical tools to apply sustainability principles in your future career. You will acquire skills tailored to meet the demands of a dynamic global landscape, exploring the intersection of sustainability and public health. Through interactive learning methods, including case studies and real-world projects, you will gain the competencies required to address the complex challenges of developing and maintaining sustainable public health structures in a rapidly changing world.

Teaching Strategies:
During the semester, students engage with the content to achieve the intended outcomes by using a range of teaching and learning strategies. This subject is designed to assist students in understanding the complexities associated with sustainable public health practices. By exploring sustainability theories and case studies, students will gain the competencies required to address the complex challenges of creating and maintaining sustainable public health structures in a rapidly changing world. In this subject, learning occurs before and during on-campus tutorials. Before tutorials, students engage in independent weekly preparatory activities (consisting of, but not limited to, online quizzes, surveys, and questionnaires) aided by online learning resources provided on Canvas (such as journal articles, news reports, YouTube videos, podcasts...), as preparation for the relevant in-class activities. Following this, the on-campus tutorials include discussions of the case studies, and classroom exercises and worksheets. These enable the students to students engage in collaborative learning through working with the tutor and other students in pairs or groups on activities such as debates and presentations.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the role of the public health workforce in promoting sustainable practices and identify necessary competencies for sustainable public health professionals.
Develop innovative and evidence-based strategies to address public health challenges from a sustainability perspective, considering ethical considerations and future directions.
Analyse the impact of globalisation, technological advancements, and socio-political factors on sustainable public health practices.
Apply sustainability principles to various aspects of public health, including research, policy development, disaster preparedness, and Indigenous health.
Understand the key principles and dimensions of sustainability and their relevance to the field of public health.

title: Sustainability and Social Justice in the City
syllabus_overview:
This subject delves into the connections between the three pillars of sustainability – social, economic and environmental - and how they intersect and compete in issues of inequality that unfold in contemporary cities in the Asia-Pacific. In particular, it deepens your study of the relationship between sustainability and social justice through an intersectional lens, examining how disparities are structured by race, class, gender and other categories of difference. It focuses on developing your skills in qualitative methods of enquiry and analysis to understand how global sustainability challenges manifest in localised contexts and enhance your professional capacities for meaningful community engagement. Taking the city as the site of analysis, you will ground your learning on a range of pertinent issues such as (but not limited to) Indigeneity and cultural preservation in the context of urban development; geographies of racism and racialised built and natural environments; inclusive citizenship in cities of immigrant diversity; and creating equitable infrastructures across urban, peri-urban, and regional areas.

Teaching Strategies:
Weekly 2 hour mass seminars (except for 2 weeks of off-campus fieldtrips) provide the main basis of instruction which entail students undertaking pre-seminar reading and activities in order to complete interactive group work and discussion on the weekly topics and engaging with micro-lectures summarising key theories and concepts. Two weeks of off-site field trips and one virtual fieldtrip to a comparative city outside of Australia are key to introducing students to conducting empirical qualitative research in localised settings. Students will learn to use qualitative methods of photography, ethnographic observation, and interviews to communicate their arguments in their assignments.
learning_outcomes: Understand the relationship between sustainability and social justice.
Critically discuss issues of inequality and approaches to 'just sustainability' in urban planning and policy
Undertake qualitative research into the experience of social, economic and environmental inequalities in urban life shaped by race, gender and class, and other categories of difference.
Develop skills in written, visual and oral presentation of arguments based on evidence
Critically discuss issues of sustainability and social justice relating to Indigenous peoples in cities.

title: Sustainability Practices in Industry
syllabus_overview:
The transition to a sustainable future requires collaboration between industry, government and other stakeholders to achieve sectoral change. The guiding vision for action on sustainability comes from the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This subject introduces you to a six-step transition management planning framework to identify sustainability practices that are context-specific and contribute towards achieving the SDGs. The framework covers system analysis, stakeholder engagement, foresighting, option development and selection, implementation and evaluation. You'll be able to apply the framework in any industry. Case studies from industries such as energy, manufacturing, agriculture and the built environment demonstrate practical applications. You will learn to apply the framework in your own context by working through each of the steps in an individual project on a system of your choosing.

Teaching Strategies:
The core pedagogical strategy for the subject is 'learning by doing'. Students will learn about a six-step transition management framework for developing and implementing sustainability practices by engaging in practical activities on each step. Each activity will build on the previous activities, developing a small sustainability implementation project over the course of the subject. Students will select the context and system they wish to focus on and will work on this system throughout the subject. The system could be their current organisation or sector, a sector they aspire to work in, or one that is of personal interest. To guide students through the application of the transition management framework, four case studies run in parallel through the subject. These case studies focus on sustainability transitions in energy, the built environment, agriculture and textile and garment manufacturing. Illustrated with video material from sustainability experts, they will help students to see how the tools from transition management have been applied to real sustainability projects in industry. Discussion boards, polls and reflection activities throughout the course encourage reflection on the material to facilitate deeper learning. Extensive additional reading is also provided so that students can choose to go deeper into specific topics that particularly interest them. The three assessment tasks are designed to build on each other as students move through the transition management framework. The first helps students to start identifying their area of focus by drawing out their interest in specific Sustainable Development Goals. The second asks students to present on the results of their system analysis, stakeholder engagement and foresighting work. The final presentation brings all the stages of transition management together into a 'pitch' for implementation of specific sustainability practices. Peer feedback is encouraged throughout, recognising that sustainability practices are cross-disciplinary and benefit greatly from other perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Build capacity to investigate and advocate opportunities for organisations to develop and implement sustainability practices
Contextualise, synthesise, and evaluate sustainability practices in order to influence future implementation
Apply transition management planning to identify, prioritise, select and implement industry-specific sustainability practices

title: Sustainability Reporting and Analysis
syllabus_overview:
In the subject Sustainability Reporting and Analysis, you will examine how business strategies and competencies translate into sustainability risks and opportunities and how such risks and opportunities are reported and analyzed. This analysis will give you an appreciation of the legislative requirements for sustainability reporting, as well as the economic and social sources of demand for such information.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject uses a variety of teaching and learning strategies to provide students with a hands-on approach to learning about how sustainability risks and opportunities arise, and how such risks are reported and analysed. Classes are interactive and are used to impart important theoretical and practical concepts. Students work through and are assessed on several exercises/case studies based on data from real companies.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate a corporate sustainability report, or equivalent (e.g., management commentary, financial report, etc)
Compare current and developing mandatory sustainability reporting requirements and their underlying frameworks for Australian firms and their global competitors
Analyse the methodologies that underly popular corporate sustainability rating systems and their application in ‘sustainability investing’
Incorporate sustainability-related information into traditional financial analysis and valuation
Identify the material sustainability issues impacting a business organization

title: Sustainable Construction and Development Management
syllabus_overview:
In this subject, you'll learn about new technologies to enhance building performance, including building and site services, facilities management, and green retrofits. It addresses building pathology, from identifying defects to implementing repairs, with a focus on project and building scales, and highlights the latest innovations. You'll receive individual feedback through in-class group reviews, with formative feedback during group projects. The teaching is designed to develop the knowledge and skills needed for assessments, enriched by guest speakers and site visits when possible. The subject introduces sustainable construction and development management, exploring climate risk and sustainable property development, sustainability concepts, explains scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, precinct-scale master planning, and sustainable construction practices, including cost planning, procurement and social considerations. It also covers designing for sustainability and building services to reduce environmental impact. The subject covers managing sustainable building adaptation and reuse throughout the building lifecycle. It includes diagnosing building defects, sustainability in leasehold properties, Sydney's conversion adaptation market, international best practices, the role of 'eco-concierge', building certification, circular economy and sustainability in building services, focusing on retrofitting and adaptation.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is taught in 12 weekly 3 hour sessions. Feedback will given throughout the subject on an individual and group basis.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced understanding of sustainable construction and management technologies, practices, and applications.
Communicate, collaborate and apply technologies effectively in a professional context.
Critically evaluate existing practices in construction using appropriate evidence.

title: Sustainable Energy Resources
syllabus_overview:
This subject examines the impact of non-renewable energy consumption on climate change, urbanisation, and economic growth, highlighting the need for sustainable energy resources. You'll model the relationship between energy use and climate change, exploring the technical, societal, environmental, and economic facets of sustainable energy. Upon completion, you'll be adept at evaluating the effects of current and emerging technologies on sustainable energy, considering ethical and community issues within various contexts. You'll also learn to apply principles of renewable energy systems, such as solar, wind, geothermal, hydroelectric, hydrogen and fuel cells, biomass, biofuels, wave, and tidal energy.

Teaching Strategies:
Teaching and learning strategies covered in this subject include on-campus lectures, pre-work sessions, and group discussions. The subject is organised into seven 5-h on-campus block class sessions throughout the course of the semester. Pre-work activities such as watching videos and reading online materials prior to each block session will be made available on Canvas. Assessment tasks are designed to assure the students’ learning of the topics covered. Learning Resource Materials (LRM) will be provided on Canvas during the preparatory week, which include reading materials, videos, reference to external websites, or text/notes on the class lectures in Word or PDF format. Students are expected to engage with preparatory class materials, attend classes, participate actively in group discussions and complete assessment tasks by their due dates.
learning_outcomes: Identify and characterise the drivers for the increasing demand in sustainable energy sources. (B.1)
Explain the interaction between energy sources and evaluate their socio-technical, economic and environmental effects. (B.1)
Develop recommendations of appropriate sustainable energy technologies for the future. (C.1)
Describe the challenges and issues of different energy technologies and sources including fossil and renewable energy and assess their trends and potential. (D.1)
Understand the concepts and principles of sustainable energy. (D.1)

title: Sustainable Energy Studio
syllabus_overview:
This studio challenges students to reimagine the world's energy systems with sustainability and resilience at the core. You will explore avenues such as optimizing fossil fuel technology to mitigate its impact, scaling the deployment of renewable energy for a sustainable energy transition, and advancing energy efficiency in generation, transmission, and use. You'll examine current systems and sustainability issues, gaining a foundational understanding of development principles related to both renewable and non-renewable sources. Additionally, you'll assess the social, environmental, and economic facets of decarbonizing emissions and the potential for a carbon-free energy future, considering the effects on communities worldwide.

Teaching Strategies:
In this studio, students will do a combination of individual self-directed study and project work as a team. The stages of the projects are the means through which students learn how to apply their knowledge to what they can achieve. The stages follow the classic engineering paradigm of assess, design and implement. Each student is required to engage in hands-on experimental learning through the completion of a design project. Students are strongly suggested to attend the studio sessions where they will form teams to work together on a chosen solution. The studio learning environment uses agile methodology where students will need to participate in weekly ‘sprints’ and ‘scrums’. Each team will emulate a real-life project management scenario and record their progress using online tools. The scrums are set up to discuss the concerns that present themselves each week; to discuss possible solutions and prioritise as a team, how to proceed during the week. Weekly sprints are scheduled for students to present their progress for that week, receive peer and tutor feedback and use this in the following week. The studio learning environment will concentrate on reinforcing fundamental concepts through problem-solving, computer simulations and design exercises. Design Thinking is the methodology used to find desirable solutions for clients, and students will use all 5 stages of the design thinking process to solve the design project problem. Students will need to engage in online learning modules. Processes are explained in the online modules that develop student technical knowledge. These short educational modules introduce the basic material in a modular fashion starting from electricity supply chain fundamentals and working up to power system operation and protection scheme design. Students will have the opportunity to raise any doubts and questions in relation to the project and receive feedback from the lecturer online and in the studio learning environment.
learning_outcomes: Design a renewable energy plan for a community that meets sustainability criteria. (C.1)
Communicate implications of technological change and sustainable energy solutions to diverse audiences. (E.1)
Analyse the factors which lead to making an informed choice between energy resources and technologies. (B.1)
Describe various technologies that have the potential to provide a sustainable environment and energy supply system. (D.1)

title: Sustainable Energy: Sources and Systems
syllabus_overview:
Sustainable energy is critical to the future of economic growth, human development and a healthy planet. As scientific research advances, the adoption of these technologies continues to grow in importance and reliability. In order to develop new technologies, an understanding of the science underpinning the technologies is crucial to the future of this sector. This subject covers the variety of sources of sustainable energy, how they can be harnessed and how we can design infrastructure to store the energy. In doing so, it equips you to tackle a range of energy problems that need to be resolved.

Teaching Strategies:
"Sustainable Energy: Sources and System" is a fully online educational program tailored for students to learn at their own pace. Students should be expected to dedicate 15-20 hours per week to complete the learning activities and work on assessment items. The course delves into the significance of sustainable energy sources in facilitating clean energy transitions, offering a variety of engaging interactive content and media. Experts lead the learning process, while students engage in collaborative activities with peers through discussion boards and social polls, fostering essential skills and knowledge in a supportive online environment. During the course, students will explore clean energy sources like solar, wind, and hydropower, while delving into the fundamental principles of physics and thermodynamics that govern energy production and system efficiency. They will develop critical thinking skills to address sustainability challenges and devise innovative solutions. The students will also work with openLCA modeling software to design sustainable projects using Life Cycle Assessments. Throughout the course, authentic case studies will be presented, and students will have opportunities to share their thoughts and experiences in discussions and live sessions. Assessments in this course are thoughtfully designed to complement student learning, providing them with a chance to apply and monitor their skill development and grasp of essential concepts. Formative feedback will be consistently provided to guide students throughout the session.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of thermodynamics and the role physics plays in the development of sustainable energy generation.
Critically review energy storage systems and evaluate their potential across different applications.
Discuss current possibilities for improving energy generation, storage and infrastructure across sectors.

title: Sustainable Engineering Design
syllabus_overview:
This subject immerses you in design, sustainability and innovation as core engineering activities through a real-world project. You'll select a problem, explore multiple solutions, and develop a prototype, honing your ability to meet stakeholder needs with an engineering mindset. Employing design and systems thinking you'll understand complex design contexts, stakeholder engagement, and requirements analysis, including legal and technical aspects. You'll also tackle design analysis, managing risks and uncertainties, focusing on manufacture, sustainability, and safety. By applying these concepts and scientific principles to your project, you'll grasp the models of design and innovation processes and the authentic practice of engineers.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject uses a variety of teaching and learning activities. These activities consist of weekly workshops, and a real-life group project with discrete activities that facilitate individual assessment. The lectures are interactive and students are encouraged to actively participate in them by making comments and raising questions. Lecture notes will be made available before the lecture. Complementary material – e.g. readings, videos, exercises - will be made available both before and after lectures. The tutorials, project and presentations complement the theory and applications presented in the lectures and represent a key component for realising the aims of the subject. Students will be required to undertake one project during this subject. This project will involve a critical assessment in sustainable engineering design and will require independent research, analysis and comment. Students will work in small teams – within larger groups - to complete the report and presentations required for the delivery of the project. They will be required to engage in interdisciplinary collaboration within the 49xxx cohort and with other professionals in other fields. The primary goal of the tutorials is to work through the different phases of the project while being able to get feedback from the lecturer, the tutors and fellow students. The aim of this process, is to have students develop understanding and confidence in handling the material and the research required to provide an engineered solution to the problem proposed. Because of its comprehensiveness, there will be only one project that will run the full extent of the session.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise research findings to ideate interdisciplinary, sustainable solutions within complex and changing contexts. (C.1)
Organise team work, manage interdisciplinary collaboration, and assess own and other team member’s contributions. (E.1)

Apply design and systems thinking problem solving approaches to define problems in an effective manner to provide fit for purpose engineered solutions underpinned by a sustainability and innovation focus. (C.1)
Identify social, environmental and economic needs and constraints for a project using sustainability frameworks, methods and tools. (B.1)

title: Sustainable Enterprise in Dynamic Systems
syllabus_overview:
This subject provides students with systemic and sustainable business models to analyse business opportunities arising from complex issues related to grand sustainability challenges. It equips students to systematically understand and analyse the dynamic interrelationships and interdependencies between business, society and the natural environment. Conceptualising business as a multiscalar activity system, students are encouraged to explore new sustainable business models that generate value for the natural environment, society and the economy. The subject enables students to understand the leading principles, practices, policies and processes that organisations implement when they adopt a sustainable business approach. By analysing contemporary practices, students have an opportunity to determine how an organisation might transition to becoming a sustainable organisation. Such sustainability transitions are positioned as opportunities for business to proactively engage with sustainability issues within their stakeholder networks. Within this framework students develop a sustainable business strategy, model or change plan that could be implemented within an existing corporation or small-medium-sized organisation.

Teaching Strategies:
Classes adopt a blended learning approach that combines inquiry based and experiential learning techniques. Through a flipped learning approach students are directed to access pre-read materials for each main content area. During the first two modules, students will develop an analysis of an organisation in relation to its social and ecological systems context and using specific sustainability frameworks, models and practices. This ongoing task is built into an online learning platform through which students will receive ongoing feedback. Lectures are delivered in a dialogic style to maximize critical engagement with the foundation concepts. Students experience collaborative learning through engagement in-class with systems mapping activities, case studies, stakeholder analysis and presentations. During the final module, students will create a sustainable transition development plan through an in-class creative brainstorming session and they will continue the development of this project through guided learning via an online. The teaching management system is the online platform used to deliver the online and digital context for each module, to share course information, enable peer interaction, and provide feedback between staff and students.
learning_outcomes: analyse systemic and sustainable business models as nested in social and ecological systems, multi-scalar and complex
apply key concepts and techniques of voluntary reporting, sustainable business models and certification systems that could progress organisations towards social and environmental sustainability
apply the principles and tools of complex systems thinking to sustainable business challenges and/or opportunities

title: Sustainable Finance
syllabus_overview:
This subject provides an overview of the field of sustainable finance. It investigates environmental, social and governance (ESG) issues and the ways in which these can be addressed using financial instruments, a sustainable financial system and investment decisions that focus on sustainability. Current industry practice is analysed and incorporated into the underlying theories. The subject draws on the experience and expertise of senior academics and industry practitioners.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject will be taught in an interactive mode with a high level of student engagement and participation. The assessment tasks are designed to provide early and ongoing feedback. Before class: Students will be provided with readings and preparation videos to prepare for class. In class: Classes will be conducted as face-to-face seminars. Class-time will be used to present and discuss concepts, answer questions about subject materials, discuss case studies, and work through guided activities and workshop questions. The learning philosophy is to enable students to master the foundation concepts and apply them in real-world applications in a collaborative environment. The in-class discussions give students an opportunity to get feedback from the lecturer and their peers. After class: Online weekly quizzes will be provided as individual assessments and accessed via the LMS. Students are expected to complete the quizzes during the allocated periods. They will receive timely feedback on the quizzes.

evaluate the techniques applied to sustainability in financial decisions
appraise the role of sustainable finance in making investment and financing decisions in organisations

title: Sustainable Urban Design and Development
syllabus_overview:
This subject provides a comprehensive introduction to sustainability principles and their application within the built environment. Students will explore the environmental, social, and economic dimensions of sustainable development, develop an understanding of Australia's sustainability initiatives, and examine the critical role of the construction industry in driving sustainable transformation. The subject investigates sustainable and climate-resilient urban development, high-performance and energy-efficient approaches for both new and existing buildings, sustainable construction materials, renewable energy applications, and innovative construction practices. Key topics include energy efficiency, adaptive reuse, energy auditing and building retrofits, operational and embodied carbon emissions, life cycle thinking, water and waste management, and sustainable project delivery. Students will also examine national and international sustainability policies, regulatory frameworks, and building performance rating systems to develop the knowledge and skills required to construct and manage resilient, low-carbon, and sustainable built environments.

Teaching Strategies:
Weekly on campus: 2-3 hr interactive lecture/workshop format. This subject uses blended learning by supplementing face-to-face teaching with additional online practices. The weekly in-class sessions are designed for active learning and students prepare for this by completing in-class tasks, exercises and discussions. Optional readings of extra materials and contents will also provide online along with the lecture slides for students to explore more on the discussed topics. Notification of in-class tasks, quizzes and assignments (and supplementary readings) occurs weekly through Canvas. Timely completion of these learning tasks allows full participation and more in-depth discussion of topics in class. The in-class sessions are structured in a lecture/workshop format to encourage active learning. Workshop activities involve both individual reflection, partner work and collaborative learning in groups through brainstorming, discussion, and scenario based activities using a range of case studies. The assessment tasks are designed around the Subject Learning Objectives (SLOs) and the Course Intended Learning Outcomes (CILOs) that relate to this subject. Online quizzes throughout the semester along with three major tutorial assignments (dates provided in advance) assess and indicate the level of understanding of basic concepts and the readings. The final assessment is a formal (online) examination that brings together the wide range of sustainable built environment topics and issues covered throughout the subject.
learning_outcomes: Understand Fundamentals of Sustainability in the Built Environment, Australia's Sustainability Initiatives and the Critical Role of Construction Industry in Transformation
Understand Climate Resilient Urban Development, Energy Efficiency and Environmental Quality in New Developments and Existing Buildings
Understand Sustainability Policies, Regulatory Frameworks, and Building Performance Rating Systems, and Compliance Strategies
Understand Sustainable Construction Materials, Methods, and Project Delivery, including Life Cycle Thinking
Understand Energy, Carbon FootPrint, Water, and Waste Management in the Built Environment, including Renewable Energy Applications
Understand Social and Economical Sustainability in the Built Environment, including the Concept of Circular Economy

title: Sustainable Urban Development
syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces sustainable development, focusing on the triple bottom line of environmental, economic, and social sustainability, alongside the ESG framework of environment, social, and governance. You'll engage with sustainable practices through case studies, guest lectures, group discussions, exercises, and field visits, with compulsory attendance for block sessions to participate in group work and earn marks. Initially, you'll explore urban resilience, examining sustainability challenges in global cities and Sydney's local strategies. Topics include climate change impacts, greenhouse gas reduction, alternative energy strategies, air quality, population growth, economic resilience planning, and social sustainability issues like housing affordability and the night-time economy. The second block delves into sustainable urban development at the precinct and building scale, discussing eco-footprints, sustainable building assessment methods, and physical development constraints. You'll evaluate sustainability performance, consider rating tools' effectiveness, and discuss sustainable transport, energy use, new builds versus retrofitting, green roofs, and urban vegetation. The feasibility of alternative sustainability evaluation methods is also covered.

Teaching Strategies:
Delivery will be over two block sessions and will include lectures on key concepts, presentations by guest lectures, evaluation of case studies and specialist material. Active learning opportunities will be integrated throughout each block and may include group discussion, class workshops, field visit(s) and presentations by student groups. In addition, some flipped learning strategies have been integrated into the subject learning philosophy, including readings and short video clips (available on UTSOnline) which must be viewed prior to the block. In addition, online reference and resource material may be provided throughout the semester, and relevant news topics that relate to subject topics may be posted on Canvas (in the Interesting Ideas tab) to demonstrate relevance of the subject content to contemporary life and professional practice. The complexity of sustainable urban development challenges cannot be solved by a single profession or individual. To replicate how these challenges are addressed in industry, each assessment task includes a group work component.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the relationships among urban structure, resource consumption, and sustainability.
Apply the principles of environmental, economic, and social sustainability to urban development.
Understand environmental risks and mitigation strategies in urban development.
Critique policies and plans using evidence-based analysis.
Develop teamwork and communication strategies.

title: Sustainable Urban Development
syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces sustainable development, focusing on the triple bottom line of environmental, economic, and social sustainability in urban design. You'll examine sustainable practices through national and international case studies and delve into urban resilience and the sustainability challenges global cities face. The course addresses climate change's urban impacts, exploring greenhouse gas reduction, alternative energy strategies, air quality, and population growth. You'll also consider economic and social planning for resilience, including equity issues. Additionally, the subject covers urban ecology principles and their application, equipping you with foundational knowledge for subsequent studies.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is taught fully online. Each week is self-paced through the learning management system. You are expected to complete a range of different learning activities throughout the week. Activities provide opportunities to learn, apply and discuss the knowledge gained in a practical manner. Feedback is provided from both peers and teaching staff throughout the activities. You are encouraged to actively provide feedback and interact with staff and students in the exercises and on the discussion board(s). Online Zoom sessions will be held regularly throughout the subject to allow you to interact with staff and students, ask questions and receive clarification and formative feedback on your assignments.
learning_outcomes: Develop coherent criticisms of existing policies and plans using available evidence appropriately.
Analyse the challenges and practical application of principles of environmental, economic, and social sustainability to urban development at the city and precinct scale.
Develop effective written and verbal communication strategies.
Examine the environmental risks posed by patterns of development, and the strategies available to manage risk and adapt urban development patterns to mitigate risk.
Describe the relationships among urban structure, urban ecology, resource consumption, and sustainability at the city and precinct level.

title: Sustainable Value Management
syllabus_overview:
This subject takes a stakeholder management view to dissect strategies, practices, and processes that foster sustainable, high-performing organisations. You'll employ a systems approach to understand the complex interactions between business activities, societal expectations, and environmental limits. The subject enables you to critique current business models and devise adaptive strategies that weave sustainability-oriented innovation into organisational frameworks, creating additional value. It arms you with the skills to identify external opportunities, engage stakeholders in meaningful dialogue, raise awareness of sustainability imperatives, and build a compelling business case for transition.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject is offered in blended learning mode during the short teaching periods of six weeks duration. The teaching and learning approach is a mix of online learning and in-class seminars typically scheduled over three evening seminars. Classes are based on blended and flipped learning approaches: students engage with learning materials (including papers, book extracts, videos, etc.) before attending seminars. Seminars include guided critical discussion of learning materials, group work on contemporary case studies, scenarios, workshops, peer discussions and learning from students own professional experiences. Discussions and application of theory, case studies and best practices are supported by online learning and communication tools and the UTS learning management system. A formative assessment provides students with feedback to direct their self-study. Ongoing general and individual feedback will be provided throughout the subject via consultation seminars. A summative assessment provides feedback on students' comprehension and application of learning. Students also receive formal feedback on assessment tasks.
learning_outcomes: Critically apply analytical decision-making tools and techniques to the valuation of financially material environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors
Demonstrate comprehension of sustainable value management in strategic planning, reporting and financing decisions in organisations
Evaluate the techniques applied to sustainable valuation of organisational activities and investment decisions

title: Synthesizing Midwifery and Research Translation (SMART)
syllabus_overview:
This capstone subject supports your transition into professional midwifery by deepening your capacity to translate research into practice, lead quality improvement initiatives, and advocate for sustainable, equitable maternity care. You will critically appraise contemporary research, develop strategies for integrating evidence into clinical decision-making, and collaborate across disciplines to improve outcomes for women, families, and communities. Emphasis is placed on research-informed practice, innovation, environmental responsibility, and the leadership role of midwives in shaping ethical, inclusive, and future-focused maternity services.

Teaching Strategies:
TEACHING AND LEARNING STRATEGIES In this subject, students will participate in a range of learning and teaching strategies that are designed to enhance learning. ONLINE LEARNING ACTIVITIES You will access online learning resources via UTS Canvas in the weekly “Before/Post class activities” which will need to be completed prior to, or after the scheduled tutorials. These learning resources include quizzes, journal articles, book chapters, modules, lectures and videos. Online resources enable you to prepare for in-class learning, clarify complex concepts and terminology and engage with sensitive or confronting topics at your own pace. Online resources are reviewed and discussed in class to share and receive feedback on learning, experiences and reflections. LECTURES/TUTORIAL CLASSES (WORKSHOPS) Lectures and tutorials are commonly combined to form interactive workshops. The workshops enable you to clarify, discuss and develop concepts pertaining to the subject’s content. You will engage in collaborative group activities and discussions during tutorials/workshops to enable peer to peer learning. CASE STUDIES, ROLE PLAYS AND STORIES FROM PRACTICE Case studies and stories from practice depict people and their families in clinical, community and social situations. You will use these scenarios to learn concepts, interpret information and develop creative solutions. You will develop critical thinking through analysis, interpretation of and reflection on issues or situations. Participating in simulated practice of midwifery communication with women and families aids in the development, learning and practise of interpersonal skills required in the midwifery role. Role plays provide a simulated environment for you to practise new skills learnt through theory and knowledge development. Scenarios from relevant situations are used to depict real life experiences by women through pregnancy, labour and birth, and the postpartum period. You will be encouraged to interact, observe and provide feedback within the facilitated debriefing, and critically reflect on your own skills, values and experiences. STRUCTURED DECISION-MAKING ACTIVITIES Working in small groups, you engage in real-time, shared decision-making activities. This will assist you to engage with practices and policies of maternity care settings and utilise knowledge to formulate responses to women and family situations, under pressure, as would be expected within a clinical practice setting. Together students learn to quickly achieve consensus for decisions. ACADEMIC WRITING Students undertake assessment tasks in the form of academic writing. Students comply with academic integrity writing practices and use information and AI technologies ethically, legally and respectfully. SEMINARS AND ORAL PRESENTATIONS Seminars require you to either individually or in groups present to the class. Group work and assimilation of information fosters development of respectful and collegial collaboration with student peers, women, professional organisations and other stakeholders. This activity develops skills in collaboration, working in a team, allocating tasks and supporting one another. It also enhances your ability to communicate your thoughts and relevant information in a clear, coherent and confident manner. PERSONAL, PROFESSIONAL AND EXPERT NARRATIVES Guest lecturers provide you with personal and professional stories in relation to the subject content. Hearing stories from both a professional and personal perspective supports you to relate your learning to real world situations.
learning_outcomes: Design and evaluate strategies that integrate research and clinical experience to enhance decision-making in midwifery practice.
Lead or contribute to quality improvement initiatives by synthesising research, policy, and contextual knowledge.
Collaborate effectively with interdisciplinary teams to implement innovative, evidence-informed solutions to challenges in maternity care.
Critically appraise and apply research evidence to inform midwifery care and improve outcomes for women, families, and communities.
Critically assess the application of sustainability and equity principles to midwifery care, and advocate for environmentally responsible and socially just practices.

title: Swallowing Disorders
syllabus_overview:
In this subject, you'll learn about the assessment and management of swallowing disorders in infants, children, and adults. This includes eating, drinking, oral health, and saliva control. You'll apply theoretical knowledge in clinical cases to diagnose swallowing disorders and create management plans. You will understand the expected pattern of swallowing, signs and symptoms of swallowing disorders, and related health and quality of life impacts. Practical activities with simulated clients will help you integrate your knowledge with case-based learning. You will also learn to apply ethical frameworks to guide your decision-making. This subject prepares you for your future clinical placements and managing complexity related to swallowing disability.

Teaching Strategies:
Preparation for Learning Before each class, students are expected to complete learning activities (e.g., reading a journal article or book chapter, reviewing videos) as outlined on the Canvas subject site. Students should use the on-line materials on Canvas to help them to be well organised and prepared for learning in each module. Resources used to prepare for class include any lecture notes, journal article or book chapter readings, multimedia materials, and class discussion points. The ‘before class’ activities enable students to participate in the active learning experiences which include problem-solving and practical ‘hands on’ applications of the learning material. Active Learning The lectures and workshops in this subject are designed to provide both a theoretical introduction to topic content, evidence about the topic, and practical scenarios for application of the theory and research into practice. Lectures are active in that they involve students engaging with peers and with the lecturer in case-based problem solving (e.g., scoring test items, analysing test results, completing quizzes, and contributing actively in small group and large group class discussions) and role-play situations to practice skills. Practice-based Learning Small and large group activities enable students to apply their knowledge to clinical situations. In this subject, students have the opportunity to learn and use clinical skills that are considered ‘fundamental’ to speech pathology and underpin knowledge in a wide range of clinical areas of practice in working with children and adults. Case-based learning is a form of authentic problem-based learning and a key learning strategy used in this subject. Example clinical cases (simulations) are analysed individually and in small groups. In simulations, students develop clinical reasoning skills and practice the application of theoretical knowledge. Students have the opportunity for hands-on learning including demonstration, peer learning and feedback, and repeated practice of skills over time. Reflective Learning Reflective practice helps to improve quality in speech pathology services. This subject involves students in critical reflections on their learning, so as to identify areas for improvement and ways to build upon understanding and skills. Peer and self-evaluation are key concepts in the use of reflective learning. Collaborative Learning The ability to work well in a team is an essential skill for Speech Pathologists, who frequently engage in team-based service delivery and management with clients, their families, and other service providers. Collaborative teamwork is vital in high quality healthcare, education, and disability services in the community. In this subject, students expected to participate in individual, pair and small group activities that include group discussions, role-plays and reflections, case studies and workshops. All activities facilitated by teaching staff who provide feedback to guide your learning. Peer feedback is also encouraged. Feedback The ability to give and receive constructive feedback is an essential component of peer-based learning. Students have several opportunities for providing and receiving feedback during class, particularly during simulations practicing clinical skills in workshops and assessment tasks. Students also receive feedback from teaching staff and on assessment tasks. Research-Integrated Teaching Speech pathology is an evidence-based profession, and it is an ethical responsibility of speech pathologists to follow evidence-based practice. Classes in this subject are informed by the best available evidence. Students are required to engage with the evidence through readings in the literature and discussion of the findings of research as applied in clinical scenarios.
learning_outcomes: Explain the principles and practices relevant to speech pathology, including ethical decision-making, clinical risk, and infection control.
Develop and evaluate clinical plans and interventions based on evidence and theoretical frameworks.
Identify advanced practice areas in speech pathology that require further training.
Apply foundational knowledge of body structures and functions, genetics, anatomy, and neuroanatomy, to diagnose and manage communication and swallowing disorders.
Identify and respond to environmental factors and life-course transitions that impact on a person’s communication and swallowing disorders and that influence assessment and management.

title: System Security
syllabus_overview:
This subject provides a comprehensive understanding of contemporary system security concepts, strategies, and practical techniques essential for securing operating systems, databases, and servers. You will learn to implement security measures throughout the design and configuration phases, ensuring robust system security and privacy. The subject places a strong emphasis on system hardening mechanisms and prominent security techniques, which you will apply in hands-on practical sessions. By testing the resilience of hardened systems against various attack vectors, you will gain critical skills in defending against real-world cybersecurity threats. This subject fosters both theoretical knowledge and practical expertise, preparing you to effectively safeguard corporate computing environments.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject uses active learning strategies, which involves a combination of lectures, workshops and practical sessions to support a research-inspired learning strategy. It also includes elements of guided self-study learning. Students will be required to review online materials, pre-readings and research literatures before taking the on-campus workshops. Within workshops, students present the current research issues following the standard procedure, and conduct practical lab in system security independently. In group activities, students engage in intensive discussion and activities on selected topics or projects. In assessment 2, students are grouped into defensive and offensive teams. The offensive team has to choose on a subset of the top ten vulnerabilities listed on OWASP project website, identify these vulnerabilities in systems nominated by the defensive team and document their findings. Defensive team Students will be tested on their ability to harden the system. Both teams verify experimental outcomes and to propose solutions to remedy the identified vulnerabilities. Students must attend workshop sessions and tutorials to complete the required assessment tasks. Feedback for assessment tasks will be given to students once the marking is finalised. Students will also receive continued feedback for their workshops and tutorial exercises on weekly basis. This will be administered by the tutor in the tutorial sessions where the deficiencies in the answers to problems are pointed out to students.
learning_outcomes: Propose and justify technical solutions and potential remedy actions to increase security. (D.1)
Identify and explain the difference between particular types of security systems. (D.1)
Communicate with peers effectively concerning ethical hacking practice. (E.1)
Identify and analyse security vulnerabilities and issues in computer systems. (D.1)

title: Systems and Service Innovation
syllabus_overview:
This subject is tailored for professionals seeking to enhance health and social care through innovation. Choose this subject to learn about the historical and contemporary perspectives on innovation, and the organisational structures, systems and strategies that support innovation within the health system. Its distinctiveness lies in the emphasis on human-centred design, ensuring innovations are not only fit for purpose, but also effectively adopted and evaluated. You will acquire skills in assessing, driving and supporting innovation, employing a systems approach that integrates lifelong learning, creativity, critical thinking, and collaboration. The course facilitates learning through interactive methods, fostering the practical application of curiosity and collaboration to real-world healthcare challenges.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is taught using a variety of teaching and learning strategies that encourage critical thinking and reflection. The strategies used emphasise active self-directed learning and engagement with the content, with the support and guidance of facilitators. Subject activities include, but are not limited to: thought provoking online resources, including mini lectures, videos, podcasts, interactive activities and opportunities to engage in discussion with facilitators and fellow students. Learning is also supported by case studies of real world examples, including classic and cutting-edge research and practice. Assessment Range Students will be given the opportunity to undertake a variety of assessments. Formative and summative feedback will be provided throughout the subject. Early low-stakes feedback will be provided in weeks 1 and 2, in the form of interactive online activities, and facilitator responses in online discussions. Formal feedback will be provided through progressive assessment tasks, worth 25%, 35% and 40%
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise current and future health innovations for their impacts on individual and population health and the safety, quality and cost-effectiveness of healthcare services, as well as challenges relating to privacy, equity, accountability and ethics.
Describe the factors that impact on the development, adoption, and spread of innovations in healthcare systems, from micro to macro perspectives.
Describe and apply human-centred and design thinking principles, tools and techniques, for the design of innovative technologies, services and ways of working.
Effectively communicate complex issues in a variety of ways for different target audiences.
Critically appraise innovation as a strategy for meeting the needs of complex and changing health and social care systems, in the context of contemporary perspectives on safety and quality.

title: Systems Administration
syllabus_overview:
This subject equips you with the knowledge and skills for deploying network servers using Windows and Linux operating systems. You will develop system administration techniques through a well-designed combination of laboratory activities, succinct lectures, and design tasks, gaining insight into the design principles and practical challenges of implementation.

Teaching Strategies:
Students are required to use the online media before attending the combined tutorial/lab as this is essential for completing the labwork. Students will collaboratively develop a threaded case study during the tutorial, applying and extending the work done in the labwork component. The initial labs will develop core skills and knowledge for network servers and this will be directly applied to the relevant case study. The lab worksheets initially assist students in practice based exercises but will progressively require more research and self-directed learning towards the end of session. Students progressively develop an engineering journal which will be used in the practical skills tests. Students will have the choice to develop their own case study which can optionally be industry or community aligned. Online audio lectures, study by the students themselves plus lab practice with onsite support from staff will be accommodated together to maximise the effectiveness and the outcomes of study.
learning_outcomes: Design basic network infrastructure and services. (C.1)
Demonstrate the attitudes and record keeping methods required to be a system administrator. (E.1)
Demonstrate skills in deploying and administering Windows and Linux based network servers. (D.1)

syllabus_overview: In this subject you will develop an understanding of a number of contemporary systematic approaches for developing information systems and you will be able to evaluate their strengths and weaknesses. You will develop the skills to identify and assess the appropriate process models and methods, taking into account all stakeholders including clients, developers themselves, and their respective organisational contexts. title: Systems Engineering for Managers
syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces you to systems engineering, an interdisciplinary field centred on designing and managing both complicated and complex systems over their life cycles. You will delve into systems theory and systems thinking, with a particular focus on complex adaptive systems that evolve and adapt over time. Engaging in a real-life sustainability-focused project, you will use diverse quantitative and qualitative methods to understand and address the complexity inherent in all natural and some human-made systems and their interactions,

Teaching Strategies:
This subject uses a variety of teaching and learning activities. These activities consist of weekly online lectures and tutorials, and a real-life group project with discrete activities that facilitate individual assessment. The lectures are interactive and students are encouraged to actively participate in them by making comments and raising questions. Lecture notes will be made available before the lecture. Complementary material – e.g. readings, videos, exercises - will be made available both before and after lectures. The tutorials, project and presentations complement the theory and applications presented in the lectures and represent a key component for realising the aims of the subject. Students will be required to undertake one project during this subject. This project will involve a critical assessment in systems engineering and will require independent research, analysis and comment. Students will work in small teams – within larger groups - to complete the report and presentations required for the delivery of the project. They will be required to engage in interdisciplinary collaboration within the 49004 cohort and with other professionals in other fields. The primary goal of the tutorials is to work through the different phases of the project while being able to get feedback from the lecturer, the tutors and fellow students. The aim of this process, is to have students develop understanding and confidence in handling the material and the research required to provide an engineered solution to the problem proposed. By scanning current media, students will also be required to analyse present problems in the wider community through the lens of systems thinking. This weekly exercise aims to emphasise the relevance and applicability of the concepts presented in this subject to current real-life situations. Because of its comprehensiveness, there will be only one project that will run the full extent of the session.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise research findings to ideate engineering solutions to complex sustainability requirements within urban contexts. (C.1)
Apply systems thinking and approaches to analyse complex natural and human-made systems, and to design engineered solutions. (D.1)
Organise team work, manage interdisciplinary collaboration, and assess own and other team member’s contributions. (E.1)
Apply professional written and verbal communication skills to present research findings and recommendations to peers and broader audiences. (E.1)

title: Systems Quality Management
syllabus_overview:
This subject teaches you to plan, implement, and enhance quality management processes, crucial for ensuring product integrity in complex production landscapes. You'll learn how quality management systems (QMS) are integral to organisational management, permeating various layers and functioning within firms. With an emphasis on the intricacies of software and systems products, the subject uses real-world examples and culminates in an industry project where you'll address and propose solutions to a QMS problem.

Teaching Strategies:
Lectures are available online. The lectures provide foundation knowledge of quality management that can, and probably will, be applied when investigating and solving a commercial quality management problem. During the tutorials problem will be presented for students to suggest ways to respond to the different stages of problem investigation. The student responses will be summarised to inform discussion about the investigation. The main learning activity of this subject is for group (4-5 students) of students to investigate and develop responses to a problem provided. Each week student teams will develop another phase of their investigation and suggested solution to the problem.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the value and costs of quality in a specific context. (D.1)

Using a quality model describe those qualities that are important in a specific context. (D.1)

1.5 hour lecture and 1.5 hour tutorial per week UTS has embraced the ‘flipped education’ model, rather than only attending lectures, students access digital resources and undertake preliminary tasks prior to coming to tutorial and lecture where they engage in collaborative, mentored activities. Collaboratively plan, develop, apply and document test quality systems (E.1)

title: Systems Thinking for Managers
syllabus_overview:
This subject introduces systems thinking to tackle management issues, blending hard and soft approaches to understand project elements and their execution environment. You'll gain tools for systems diagnosis, thinking, and business modelling to analyse project issues, design solutions for internal stability, and address external factors beyond your control. This knowledge is key for maintaining project adaptability and managing environmental influences.

Delivery of this subject will include lectures on key concepts, presentations by guest lecturers on applications of concepts, and active learning opportunities through targeted activities that will be integrated throughout the sessions through group work and in-class presentations by student groups. During the classes students will engage in interactive activities including peer review, team discussions, and interactive workshops to learn to apply what they have learnt. Feedback will be provided during the class through in-class discussions, structured peer review and comments on assessments both in class and after the classes on post semester work. In addition, some flipped learning strategies have been integrated into the subject learning philosophy, including the use of pre-readings and/or multimedia content which must be completed prior to the first session. Online reference and resource material will be provided that will be available throughout the semester, and relevant topics that relate to subject topics will also be posted on the Canvas (learning management system).

Demonstrate a capacity to apply software tools to create and analyse selected systems thinking models.

Explain the basic concepts of systems thinking as applied to management problems, by exploring hard systems, soft systems, coercive systems and complex systems thinking approaches through interactive activities during classes.
Critique a systemic thinking approach to practice.
Explore and understand systems thinking and systems diagnosis tools used to address complex issues faced in organisations and projects by participating and engaging in teamwork during the classes.

title: TD: Change-making for social impact
syllabus_overview:
For help with deciding which Transdisciplinary Elective subject to study, do a web search for "UTS TD electives." How can we transform ourselves and the systems we live in? This subject invites students to explore the deep connection between personal transformation and systemic change. Through embodied, reflective, and collaborative learning, students engage with practices from mindfulness, complexity science, implementation science, decolonial thinking, and First Nations and other diverse knowledge systems. Across two integrated phases—self-transformation and systems evolution—students learn to sit with the discomfort of change within complex systems, understand the roots of suffering and injustice, and take ethical action in response to real-world challenges co-designed with our industry partner Stockland. Through creative, non-written assessments, students map their inner shifts, design micro-interventions within complex systems, and showcase ripple effects of their work through ritual, installation, and action pledges. Learning flows between immersive in-person sessions, interactive online sessions, and reflective practices, supporting students to build purposeful, relational, and sustainable approaches to social impact within the communities they care about.

Teaching Strategies:
The teaching and learning strategies in TD Change Making for Social Impact are grounded in transformative, experiential, and community-based learning. Each week invites students to move through cycles of seeing, being, and doing, beginning with embodied, face-to-face activities that engage emotion, ethics, and complexity, followed by reflective and interactive online sessions that deepen insight and prepare for real-world application. The subject integrates practices from mindfulness, systems thinking/complexity science, decolonial theory, and implementation science, supporting students to explore their own purpose, identity, and agency as they co-design micro-interventions with their communities. Students learn through collaborative inquiry, visual mapping, creative storytelling, ritual, and action, making learning personal, practical, and powerful.
learning_outcomes: Design communication strategies to persuade organisational and community leaders to implement innovation in professional or social contexts to achieve impact
Articulate the current and future structures, processes, and practices that influence change and innovation across organisations, networks and systems
Develop strategies to mobilise and connect people and the organisations, networks and systems they work and live in to create and implement innovation
Analyse and map systems, organisations and individuals utilising language, principles and tools of complexity to identify leverage points for change and impact

title: Taxation Law
syllabus_overview:
This subject develops your conceptual and analytical skills relating to the Australian tax system. You will analyse the current tax system and consider the many changes it is presently undergoing. You will explore the concept of assessable income, taxable income and allowable deductions and offsets, learn to apply the various types of taxes including Marginal Tax Rates (MTR), Fringe Benefits Tax (FBT) and Goods and Services Tax (GST), explore international tax and gain an understanding of the laws surrounding the taxation of superannuation, trusts, partnerships and companies. You will develop your ability to interpret and apply the law through analysis and calculations. By completing assessable problem questions, you will actively learn how to reliably calculate tax liability for clients.

Teaching Strategies:
Strategy 1: Preparing for professional practice in taxation law By completing readings and preparatory work prior to each class, students establish a strong foundational understanding of key issues and controversies of taxation law. Preparation allows students to better engage with complex content. As part of preparation, students are required to respond to questions prior to class. Students receive ongoing feedback on their understanding of core concepts by active participation in class discussion, which involves engaging with the teacher and peers. Online learning and preparation occurs from Week 1 onwards. Online materials will include précis outlining sources of law, research skills in accessing tax materials, jurisdictional issues such as residence and source, and constitutional power to tax. Strategy 2: Developing critical analysis through research of case law, tax rules and legislation Students undertake research of relevant legislation, tax rules and case law. Research is synthesised and summarised by students and applied in practically-oriented hypotheticals and problems. Essential to student learning is mastery of literacy and numeracy skills, allowing students to analyse facts, explain assumptions and determining taxpayer liability. This will also involve a development of students’ ability to apply law alongside mathematical calculation to produce reliable numerical and legal outcomes. Strategy 3: Active learning through problem solving To effectively grasp the core concepts of taxation law, students are encouraged to actively engage with problems throughout the subject. Active learning is the only way to test and amend understanding of tax rules, case law and legislation, based on regular feedback during class. By responding to preparatory questions and completing assessable problem questions, students are able to actively learn how to reliably calculate tax liability for hypothetical clients. This process may involve determining assessable income, and understanding how this is determined, as well as specific and general deductions. Other core concepts such as trading stock, accounting methods and timing, bad debts and capital gains tax calculations are tested and mastered by applying knowledge through problem solving. Strategy 4: Feedback to encourage critical reflection and self-improvement Feedback is provided throughout the session by teachers and peers. Feedback comes in a number of forms, including responses to completed preparatory questions and discussion during class. Students are also encouraged to deepen their understanding of subject content by posing questions to teachers and peers throughout the session. Formal feedback is provided by teachers for each assessment. Informal feedback is provided via in class and online discussion with peers and the teacher.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and apply taxation legislation and rules to practical situations.
Apply critical analysis and effective communication skills to generate solutions to legal issues relating to taxation law.
Analyse and evaluate the implications of taxation on various entities and scenarios.
Understand key taxation concepts and accurately calculate tax obligations.

title: TD: Envisioning futures worth wanting +
syllabus_overview:
For help with deciding which Transdisciplinary Elective subject to study, do a web search for "UTS TD electives." This subject introduces you to futures studies, a field vital for tackling complex issues in business, government, and society. You will work individually and in teams to respond to a challenge set with our industry partner, the City of Sydney council, to explore and propose a future worth wanting set in "Sustainable Sydney 2050." You will learn and apply practical techniques and theoretical frameworks to: examine how change happens in complex systems, identify and interpret emerging signals of change, and engage peers and partners in exploring possible futures. You will also critically reflect on how your values and personal perspective, and those of individuals, communities, and organisations shape the way we imagine and create futures worth wanting.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject combines authentic assessment through an industry partner challenge, with classroom and online learning. Using a participatory futures project to frame the subject, students will complete reading and learning tasks to understand key concepts, then apply those concepts through hands-on activities and receive formative feedback in facilitated tutorial workshops.

title: TD: Pathways to societal transitions
syllabus_overview: For help with deciding which Transdisciplinary Elective subject to study, do a web search for "UTS TD electives." Artificial Intelligence seems to be everywhere – embedded in phones, homes, workplaces – but what are the physical infrastructures that make it possible, and how are they reshaping communities and our environment? This subject takes students beyond the screen to investigate the hidden, material side of AI. From data centres and fibre-optic cables to the vast demands for energy, water, and land, students will explore how rapidly expanding digital infrastructure is transforming communities and environments globally, and in their own backyard. Students will hear from a diversity of industry experts working across sectors who are making digital infrastructure expansion possible, and learn how the challenges and opportunities this expansion presents affect sustainability efforts globally, and in Australia. In multidisciplinary teams, students will investigate how digital infrastructure expansion is unfolding in their local community and codesign future scenarios that balance environmental priorities with societal demand for AI. Through this process, they will use a range of ethnographic and creative research methods, including photography, video, and story-making, to learn from their local community and communicate possible futures. This process will be assisted through regular engagements with our industry partner, Lane Cove Council, who will provide first-hand insights into how digital infrastructure expansion is shaping their community. Students participating in this subject will develop skills and confidence in understanding and responding to complex, real-world challenges in multidisciplinary teams, using effective systems approaches to change-making. It is relevant to students from all disciplines including (but not limited to) computer and data science, social sciences, fine arts, communications, science, law and medicine.
learning_outcomes: Identify significant issues and emerging opportunities to create positive change in real-world contexts.
Develop a cohesive rationale for proposals and communicate ideas persuasively to diverse audiences.
Integrate different perspectives to unpack and analyse complex challenges that the digital infrastructure industry is creating for local communities and environments.
Synthesise your learning and research to generate insights about transdisciplinarity and your own role in imagining digital futures, and steps to bring about positive social change.
Apply transdisciplinary and creative research methods and collaboration in teams to generate responses to complex challenges.

title: TD: Reframing, remixing, reimagining society
syllabus_overview:
For help with deciding which Transdisciplinary Elective subject to study, do a web search for "UTS TD electives". In this subject, students challenge their personal and disciplinary mental models, worldviews, biases and assumptions to rethink how current societal problems are framed. Working on a real-world challenge posed by UNICEF, students explore different disciplinary and professional perspectives on youth involvement in climate action. In teams, they creatively remix different approaches to develop innovative responses to the challenge. Through this, students test their emerging expertise, learn to collaborate across differences, and develop insights that have the potential to create new pathways for real-world action.

Teaching Strategies:
Most learning in this subject happens through collaboration in multidisciplinary teams during in-person classes. In these sessions, students work on the partner challenge while building their understanding of key concepts and frameworks through dialogue with peers, educators, and industry partners. To prepare for each class, students complete individual Learning Tasks and engage with online modules that support the development of their ideas and proposals. In the 12-week version of the subject, students also participate in online plenaries and team check-ins, while students in the 2-week intensive attend in-person lectures. Throughout the process, students receive ongoing formative feedback from peers, educators, and industry partners.
