Integrate different perspectives to analyse complex challenges.
Synthesise your learning to generate insights about transdisciplinarity and your own role in fostering positive social change.

title: TD: Shaping technologies that shape us
syllabus_overview:
For help with deciding which Transdisciplinary Elective subject to study, do a web search for "UTS TD electives." This subject equips you with critical thinking, creative, and collaborative skills to address complex real-world challenges, enhancing your professional capabilities. In response to an industry partner brief from Microsoft, you will explore the wide-ranging impacts, opportunities, and profound questions posed by the exponential growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, applying your disciplinary lens while learning to work with other perspectives. By engaging with a range of thought provoking multi-media learning resources, highly interactive classroom activities, and a range of practical tasks, you will develop key insights into the challenge space and deliver a distinctive agenda for the sustainable development of these transformative technologies.

Teaching Strategies:
Experiential problem-based learning; interdisciplinary collaboration; blended learning (technology-mediated instruction); authentic assessment. By collaborating as a cohort and in small group settings, students will examine complex technological trends through the lens of their emerging disciplinary positions and diverse stakeholder perspectives. Interactive Canvas modules will enable students to engage with a range of provocative and engaging multi-media learning resources, including podcasts, videos, selected peer-reviewed articles, and industry reports. These resources will support authentic, practice-based learning to develop intellectual agility, creative skills, and collaboration capability that students can use for the rest of their professional lives. Throughout the subject, students will have ongoing opportunities for formative feedback by peers and academic staff, incrementally building skills they can apply in real-life settings (especially with a view to increasing employability).

For help with deciding which Transdisciplinary Elective subject to study, do a web search for ''UTS TD electives.'' This subject introduces students to ways of thinking differently about the ‘wicked’ problems we face when tackling big issues around sustainability. Students draw on a range of approaches from across our disciplines and professional domains to explore the complex social and environmental context in which every problem is situated and networked with other problems. Striving towards regenerative sustainable futures, these novel ways of thinking enable students to move away from conventional problem-solving approaches to discover new avenues for action. By working in multidisciplinary teams on complex industry or community challenges, students develop their relational and analytic skills. Students devise their own questions based on insights they’ve uncovered, and communicate their proposals for addressing current or emerging global challenges to a range of diverse audiences.

For help with deciding which Transdisciplinary Elective subject to study, do a web search for "UTS TD electives." This subject explores the profound impact of ubiquitous technologies on our behaviours, aspirations, and daily lives. Students develop skills in complex systems thinking, enabling them to navigate real-world challenges around technologies of everyday use and reimagine these technologies with proposals promoting inclusivity and sustainability. Students also engage with industry or community partners for practical experience, working in multidisciplinary teams on hands-on projects and collaborative workshops. This subject prepares students for innovation, sustainability, or community development careers, addressing complex challenges and driving systemic change. Students will translate their learnings into practice by addressing a complex real-world challenge posed by an industry partner. As students collaborate in multidisciplinary teams and experiment with different disciplinary approaches to reimagine technologies, they have the opportunity to critically reflect on technology futures in their own disciplines and consider the implications to their future study and profession.

title: TD: Transdisciplinary action lab
syllabus_overview:
For help with deciding which Transdisciplinary Elective subject to study, do a web search for "UTS TD electives." In this subject, you'll explore real-world challenges posed by the industry partner, MIRO. You’ll take on the role of a decision-maker grappling with uncertainty when facing these pressing challenges and devise practical ways to address them. Working in multidisciplinary teams, you will ideate solutions, field-test them in real-world settings, assess their impact, and propose actions that promote desired outcomes. By crafting responses to complex issues and taking action towards better futures, you'll develop skills in critical thinking, transdisciplinary collaboration, and entrepreneurial mindset. You'll apply these insights to propose enhancements and reimagine future disciplines and future professions.

Teaching Strategies:
In this subject, learning will take place in a collaborative, immersive, and experiential environment. Online modules and plenary sessions will introduce key concepts and frameworks to deepen their understanding. Teaching staff and peers will provide continuous formative feedback as students refine their initiatives.

title: Teaching Across the Curriculum
syllabus_overview:
This subject focuses on the practical and creative ways in which teachers can incorporate aspects of the curriculum into integrated units. It is based on the philosophy that learning is most successful within meaningful contexts and when it is holistic rather than fragmented. Ways in which cross-curricular teaching can be programmed, assessed and evaluated are also explored. In recognition of the demands of programming for teachers, the integration of ICT is also examined.

Teaching Strategies:
Students will be supported to undertake authentic project-based learning and group work. This will be complemented by independent student reading and research, along with participation in online discussion. Other teaching and learning strategies will include lectures/lecturettes, case studies, videos, discussion of readings, short student-led presentations, interest-based investigations and collaborative writing. Students will receive ongoing, lecturer and peer feedback through discussion, presentation and project-based learning activities.
learning_outcomes: Explore the possibilities of teaching from a number of different perspectives
Apply critical analysis in planning and programming for teaching across the curriculum
Creatively demonstrate how an integrated curriculum capitalises on the interdependent nature of subject disciplines
Implement, manage and evaluate suitable learning experiences in an integrated curriculum
Explain the practical possibilities for teachers in the philosophical concept of holistic learning
Explain how the integration of teaching across the curriculum reinforces student learning and enhances a sense of purpose within meaningful contexts
Produce accurate and cohesive academic texts

title: Teaching and Learning with Digital Technologies
syllabus_overview:
This subject explores the use of learning technologies to foster design, critical thinking, creativity, and learning in a digital world. You will examine how different technologies can facilitate authentic, active, and collaborative learning within your discipline. The subject encourages you to engage with relevant e-learning theories and pedagogies for diverse environments, including face-to-face, online, and mobile settings. Additionally, you will address contemporary social and curriculum issues, as well as emerging technologies, in the context of high school education's information and communications technology.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is offered in a either weekly or block classes (Saturdays) and independent study activities. This approach to the subject is designed to cater for the wide range of students’ background experiences, capabilities, interests and commitments. It is also designed to encourage students to engage in peer support activities and develop autonomous learning strategies. The subject includes structured workshops, tutorials, discussions, webinars, screencasts, individual research and engagement in assessments that critically examine and apply current thinking in the area. Early formative feedback will be provided after assignment one and two proposals. Independent study activities. Throughout the session, students will engage in pre-class independent study mode (ISM) activities relevant to their interests as outlined on Canvas. They will exchange ideas with peers and staff in a range of online fora. The online and offline learning tasks will help students to ‘co-own’ the learning process. Attendance at classes and participation in online activities are important in this subject because it is based on a collaborative approach, including interchange of ideas with other students and staff. An attendance roll will be taken at each class. Where possible, students should advise the lecturer in a timely manner if they are unable to attend.

title: Teaching EAL/D and Literacy in Primary Schools
syllabus_overview:
In this subject, you will learn how to enable English Language Learners to develop literacy across the disciplines in the formal schooling sector. You will look at how both English as an Additional Language or Dialect [EAL/D] and Literacy are framed in curriculum documents, and subsequently translated into teaching and assessment activities in school settings. Taking an approach of “high challenge, high support” you will explore how teachers provide explicit and targeted language and literacy support to help students achieve learning goals. The Australian context is the primary focus for the content, but you will also find the subject relevant if you are working within settings where English is not the dominant or official language.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject uses a range of teaching and learning strategies in face-to-face mode. Weekly topics are introduced through lectures, readings and practical activities that explore current theory, research and classroom practice in EAL/D education. Tutorials and workshops provide opportunities for students to analyse authentic classroom materials, engage in discussion, undertake collaborative problem-solving, and practise planning and implementing EAL/D pedagogy through microteaching activities and professional planning tasks. While tutorials encourage collaboration and peer feedback, all assessment tasks are completed and submitted individually. Students are strongly encouraged to attend all classes to maximise opportunities for participation and professional learning. Students complete 30 hours of supervised practicum in a school. Under the guidance of an experienced teacher, the students develop teaching, learning and assessment resources, and implement these to address the needs of EAL/D and literacy needs of students. Towards the end of the placement period, students are assessed by a UTS supervisor. Successful completion of the practicum requirements is a minimum requirement for passing the subject.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of EAL/D teachers and the scope the role in a school
Know and use the policy and curriculum documents that orient the provision of EAL/D support in Australian schools, K - 12
Identify learners’ language needs as the basis for planning and implementing teaching and learning strategies to enhance language development
Identify the particular needs of indigenous students in schools and how their learning needs can be supported
Communicate clearly and competently in an academic setting, theory and research as well as application of ideas
Know and use appropriate assessment practices to diagnose, support and evaluate students in the classroom, in partnership with other teachers, and as the basis of curriculum planning
Demonstrate knowledge of the current issues within the EAL/D sector and how these affect the work of teachers and learning of students

title: Teaching English in International Contexts
syllabus_overview:
This subject develops students’ understanding of the teaching/learning of a second or subsequent language, particularly in contexts outside Australia. It examines a range of practices for teaching English to speakers of other languages and raises awareness of cultural and linguistic diversity and the impacts on language learning. This subject is specifically designed for all students undertaking an International Professional Experience (IPE) program. Priority for enrolling in the subject is accorded to students who have expressed an intention to undertake an IPE program.

Teaching Strategies:
In class time , the teaching and learning strategies will include: discussions, material and strategy analysis, guest speakers, presentation of strategies and ideas to peers, feedback and suggestions, analysis of documents and viewing of practice. Students will be expected to prepare fully for class so that they are able to contribute in a knowledgeable manner. Group and class work will be done in a respectful and collaborative manner, understanding that topics at times deal with cultural, political and emotional issues. Full attendance is required on a weekly, face-to-face basis. A short formative assessment task will be given in Week 2. This will enable the lecturer to provide feedback about individual academic language needs. Outside class time , students will read view a short weekly presentation on-line that will assist them to engage and understand the weekly, prescribed readings. Close and critical reading of these required texts is a necessary part of students’ learning in the subject, and evidence of this will be seen in students’ response to the assessment tasks.
learning_outcomes: Increase awareness of English language structures and functions, including issues that might arise for EFL learners.
Examine the principles and practices of teaching English in an overseas context.
Acquire a range of strategies for teaching English in an overseas context, preparing lessons and resources, with a special emphasis on using oral language for authentic communicative purposes
Develop an awareness of cultural and linguistic diversity, and how languages work together to support learning.

title: Teaching English for Academic Purposes
syllabus_overview:
In this subject, you will develop research-informed knowledge, skills and practices to teach English for academic purposes (EAP) in a wide range of tertiary education contexts including: tertiary preparation courses, academic language support programs in universities, and embedded academic language and literacy in other discipline subject areas. You will apply theoretical and practical knowledge to evaluate curricula and teaching resources, and to design a unit of work and assessment tasks for a group of learners in a chosen program context.

Teaching Strategies:
Teaching and learning environment Teaching and learning takes place in the on-campus classroom and online via Canvas. Lecturer input, modelling and scaffolding Each week, the lecturer introduces new materials through an online lecture, with links to subject readings and learning activities. Students are expected to view the video, access and complete the readings, and participate in learning activities. Student learning activities In-class and online student learning activities in the tutorials and online via Canvas enable students to prepare for and check their interpretation of concepts presented in the lecturer input and readings. The tutorials provide opportunities for students to participate in discussions and collaborate with peers on related tasks. They also allow for tutors to monitor students' learning, and for students to receive tutor and/or peer feedback on their understanding and application of key concepts and theories.

Produce written academic texts which are accurate, cohesive and coherent, and which demonstrate correct citation and referencing
Explore key issues in the teaching and learning of English for academic purposes
Analyse and describe approaches and practices in the teaching and assessment of academic English in different contexts with reference to theory

title: Teaching for Learning
syllabus_overview:
This foundational subject of the Graduate Certificate introduces you to learning and teaching in higher education, drawing on your experiences and key scholarship to explore practice-based learning models within the curriculum. It encompasses practice-oriented education, international engagement, and research-inspired learning, with a focus on using innovation and technology to create dynamic, blended learning environments. You will analyse how these approaches promote social justice, Indigenous education excellence, and responsible leadership, shaping your teaching values. Engaging in critical dialogues and reflexive activities, you will critique and enhance your confidence in developing an authentic voice as a lecturer and tutor.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject is designed to support a student-centred approach to learning and invites participants to reflect as a developing teacher. Learning activities include formal participation in online discussions responding to question prompts and sharing key aspects of reflective thinking. Small comprehension activities within module content aim for engagement with online material and plan for the application of core concepts in teaching contexts. An enabling process through reflection, dialogue and modelling teaching skills aim to enhance learner development towards becoming an inclusive higher education teacher. A range of asynchronous online activities that are self-paced offer the opportunity to learn from and give feedback to peers. Continuous feedback is provided verbally as well as written in the online comments and supporting formative and summative assessments. Peer feedback is collegial and strongly encouraged as part of the learning activities and is built into the assessment process.
learning_outcomes: Engage with key principles supporting inclusive teaching practices through introductory knowledge of cultural, historic, and contemporary contexts that influence the lives of Indigenous Australians
Reflect on prior experiences to identify key learning priorities supporting developing teacher self
Enhance multi-modal teaching skills to communicate effectively in a range of contexts
Analyse how learning design, constructive alignment in curriculum, feedback and assessment optimises student learning
Identify and describe key educational principles that underpin strategic priorities in relation to your teaching

title: Teaching Language for Meaning
syllabus_overview:
This subject provides language and literacy teachers with knowledge about English grammar and vocabulary, and how to teach it. The presentation of this knowledge aligns with contemporary curriculum and syllabus documents. Knowledge about English grammar and vocabulary is expressed in a metalanguage teachers can share with their students. This knowledge enables students to: reflect on how English works recognise the main features of the English language understand, appreciate and compose spoken and written texts in ways that align with their language learning needs and goals, and curriculum outcomes Knowledge about how to teach English grammar and vocabulary enables teachers to design sequences of teaching and learning that support language and literacy development across the stages of school and post-school education

Each week students will have four stages of engagement with the subject: Listening to a recorded lecture, supported by slides. Completing set readings and follow up reflection and practice tasks, relevant to the week’s topic. Participating in a 90-minute tutorial, with structured activities to clarify, consolidate and extend understanding of content covered in the lecture and readings Completing extension tasks, such as further reading, critical evaluation of teaching approaches and materials, and small-scale text analysis and lesson- planning tasks.

Evaluate critically approaches to the teaching and learning of English grammar and vocabulary for students learning English as an additional language or dialect.
Examine texts to identify and select patterns of grammar and vocabulary use of most relevance to the English language learning needs of one or more specified student profiles.
Analyse texts to understand how grammar and vocabulary choices have been used to make different kinds of meaning and to achieve specific social purposes.

title: Tech Law, Policy and Ethics (Law Tech Capstone 1)
syllabus_overview:
This subject explores the policy and ethical issues that technology presents for legal practitioners. You’ll examine the role of lawyers in regulation of technology, shaping policy and supporting vulnerable populations using technology. You will also explore ethical and policy issues arising from innovative technology that poses new threats at the same time as providing new opportunities to find solutions to some of the world's wicked problems. This subject is taught by academics and guest lecturers who specialise in legal technology. You’ll engage in weekly discussions on various aspects of legal issues arising from disruptive technologies and present lightning talks that engage with these issues. Classes examine the key role that lawyers can play in ethical policy-making and draw on professional conduct obligations, international human rights law and humanitarian law. You will also become familiar with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and consider which of them may be supported by the use of technology.

Teaching Strategies:
Strategy 1: Students’ Preparation for Learning Students engage in independent study to develop, deepen and consolidate knowledge and understanding of relevant issues. Students read policy documents, legislation and articles and listen to TedTalks and similar online resources before attending seminars (see Strategy 2 below) to prepare for tutorial activities including collaborative discussion. It is a goal for students in this subject to familiarize themselves with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and consider which of them may be more readily achieved with the use of technology; and the key role lawyers can play in ethical policy-making. Strategy 2: This subject is taught by academics and guest lecturers who specialise in legal technology. Students build on their preparation and engagement through participation in interactive seminars. Each week, students engage in discussion and oral presentations (including lightning talks) on various aspects of legal issues arising from disruptive technologies. Students receive immediate feedback from their tutor and peers (see Strategy 4 below). Students have the opportunity to ask questions of their peers and of the teacher to assist them in consolidating their own learning. By testing their knowledge and learning from others the class discussions allow students to gauge how successful they have been in their critical reading, Students identify their Lightning Talk topic at least two weeks prior to the online presentation. Students are given guidance as to the best resources for their research and have access to an exemplar provided via Canvas. These presentation and distillation skills are important because lawyers need to be able to explain or summarise complicated concepts into brief descriptions in plain English so that they may readily be understood by their client or the Court. Collaborative in-class activities will include hypothetical problems based on real cases and engaging with policy questions about the role of the law in technology. Strategy 3: Online learning Students access material for self-directed learning and engage in student-led discussion on key topics on Canvas. Throughout the session, students share their questions and ideas on this open discussion forum, with prompt guidance and contributions from the Subject Coordinator. Strategy 4: Ongoing Feedback Detailed guidance as to the assessment criteria and the provision of timely feedback form an important part of the learning process. The marking criteria for assessment tasks 1, 2 and 3 are provided prior to the commencement of formal classes. Students provide each other with peer feedback during in-class activities and are instructed to use comparative feedback strategies to strengthen their understanding of the subject. Subject Delivery: Three hour seminars once a week, over 12 weeks.
learning_outcomes: Prepare and present lightning talks to the rest of the seminar
Evaluate the capacity for existing statutory instruments to regulate policy issues raised by disruptive technologies

Evaluate new risk, obligations and ethical issues for the courts and practitioners arising from the use of technology in the delivery of justice and legal services and collaborate in groups and online to generate ideas and possible solutions to the challenges arising from new technologies
Identify and analyse policy and ethical considerations arising from recent technological advances and the policy response of governments and international organisations to these developments

Explore and critically reflect on the way that disruptive technologies challenge regulators across global jurisdictions, in particular the UN Declaration of Human Rights and the UN’s 17 Sustainable Development Goals

title: Teaching for Learning
syllabus_overview:
This core subject introduces you to learning and teaching in higher education, with a particular focus on key theoretical frameworks and practical strategies related to constructive alignment, student-centred learning, and active learning. It provides an opportunity to reflect on the comparative context of higher education in Australia and Pacific Island nations, with particular attention to the experience of Indigenous students in tertiary education. It builds on your own experiences of learning and teaching and enables you to contextualise your experience with reference to key scholarship, and to explore models for learning that enhance your understanding of tertiary student experience.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject integrates distance study with intensive block face-to-face instruction in a studio format. Your distance study is supported by materials, resources and activities that you can access in an online environment in Canvas. These online resources will enable you to prepare for the intensive block, and to review content and submit final assessments after the intensive. During the intensive block, you will work collaboratively with other participants from Solomon Islands National University (SINU) on a range of authentic activities in a studio format to develop your understanding of key educational theories and receive peer feedback on your draft action plan for enhancing your own teaching practice. Before, during and after the intensive teaching block, you will engage in structured reflections in an individual journal. Both your journal and your action plan can form the basis for work in later subjects, which provide opportunities to revisit and revise your earlier work as your knowledge and skills develop. Teaching staff provide continuous formative feedback through online and in-class interactions, as well as structured written or verbal feedback on formal assessments. Although all formal assessment is individual, peer feedback and collaboration are integral to the intensive teaching blocks. All assessments are designed to focus on your personal professional development priorities for your tertiary teaching practice. If it is appropriate for your goals, you may combine the second and third assessments submitted for this subject with the parallel assessments in the Feedback and Assessment subject, submitting a single integrated assessment that addresses the assessment criteria for both subjects. Submission formats are flexible for many assessment components and, where flexibility is possible, we invite you to demonstrate your skills in the format best suited for your personal goals.
learning_outcomes: Communicate about teaching skills effectively in a range of contexts
Reflect on your prior experiences of tertiary teaching to identify key learning priorities for developing your teaching skills
Identify and describe key educational principles that underpin strategic priorities in relation to your teaching
Analyse how learning design, constructive alignment in curriculum, and feedback and assessment optimise student learning

Reflect on key principles supporting inclusive teaching practices, and analyse the cultural, historic, and contemporary contexts that influence the lives of Indigenous peoples in the Solomon Islands and Australia

title: Technical Direction for 3D Animation and Graphics Projects

Technical Directors craft tools, maintain software, and manage the production pipeline. They work in animation and VFX studios and in the games industry. You'll need robust coding skills and a fundamental knowledge of Python.

Learning at the UTS Animal Logic Academy takes place in a collaborative, immersive and experiential studio that mirrors professional conditions. Teaching focuses on creative problem-based learning strategies. The cohort work with academic and industry mentors using collaborative dynamic workflows and problem-solving production practices. Learning approaches centre on developing critical analysis, creative and technical ability. Assessment focuses on the quality and applicability of innovative solutions and practices. Students will engage with existing projects in production at the Academy as they develop the technical direction skills.

Contribute constructively to collaborative team dynamics and projects, enhancing the overall output through technical direction. (E.1)

title: Technique: The Architectural Model
syllabus_overview:
Students learn to transform architectural plans into detailed handcrafted models, focusing on iconic houses. You'll master analogue model-making at scales of 1:100, 1:50, and 1:20, from rapid concept models to intricate presentation pieces. Emphasis is placed on sustainable practices, efficient use of materials, and the use of analogue tools.

Teaching Strategies:
Iconic Houses – Technique and the Architectural model is a subject run through a workshop typology. The Elective Leader Jenna Rowe is a registered practicing architect with over 18 years experience in architectural model making – much of the subject will involve hands-on making and guidance through tutorial workshops. The aim of this elective is to emulate the environment of an architectural practice with Workshops structured similarly to a working day – to enable students to also gain insight into professional practice. Sketching and prototyping will be heavily utilised, as will learning strategies related to time management and task planning. Architectural documentation of the houses to be modelled will be studied and interpreted within groups. Students will learn to determine the construction technique of the houses, from the overall structure to the detailing of the joinery – to assist in a means translation into the architectural model. Students will gain an understanding of construction sequencing, drawing on knowledge gained from their various undergraduate subjects. Students will experience one-on-one guidance, and also peer guidance, through a learning-by-making approach. Pre-prepared prototypes of different model making techniques will be made available to the students, and the elective leader will make available a series of specific model making tools for the students to try and test in the fabrication of their own prototyping and exploration.
learning_outcomes: Gain material knowledge - deciphering appropriate model making materials and sustainable practice.
Develop peer learning skills - through collaboration and knowledge sharing.
Develop architectural model making techniques - refining modes of architectural representation through analogue model making technique.
Translate drawings to models - reading and interpreting conventions of architectural documentation and the translation of 2D representation to 3D representation.

title: Technological and Applied Studies Teaching Methods: Engineering Studies
syllabus_overview:
In this subject, teacher-education students apply engineering studies content knowledge to create a metal artefact, mirroring the process they will guide their future senior secondary students through. You will learn to sequence lessons, program curricula, and select effective teaching strategies and resources. The subject covers the creation of key programming documents, including scope and sequence structures, and mapping learning outcomes to projects and experiences. Lesson planning within a unit of work is addressed, considering time management, contingencies, and resources. Work Health and Safety management and risk assessment are also key components. You will learn to translate syllabus content into practical, engaging learning programs. Through lectures, syllabus analysis, and practical tasks, complemented by presentations, group discussions, and online interactions, you receive constructive feedback. Workshop sessions enhance your practical skills and resource development. Assessments include producing both documentation and a physical artefact, contributing to your portfolio of teaching resources.

Teaching Strategies:
The curated asynchronous online content and tutorials in specialist labs employed in this subject enable teacher-education students to create documentation that interprets Engineering Studies syllabus content into actionable and relevant programs for learning. Students analyse the Engineering Studies syllabus and relate it to theory and practical tasks for the classroom. Students collaborate on generating appropriate project ideas which are organised into logical sequences. Presentations and group discussion supported by online interaction enable validated feedback. Students critically reflect upon their generated ideas with respect to emerging methods for teaching Engineering Studies. syllabus_overview:
This subject provides foundational knowledge in managing technology and innovation within organisations, covering the full development cycle from ideation to implementation. You'll learn to analyse and design innovation processes, using a range of tools to tackle the complexities of innovation. The subject is structured into six self-paced online modules over six weeks, with interactive activities, videos, and discussions in CANVAS. Three live sessions offer collaborative learning and personalised feedback. Assessments are cumulative, enabling you to refine your work based on earlier evaluations.

Teaching Strategies:
Our teaching and learning strategy integrates flipped learning, organising active learning experiences, fostering an interactive and collaborative environment, and providing feedback with time for personal reflection. Through exploring real-world scenarios each class, students apply concepts to practical decision-making challenges. Prior to workshops, individual preparation ensures active engagement during discussions. The interactive workshop structure, involving smaller group discussions, encourages collaborative analysis of case studies, linking theoretical concepts in judgment and decision-making to practical scenarios. Hands-on activities, such as decision modeling, enhance engagement and immerse students in decision-making contexts. Utilising tech tools facilitates dynamic discussions and resource sharing. Continuous learning checks, including post-class discussions that provide feedback and time for personal reflection, ensure alignment with learning objectives and achieving the learning outcomes.

title: Technology Law, Policy and Ethics (Capstone 1)
syllabus_overview:
This subject explores the policy and ethical issues that technology presents for legal practitioners. You’ll examine the role of lawyers in regulation of technology, shaping policy and supporting vulnerable populations using technology. You will also explore ethical and policy issues arising from innovative technology that poses new threats at the same time as providing new opportunities to find solutions to some of the world's wicked problems. This subject is taught by academics and guest lecturers who specialise in legal technology. You’ll engage in weekly discussions on various aspects of legal issues arising from disruptive technologies and present lightning talks that engage with these issues. Classes examine the key role that lawyers can play in ethical policy-making and draw on professional conduct obligations, international human rights law and humanitarian law. You will also become familiar with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and consider which of them may be supported by the use of technology.

Teaching Strategies:
Strategy 1: Students’ Preparation for Learning Students engage in independent study to develop, deepen and consolidate knowledge and understanding of relevant issues. Students read policy documents, legislation and articles and listen to TedTalks and similar online resources before attending seminars (see Strategy 2 below) to prepare for tutorial activities including collaborative discussion. It is a goal for students in this subject to familiarize themselves with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and consider which of them may be more readily achieved with the use of technology; and the key role lawyers can play in ethical policy-making. Strategy 2: This subject is taught by academics and guest lecturers who specialise in legal technology. Students build on their preparation and engagement through participation in interactive seminars. Each week, students engage in discussion and oral presentations (including lightning talks) on various aspects of legal issues arising from disruptive technologies. Students receive immediate feedback from their tutor and peers (see Strategy 4 below). Students have the opportunity to ask questions of their peers and of the teacher to assist them in consolidating their own learning. By testing their knowledge and learning from others the class discussions allow students to gauge how successful they have been in their critical reading, Students identify their Lightning Talk topic at least two weeks prior to the online presentation. Students are given guidance as to the best resources for their research and have access to an exemplar provided via Canvas. These presentation and distillation skills are important because lawyers need to be able to explain or summarise complicated concepts into brief descriptions in plain English so that they may readily be understood by their client or the Court. Collaborative in-class activities will include hypothetical problems based on real cases and engaging with policy questions about the role of the law in technology. Strategy 3: Online learning Students access material for self-directed learning and engage in student-led discussion on key topics on Canvas. Throughout the session, students share their questions and ideas on this open discussion forum, with prompt guidance and contributions from the Subject Coordinator. Strategy 4: Ongoing Feedback Detailed guidance as to the assessment criteria and the provision of timely feedback form an important part of the learning process. The marking criteria for assessment tasks 1, 2 and 3 are provided prior to the commencement of formal classes. Students provide each other with peer feedback during in-class activities and are instructed to use comparative feedback strategies to strengthen their understanding of the subject. Subject Delivery: Three hour seminars once a week, over 12 weeks.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate new risk, obligations and ethical issues for the courts and practitioners arising from the use of technology in the delivery of justice and legal services and collaborate in groups and online to generate ideas and possible solutions to the challenges arising from new technologies.
Identify policy and ethical considerations arising from recent technological advances and the policy response of governments and international organisations to these developments.

Explore and reflect on the way that disruptive technologies challenge regulators across global jurisdictions, in particular the UN Declaration of Human Rights and the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals.
Investigate how existing statutory instruments can regulate policy issues raised by disruptive technologies.
Prepare and present lightning talks to the rest of the seminar.

Gaining the necessary skills via a review of methodological strengths and limitations, understanding when and how techniques should be applied and how they should be presented are key for your degree. This subject aims to equip you with these skills will foster your professional skills by tailoring each to your research interests. To create a customised learning experience you will work in collaboration with a supportive team comprising of your subject coordinator and your supervisor. Together this supportive team, where you are at the centre, will engage in a self-directed journey to help you investigate how to close research gaps by using critical thinking, problem solving, effective communication abilities and most importantly research methods. This will be all in preparation for demonstrating research ability at this level

The session will also include exploration of learning opportunities and how they are suited to particular types of research aims. The remainder of the subject is an independent learning journey conducted in conjunction with your supervisor. You will define your goals, needs and strategies for meeting these. In some instances, your needs will be to enhance your existing research skills and in others, you will develop new skills. Together with your supervisor, you will identify what is appropriate to enhance your ability as you attend workshops and online courses. The increasing development of your skills will assist you in writing and refining your research as well as build on your ability to become a proficient researcher.

title: Territorial Mappings
syllabus_overview:
This elective examines the dramatic reduction of New South Wales' waterways due to climate change, focusing on swamps as misunderstood sites of ecological and cultural significance. You will contribute to creating an 'Atlas of the Lost Swamps of Sydney', uncovering the history of these ecosystems through research, site visits, and mapping areas transformed by human activity. The course equips you with skills in critical cartography and in-depth archival research, highlighting the importance of swamps as carbon sinks and resilient habitats.

title: Textiles: Digital and Screen Print Design
syllabus_overview:
This subject delves into both traditional hand silk screen and modern digital print design for fashion and textiles. You'll learn about screen preparation, pattern repeats, textile print layouts, stencils, overprinting, various inks, photographic transfer, halftone, colour variations, sublimation, and digital printing techniques. Here, print design transcends mere decoration, serving as a medium to express contemporary stories that resonate with current social and cultural climates. Through lectures, you'll discover innovative designers who blend analogue and digital realms, creating new aesthetic possibilities. Emphasis is placed on cultivating a sustainable, conscious, and professional approach to textile practice.

Teaching Strategies:
Subject is delivered in weekly sessions of a one hour lecture (series of six in total) and two and a half hours of tutorial. Face-to-face studio classes incorporate a range of teaching and learning strategies including technical demonstrations in digital design studios and silk screen print workshops, open group discussions and crits, studio based learning activities and student presentations. These are complemented by independent student research and individual design projects.

In this twelve-week on-campus elective, you'll delve into the world of natural dyes, mordants, and resist patterning. Engage in workshops that encourage innovative colouring and patterning of cloth. You'll learn resist patterning methods and unique printing techniques, including binding, stitching, and clamp resist. The course also covers the interaction of natural fibres with various natural dyes and mordants. You'll develop sophisticated textile concepts and a refined colour sense, all while maintaining a focus on professional and sustainable print room practices.

title: Texts in Society
syllabus_overview:
This subject focuses on how language is used to shape meaning, identities, relationships, and the world around us. ‘Discourse’ refers to language in use and language that is beyond the level of sentences and grammar. ‘Genres’ are relatively stable and recognisable ways of organising texts and doing things with language. In this subject, you will look at different ways of doing discourse analysis (such as critical discourse analysis, conversation analysis, and multimodal discourse analysis) and at different ways in which discourse and genre may be socially organised in institutional terms (e.g. education, health, law, religion) and in social terms (e.g. class, gender, race, ethnicity, disability). You will focus on the analysis of real texts (written, spoken, visual, media) and what this tells us about broader social relations and ideology in society. You will be encouraged to develop analysis of discourses and genres in your own workplace or other domains of social life and to apply these skills to pedagogical contexts.

Teaching Strategies:
In this subject, you will engage in a combination of asynchronous and synchronous learning activities. You will work through lectures, readings and online materials independently before participating in weekly tutorials. Tutorials will focus on applying concepts and methods of discourse and genre analysis to a range of texts and contexts. Throughout the subject, you will engage with naturally occurring texts from real-world contexts, applying analytic approaches to understand how discourse operates in society.
learning_outcomes: Explain relationships between language, power and ideology across diverse social and cultural contexts
Produce written academic texts which are accurate, cohesive and coherent, and which demonstrate correct citation and referencing
Analyse and interpret genres in social and institutional contexts
Analyse and interpret spoken, written and multimodal texts using relevant discourse analytic approaches
Explain how texts in society reflect and shape social and cultural contexts

title: The Agency
syllabus_overview:
In this subject, you'll work in teams acting as agencies to address real client briefs from various sectors. You'll select a client, collaborate to creatively solve their problems, and develop an integrated communication strategy. Your team will craft a presentation deck and pitch your strategy to industry panels, learning effective pitching techniques such as storytelling, research insights, and campaign mock-ups. This practical experience prepares you with professional skills and knowledge aligned with industry standards.

Teaching Strategies:
Students collaborate in group activities in writing a reverse brief, brainstorming possible strategic options, and preparing the pitch. Class activities incorporate small group discussions, presentations, videos, and case studies that are designed to stimulate problem solving and creativity in the student learning experience. They receive constructive feedback on their pitch from their client. Presenting strong pitch cases to industry panels helps students gain confidence and build networks with those professionals. This industry-student collaboration not only gives students an opportunity to test out the skills learnt in their degree and develop industry experience, but also assists them with their move into their professional field. Lectures by industry experts are followed by tutorials and/or client meetings for the first six weeks. From weeks 6 to 8, the subject coordinator provides optional drop-in sessions to discuss project progress and directions. Formative feedback on team progress towards assignment one is given during tutorials to each team on a weekly basis from week 3. Students are expected to undertake preparatory reading and research for discussion in tutorials every week. Students may be offered to attend immersion activities in their client’s workplace or external to UTS to assist them understand the client’s business and communication issue.

Collaborate supportively and professionally as a team
Evaluate and reflect upon their own performance and that of their peers
Analyse a situation and develop a communication strategy
Integrate campaign elements with the team in response to a client brief

title: The Bio Kitchen
syllabus_overview:
In order to combat climate change there is an urgent need to transition from unsustainable manufacturing and consumption practises, and to develop sustainable materials and systems that promote ecological resilience, repair, and that support the health of our planet. For designers, the transformative possibilities of bio-based materials can offer alternative approaches for thinking through the future of fashion, consumer products, systems of manufacturing, as well as architecture and the built environment. The Bio Kitchen provides students with an understanding of bio-based material futures. This is a hands-on laboratory where students learn design principles and practices for undertaking materials research, using these to speculate on the possible social and scientific applications for bio-based materials and biotechnologies in the future. In this design lab the kitchen operates as both a vibrant system and as a practical studio space for futures-oriented material thinking. Students will undertake experiments with starches, bioplastics, agar, gels, protein and cellulose manipulations, with the opportunity to view and interact with material recipe demonstrations, before recreating, improvising and expanding on these experimental recipes themselves.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is taught fully online and will use Canvas for communications outside of class times. Please make sure to check the Canvas site regularly, and check your UTS email regularly. Canvas will host subject information including weekly tasks and schedule, learning resources, reccomended readings, and assessment task briefs. A Zoom link for the weekly studios will be provided ahead of Week 1.
learning_outcomes: Plan and conduct observational, engaged, and iterative bio-based materials testing.
Communicate design ideas and systems thinking through visual and verbal methods.
Articulate the nature of a situated context through sensitive experimental design research.
Demonstrate foundational knowledge of bio-based materials and their potential future applications.

title: The Asia Pacific in the 21st Century
syllabus_overview:
In this subject, you will study contemporary challenges and politics of the Asia-Pacific, a region with diverse and interconnected political, economic, social, and environmental landscapes. The subject helps you to analyse the region's key trends, challenges, and opportunities within the Asia-Pacific, as well as external dynamics that affect the region. The subject invites you to assess conflicts and regional cooperation among key actors from East Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific. Additionally, this subject enables you to explore nuclear politics, peacebuilding, and climate justice in the region from Pacific, Indigenous, and feminist perspectives. The subject offers case studies and theories for a critical engagement with the Asia-Pacific region and its place in the 21st century as a vibrant, contested, and dynamic region in global politics.

Teaching Strategies:
You will be guided through a series of six online modules. You will be supported to develop skills in communicating complex analyses to an informed but non-expert audience as a core workplace skill, as well as to an academic audience through assessments that encourage engagement with theories and scholarly literature. You will participate in collaborative activities to share insights and observations with peers from various professional contexts. You will engage interactively through online discussion boards and embedded comments. The subject will be scaffolded towards engaging in a simulation exercise that will apply your learning of the geopolitics of the Asia-Pacific region. To ensure practice-relevant outcomes, this subject uses authentic activities and assessments. For example, Assessment 1 provides the foundations for you to research the role you will play in a simulation activity, which forms the ungraded first part of Assessment 2. Throughout the modules, you will be supported to identify and analyse key actors and dynamics in the Asia-Pacific, focusing on contemporary and emerging challenges for the 21st century. Synchronous online seminars provide an opportunity to revise key concepts, further develop connections with other students, and to prepare for assessments. You will receive formative feedback on assessment tasks both from your lecturers and peers, throughout your learning in the subject.
learning_outcomes: Identify domestic, regional, and international policies of actors in the Asia-Pacific.
Analyse how historical and contemporary challenges shape current political, social, and economic landscapes in the Asia-Pacific.
Evaluate regional stability and security in the Asia-Pacific using concepts and theories introduced in the subject.
Communicate complex ideas and arguments related to geopolitical analysis of the Asia-Pacific region consistent with professional and academic standards.

title: The Biosphere
syllabus_overview:
The Biosphere, encompassing all life on Earth, is unique to our planet. This subject introduces you to environmental sciences, tracing the evolution of Earth's structure and species, and examining current environmental changes. You'll explore interactions among living organisms, non-living elements, and external factors such as the atmosphere and solar energy. The subject also focuses on human impacts on the biosphere, addressing critical issues such as climate change, sustainability, and resource depletion.

Teaching Strategies:
You will learn in this subject via online lectures, on-campus discussion workshops, self-paced online learning modules, and the field trip. The learning activities are complementary and designed to support you in developing your conceptual understanding, skills and application of knowledge. Lectures – The backbone of your learning will be the weekly two‑hour online lectures, which draw on current research to present the latest scientific understanding of the biosphere—its structure, the processes that shape it, the diversity of ecosystems, and the impacts of climate change and human activities on life on Earth. These lectures are closely integrated with the Online Learning Modules and Discussion Workshops. Attending the lectures is essential for developing a strong grasp of the subject matter and building the foundational knowledge required for your course. Online Learning Modules – The self‑paced Online Learning Modules (OLM) are designed to introduce you to the environmental issues that will be explored in the upcoming Discussion Workshops. The OLMs are available on Canvas and should be completed in your own time during the week they are released. Each module takes approximately one hour to complete, and automated feedback is provided when you finish. The OLMs alternate with the Discussion Workshops throughout the session. Refer to the subject schedule on Canvas for the list of topics and their corresponding weeks. Collaborative Discussion Workshops - In addition to strengthening your understanding of key concepts, the Collaborative Discussion Workshops help you develop essential critical‑thinking and communication skills that are valuable in all career paths. These workshops also play a crucial role in preparing you for the hands‑on research activities conducted during the Field Trip. For these reasons, you are strongly encouraged to attend all Collaborative Discussion Workshops. Refer to the subject schedule for specific weeks and topics for each two-hour workshop. Field Trip - The Field Trip is a core component of this subject, and attendance is strongly encouraged. title: The Carbonisation of Society
syllabus_overview:
This subject will build your understanding of human-environment relations and the social, political, and economic origins of environmental crises such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution. You will explore different theorisations and evidence of how humans have impacted the natural environment and the ‘carbonisation’ of our global societies and economies through processes such as colonisation, marginalisation, industrialisation, and globalisation. You will learn about how social, political, and economic relations have combined and interacted over time to create the current social and environmental challenges we face and consider how we can support a future where humans live in harmony with their environment. The subject assessments develop your research and critical analysis skills for building and communicating an argument in written form and through verbal presentation.

Teaching Strategies:
You will engage in weekly 1.5 hour lectures that will guide you through the socio-economic events and paradigms which led to the 'carbonisation' of global society to help you think critically about proposed solutions for environmental challenges and understand the drivers of societal change. Lecture content will be supplemented by asynchronous, student-led exploration of the weekly subject readings and audio-visual content on the concepts and content for that week's topic. Weekly 1.5 hour tutorials will provide you with an opportunity to engage with other students through collaborative activities to further enrich your understanding of the subject content. The subject assignments will help you to engage with subject content, develop your critical reading and writing skills, and support a shared learning environment. You will receive formative feedback on assessment tasks from your instructors to refine your skills and ensure your comprehension of course content.
learning_outcomes: Develop skills in written, oral, and visual presentation.
Develop skills in independent research, drawing from academic and grey literature to demonstrate links between socio-political dynamics and environmental sustainability.
Analyse the relationship between socio-environmental crises and the historical development of global society.
Critically analyse and synthesise academic literature and relate findings to subject themes and key theories of environmental and sustainability studies.
Explain the social, political, and economic causes of climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution by using historical and contemporary case studies.

title: The Challenge Studio

Employing creative and technical problem-solving, you'll extend your skills to generate innovative solutions that surpass individual capabilities. Throughout the process, you'll critically assess your work, incorporate stakeholder feedback, and strive for excellence in production values. You will also reflect on team dynamics, forecast future possibilities, and adopt ethical research practices, particularly when engaging with Indigenous stakeholders.

title: The Child in the Contemporary World
syllabus_overview:
The contemporary world has changed more in the past two decades than it has in the last century. This subject examines the sociocultural and environmental influences on the health and wellbeing of children. Students gain an understanding of the unique challenges experienced by children and young people, exploring the role that the modern world has on the social, developmental, physical, intellectual, emotional, environmental and spiritual dimensions of a child’s health and wellbeing. Students examine different theories relating to children and health whilst taking into consideration the multifactorial elements of typical and atypical development.

Teaching Strategies:
Orientation activities The “Get started” module contains vital information for students about studying online at UTS. In preparation for the session students have access to activities during orientation week. These activities are designed to introduce students to the subject and their peers, and will assist them to prepare for the subject's learning and assessment tasks. Students are expected to work through the introductory module so they have a good understanding of how online study works at UTS and the expectations on them as online learners. Independent learning activities This subject is taught using a variety of teaching and learning strategies. An overarching theme of the approaches to teaching and learning is to support students to actively learn with the support of a facilitator who can assist and coach them. Understanding and critical thinking skills will be encouraged via a range of activities, including but not limited to: On-line resources to prepare students for active engagement with the subject content Thought provoking readings, videos and other activities to stimulate thinking, promote understanding and support analysis and evaluation Problem solving, discovery-based and critical thinking activities via a range of guided and self-directed learning opportunities Learning that is supported by real world examples, case studies, illustrations and data Real-time feedback to student responses to key online activities Opportunities for students to reflect on, explain and record their input under advice and guidance. Readings, videos and activities will be available online relevant to the topic of the week. This will help students to progress through the subject and complete assessment items effectively. The online material aims to enhance student’s understanding of the topic or delve deeper into a more specific area, compare experiences and ideas with others and gain feedback. Information and links to learning activities can be accessed via Canvas. Zoom meetings Students are strongly encouraged to attend all scheduled Zoom meetings as they will provide opportunities for group activities, discussion, self-assessment, peer review and formative feedback from the subject coordinator and the teaching team. Additionally, they will also help students prepare for the subject’s assessment tasks. The schedule for this subject’s zoom meetings is below in the program section. Feedback Feedback in this subject takes several forms including self-assessment, peer review, automatic feedback from interactive activities and the teaching team. Formative feedback throughout the subject aims to increase student’s performance in summative assessments.

title: The Environment, Health and Sustainability
syllabus_overview:
Every year, 12.5 million people die from living or working in an unhealthy environment due to air, water, and soil pollution, chemical exposure, ultraviolet radiation, and natural disasters. This subject engages you in dialogue and debate with peers, researchers, and practitioners across sectors to examine the relationship between health and the environment. You will investigate the evidence and pathways that impact health and wellbeing using an ecological approach. You will explore how human intervention in the environment can exacerbate or reduce health risks. Global challenges, such as climate change, ocean acidification, human population growth, and rising costs of water, energy, sanitation, and waste management, will be examined in relation to health and the Sustainable Development Goals. You will consider how health and other sectors can work together to prevent disease burdens and provide the leadership needed to find sustainable solutions, strengthening human resilience and adaptive capacity. Innovative system changes will be explored, and you will be introduced to the concept of planetary health.

Teaching Strategies:
The subject is designed to be student-centred and highly interactive. It will be taught online and face-to-face, and will include a series of workshops in which students will have the experience of being an expert in your field. Students will be asked to complete activities in preparation for the workshops such as short readings, watching online videos, or participate in online activities. These online activities will prepare you for active participation in each of the workshops. The workshops will be a combination of lectures, expert interviews, a field trip to an urban development site (Week 6), and student-centred activities that will include collaboration with peers, critical analysis, discussion, scenario development, and exploration of real-world case studies. Case studies will be explored in dialogue with peers and teachers. Active participation will be essential in achieving the learning outcomes for each topic area and assessments. During the session students will develop an awareness that this is a rapidly evolving area of knowledge. Canvas will provide a venue to collaborate, discuss subject content, and concepts and assignments at any time. Early and continuing feedback will be provided by peers and teachers both in-person, through the Canvas discussion board throughout the course of the subject and on assessment tasks.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate on interdisciplinary approaches to promote ecosystem and health awareness.
Evaluate the roles and responses of various professions in environmental and population health protection.
Critically assess the impact of environmental issues on health equity and sustainability.
Understand the relationship between human health and ecosystems.
Identify and evaluate health-related policies and strategies across various scales.

title: The Economics of Fashion
syllabus_overview:
In this subject you build your understanding of economics through a lens of the fashion industry. You learn about different economic theories, worldviews and value systems, and how these shape business thinking and operations within fashion. Emergent economic models, such as doughnut economics, are presented alongside dominant economic theories. You are introduced to consumer psychology and citizen behaviour and how these intersect with fashion and economics.

Teaching Strategies:
Learning is this subject is facilitated through in-person lectures, readings, resources on Canvas and through teacher-student and peer-to-peer interaction in tutorials.

title: The Ethics of Data and AI
syllabus_overview:
This subject addresses the ethical dilemmas surrounding data-driven AI systems in decision-making across various sectors. You will engage in debates on AI's function and development, informed by humanities and social science perspectives. The course emphasises moral and ethical considerations like transparency, fairness, and algorithmic bias, and applies these to real and hypothetical case studies concerning data ethics, regulation, and accountability.

Teaching Strategies:
This subject is made up of three modules delivered on campus and online over 12 weeks. The modules in this subject are designed to introduce key ethical, and regulatory concepts and practices in the fields of data analytics and artificial intelligence. Real and hypothetical examples scenarios are provided to demonstrate how these concepts are applied and both the positive and negative social impact that can result from the incorporation or the lack of ethical data practices. Within each online module, content will be delivered through a mixture of short video presentations, interactive worksheets, quizzes/ questionnaires and short summary/comprehension/annotation exercises for selected readings and concepts using the online ‘essay’ feature in Canvas. These interactive elements, which incorporate formative feedback, form the basis of weekly tutorial discussions which are moderated by teaching staff over the 12 weeks. Tutorials involve group reflection on case studies to allow students to evaluate the design of data and artificial intelligence systems for their ethical vulnerabilities and the potential impact of these. Students will apply regulatory frameworks to enhance system design to be more socially appropriate.

Apply knowledge of data ethics to understand the impact of Artificial Intelligence on organisations, individuals, society, and our future

title: The Future of the International Order
syllabus_overview:
This subject equips you with an understanding of the factors influencing the international order, vital for forecasting global trends and informing policy decisions. You will dissect the complexities of the international system and the array of actors that shape it, including states, international organisations, and NGOs. In this subject you will learn how to use core theories of International Relations, such as Realism, Liberalism, Constructivism, and Postcolonialism, to deepen your analysis. You will reflect on both the historical evolution of the international order and its possible futures, reflecting on the interplay of power and norms. Through theoretical analysis and case studies you will gain a nuanced understanding of the international order and its significance for global politics.

Teaching Strategies:
You are guided through a series of six online modules framed around active learning. Each module draws on a wide range of contemporary and historical empirical and theoretical content. You are expected to engage interactively through online discussion boards and activities, and you will be scaffolded towards conducting your own analysis on current and historical challenges in the international order. This subject uses an authentic learning approach where you will develop a reflection on your worldviews, an essay and a policy brief to communicate your analysis to diverse audiences. You will have opportunities to practice and refine the application of core theories within International Relations to key contemporary challenges. Synchronous online seminars provide an opportunity to revise key concepts, further develop connections with other students, and to prepare for assessments. You will receive formative feedback on assignment tasks both from lecturers and peers, including early formative feedback, via discussion boards, Canvas activities, and in Live and Online zoom sessions.
learning_outcomes: Create self-reflexive, analytical, and persuasive arguments about worldviews and the international order.
Analyse contemporary and historical case studies using International Relations theories.
Communicate effectively about complexities within the international order with consideration of political sensitivities.

title: The Future of Work
syllabus_overview:
This subject provides an internship-like experience for students. Students explore contemporary debates concerning the future of work and employment. Critical insights are developed into changes now taking place in the labour market and students have opportunities to reflect on their own working futures in light of these changes. The subject covers new forms of work, including debates around digital labour, creative labour and affective labour; entrepreneurship and the demand to create your own work; free labour and the changing relations between work and remuneration; flexible work and the erosion of boundaries between work and leisure. Opportunities are provided for students to apply knowledge and insights gained through observational workplace experiences, as well assessing their own transferable workplace skills via skills audits.

Teaching Strategies:
In this subject, students learn about different debates concerning the future of work and employment in instructor-led interactive lectures, small group discussions of readings, case studies, and student group work. Students are expected to undertake independent reading prior to each class and to participate in collaborative online peer discussions between classes to develop a detailed understanding current debates concerning work and employment, They develop the capacity to analyse specific industries using both scholarly and popular resources that support their engagement with key topics. Feedback on their use of ideas and concepts explored in the subject to analyse different workplaces will be provided to students in class ahead of the first formal assessment task.The subject involves workplace analysis and industry engagement. Students are expected to work collaboratively in class and online to develop materials for the student led activities that form the basis of the industry engagement. Detailed guidance on the nature of transferable professional skills will be given and exercises will be conducted in class to prepare students to undertake a skills audit.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on the relationship between their university studies and their career aspirations
Debates the future of work and employment
Analyse how work is changing in specific industries using ideas and concepts explored in the subject
Reflect critically on their transferable professional skills

title: The Global Professional: Industry Engagement Project
syllabus_overview:
This capstone subject offers you the chance to apply and develop your intercultural and global citizenship skills within a professional setting. You will be supported to self-source an internship with an organisation in your field of interest and in a role that strengthens your intercultural competencies. With the global workplace serving as a backdrop for exploring cultural complexities, you will undertake a major project to observe and critically evaluate organisational and industry cultural practices, systems, and policies related to diversity, equity and inclusion, including attention to protocols working with and for Indigenous Australians. Through this workplace learning, you will develop your capacity to enact positive social change in your future places of work and industries of practice. On-campus workshops and online learning will support your preparation and progression through the internship.

Teaching Strategies:
The main learning activities in this subject are the experience of work and independent critical inquiry on the complex cultural and intercultural practices, systems, policies of professional settings and industries. In order to maximise flexibility and to enable students to undertake their work placements when and where best suited to their interests, internships will be self-sourced. There will be preparatory workshops focused on an introductory briefing on internship requirements and internship search strategies prior to the session commencing and continued once session starts with workshops on goal setting for professional development and applying research methods for workplace observations. Once on their internships, students will complete asynchronous self-paced online modules that engage with relevant cultural, intercultural and sociological studies which will provide theoretical scaffolding around their workplace/industry observations. Students will also engage in online group discussions. De-briefs with the subject coordinator will occur towards the end of the internship where students will critically reflect on their professional development. Students will be provided academic support including advice during the placement, provision of academic resources on reflective learning, research skills, international studies and work in progress online discussions.
learning_outcomes: Analyse diverse perspectives, frameworks and scales of sustainability and their possible impacts on marginalised social groups.
Apply skills in planning and writing assignments, individually and in groups.
Develop self-awareness and critically reflect on personal and professional sustainability pathways.
Identify and explain key sustainability concepts and practices.
Recognise specific issues of sustainability relating to Indigenous peoples.

title: The Innovation Lab
syllabus_overview:
In this subject learners develop experimental projects to explore strategies to bridge the gap between their organisation’s current paradigm and the identified desired future state. This includes setting a strategic challenge, engaging in considered process of innovation, as well as proposing the network/environment within and around the organization that serves as a context for the experimental projects. Projects bring together CISI learning with a focus on conditions that foster shared personal and collective vitality that simultaneously catalyze innovation ecosystems responsive to change and complexity.

Teaching Strategies:
This bespoke Lab offers an opportunity for participants to apply their learning within the program to develop a strategic and bold future-oriented direction for organisational transformation, tailored to the context of participants’ practice. In this subject, participants undertake experimental project which can be critical, formative, and/or strategic. Throughout the Innovation Lab learners evolve their innovation ecology by working with peers, academics, industry mentors and colleagues to generate feedback as part on ongoing innovation loops and will be supported through a library of self-directed modules to support your research, online mentoring and face to face workshops. Through establishing the context for innovation work – the necessary conditions, structures, and networks – participants catalyse discussion about innovation practices in their organisations.
